reigns.tagline: The vassal king who built the world's first superpower
reigns.previously: The Medes rule Iran from Ecbatana. Persis is a small vassal kingdom.
paragraphs: Around 550 BC the Medes ruled Iran from their capital, Ecbatana. Their king Astyages had a vassal in the south-west: Cyrus, king of Anshan in Persis. Herodotus says Cyrus was also his grandson. Cyrus rebelled, and when the Median army marched against him its general Harpagus switched sides. Ecbatana fell, and a minor Persian king suddenly owned an empire.

He kept going. He beat Croesus of Lydia, the richest king anyone knew of, and took his capital Sardis around 547 BC. In 539 BC Babylon opened its gates without a fight. Cyrus had a clay cylinder inscribed, boasting that he'd restored temples and let uprooted peoples go home. The exiled Jews went back to rebuild their Temple, and the Book of Isaiah calls him the Lord's anointed.

He built a garden capital at Pasargadae. Around 530 BC he marched against the Massagetae, horse nomads beyond the Caspian, and was killed. His plain stone tomb still stands at Pasargadae. His son Cambyses inherited an empire running from the Aegean to Central Asia.

claims.text: Astyages dreamed his baby grandson would replace him and ordered him killed. A herdsman raised Cyrus instead, and Harpagus, who had failed to kill the baby, was tricked into eating his own son.
claims.note: Herodotus tells it and admits he heard other versions. Abandoned babies who grow up to be kings are a classic folk-tale pattern.

claims.text: Queen Tomyris of the Massagetae dipped his severed head in a skin full of blood, so he could drink his fill.
claims.note: Herodotus calls it the most believable of the stories he heard. Xenophon has Cyrus die peacefully in bed, and Ctesias gives yet another death.

claims.text: The Cyrus Cylinder is the world's first charter of human rights.
claims.note: The cylinder is real and in the British Museum. Most historians read it as standard Babylonian royal propaganda; the human-rights label is a modern one.

reigns.hook: Cyrus's body comes home to Pasargadae. His eldest son Cambyses takes the throne, and he has his eye on the one great kingdom his father never touched: Egypt.

reigns.tagline: He conquered Egypt, and the Greeks called him mad
reigns.previously: Cyrus the Great is killed on the steppe, around 530 BC.
paragraphs: Cambyses took over the biggest empire on earth and set out to make it bigger. In 525 BC he beat the Egyptian army at Pelusium, on the edge of the Nile Delta, and took Memphis. The young pharaoh Psamtik III was captured. Cambyses was crowned pharaoh, took Egyptian titles, and Egypt's own records treat him as a proper king.

Greek writers remembered him very differently. Herodotus, writing a lifetime later and listening to Egyptian priests, paints a drunken madman who mocked the gods. He also tells of campaigns south into Nubia and west into the desert that went badly wrong.

Back home there was trouble. Before leaving for Egypt, Darius later claimed, Cambyses had secretly had his brother Bardiya killed. In 522 BC a man calling himself Bardiya seized the throne anyway. Cambyses turned for home to deal with him, but died on the way, in Syria, from a wound in his thigh.

claims.text: Cambyses stabbed the sacred Apis bull of Memphis in the thigh, and it died.
claims.note: Herodotus says so. But Egyptian inscriptions record an Apis bull buried with full honours in Cambyses's reign, which makes the story look like priestly spite.

claims.text: An army of 50,000 sent to the oasis of Siwa was swallowed by a sandstorm and never seen again.
claims.note: Only Herodotus tells it. Explorers have claimed to find traces in the desert, but nothing has been proved.

claims.text: His fatal wound came from his own sword, which slipped from its sheath as he leapt onto his horse.
claims.note: Herodotus again, who adds that it struck the same spot where he'd stabbed the Apis. Darius's Behistun inscription just says he died his own death.

reigns.hook: Cambyses is dead and has no son. On the throne sits a man who says he's Bardiya. Seven Persian nobles are sure he's a fake, and one of them is called Darius.

reigns.tagline: The brother, or the impostor
reigns.reignEnded: Killed by Darius and six nobles
reigns.previously: Cambyses is far away in Egypt when a rival claims his throne.
paragraphs: In 522 BC a man claiming to be Bardiya, younger son of Cyrus the Great, took the Persian throne while Cambyses II was in Egypt. Cambyses died on the way home, and the new king won support by cancelling taxes for three years.

Darius, writing his own version on the Behistun rock, said the real Bardiya had been secretly murdered and this was an impostor, the magus Gaumata. Darius and six nobles killed him in September 522. Many historians suspect Darius invented the impostor story.
reigns.hook: Darius takes the throne and spends a year crushing revolts.

reigns.tagline: Seven conspirators, one horse, and a king of kings
reigns.cameToPower: Killed the king with six nobles
reigns.previously: Cambyses dies on the road home. A man called Bardiya holds the throne.
paragraphs: Darius told the story his way, carved on a cliff. The man on the throne wasn't Bardiya at all, he said, but a Magian priest named Gaumata in disguise. On 29 September 522 BC Darius and six fellow nobles cornered him in a fortress in Media and killed him. Then the empire exploded. Rebels rose in Babylon, Media, Persis and beyond, and Darius spent a year crushing them.

He had his version cut high on the rock at Behistun in three languages, Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian, above a relief of captive rebel kings roped together. He was a superb organiser: provinces called satrapies paying fixed tribute, a gold coin called the daric, and the Royal Road, with relay stations from Sardis to Susa.

He began the palace city of Persepolis. Around 513 BC he crossed into Europe against the Scythians, and in 499–494 BC he crushed a revolt of the Ionian Greeks. Athens had helped the rebels, and when the Athenians beat his punitive force at Marathon in 490 BC, he planned a bigger war. He died in late 486 BC, with Egypt in revolt, and was laid in a cliff tomb at Naqsh-e Rostam.

claims.text: The dead 'Bardiya' really was an impostor called Gaumata.
claims.note: That's Darius's own account at Behistun, echoed by Herodotus. Many historians suspect the real Bardiya was killed and the impostor story covered a coup.

claims.text: The seven agreed that whoever's horse neighed first at sunrise would be king, and Darius's groom rigged the contest.
claims.note: Herodotus tells it, with two versions of the groom's trick involving a mare. A good story written down long afterwards.

claims.text: The Behistun inscription was the key to reading cuneiform.
claims.note: Copied by Henry Rawlinson in the 1830s and 1840s, its Old Persian text let scholars crack Babylonian, much as the Rosetta Stone did for hieroglyphs.

reigns.hook: Darius leaves an unfinished war with Greece and a revolt in Egypt. His chosen heir is a younger son, Xerxes, whose mother Atossa is a daughter of Cyrus the Great.

reigns.tagline: He whipped the sea, burned Athens, and still lost
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Darius I and Atossa
reigns.cameToPower: Chosen heir over an older half-brother
reigns.previously: Darius the Great dies in 486 BC, with Egypt in revolt.
paragraphs: Xerxes began by stamping out revolts in Egypt and Babylon. Then he turned to Greece. In 480 BC he crossed the Hellespont into Europe on bridges of boats lashed together, leading one of the largest armies the ancient world had seen. At Thermopylae a small Greek force under the Spartan king Leonidas held him up for days before being wiped out. Athens was emptied and burned.

Then it went wrong. In September 480 BC the Greek fleet lured his ships into the narrow strait of Salamis and smashed them, while Xerxes watched from a throne on the shore. He went home, leaving his general Mardonius behind. In 479 BC the Greeks beat Mardonius at Plataea, and the invasion was over. For the Greeks it became the founding story of their freedom.

At home he finished much of Persepolis, including the Gate of All Nations with its giant winged bulls. In 465 BC he was murdered in his palace in a plot led by Artabanus, a powerful official at court. In the bloody scramble that followed, a younger son, Artaxerxes, came out on top.

claims.text: When a storm wrecked his first bridge, Xerxes had the Hellespont given 300 lashes and the bridge builders beheaded.
claims.note: Herodotus tells it. Some historians think a Persian ritual was misunderstood or exaggerated by hostile Greeks.

claims.text: His army had 1.7 million infantry.
claims.note: That's Herodotus's figure. Modern estimates are far smaller, usually somewhere between about 100,000 and 300,000; feeding millions would have been impossible.

claims.text: He is King Ahasuerus of the Bible's Book of Esther.
claims.note: Ahasuerus is the Hebrew form of the name Xerxes, so most scholars make the link, but no Persian record backs up the Esther story.

reigns.hook: Xerxes is dead, and his eldest son Darius is soon killed too, blamed for the murder. The winner is a younger son, Artaxerxes, and he'll hold the throne for forty years.

reigns.tagline: Long hands, deep pockets and forty years on the throne
reigns.previously: Xerxes is murdered in his palace in 465 BC.
paragraphs: Xerxes was dead, killed in a palace plot, and the court was a crime scene. The eldest son, Darius, was blamed and put to death. Then the young Artaxerxes turned on Artabanus, the official behind the plot, and killed him too. Greek writers tell it in different ways, but the result is clear: the third son had the throne.

Egypt rebelled almost at once under a Libyan prince, Inaros, and Athens sent a fleet to help. Persia took years to answer, but its general Megabyzus crushed the revolt and trapped the Athenians on an island in the Nile. Persia had learned that gold could beat Greeks more cheaply than armies. Themistocles, the Athenian hero of Salamis, now an exile, came to the king's court and lived off three Persian cities.

The Bible remembers Artaxerxes kindly. Nehemiah, his cupbearer at Susa, got leave to go home and rebuild the walls of Jerusalem. After about forty years the king died late in 424 BC. He had one son by his queen, Damaspia, and a crowd of sons by other women.

claims.text: Artaxerxes got his nickname, 'long-handed', because his right hand was longer than his left.
claims.note: Plutarch says so. Some historians think 'long reach' was a compliment to his power, later taken literally.

claims.text: Athens and Persia signed a formal peace, the Peace of Callias, around 449 BC.
claims.note: Fourth-century Greek orators cite it, but Thucydides never mentions it, and the historian Theopompus called the text a forgery.

claims.text: Artaxerxes and Queen Damaspia died on the same day.
claims.note: Only Ctesias, a Greek doctor at the Persian court a generation later, tells it. He loved a dramatic coincidence.

reigns.hook: The queen's son, Xerxes II, gets the crown. His half-brothers by concubines are watching, and one of them has already worked out how long a king can last.

reigns.tagline: Forty-five days, one feast too many
reigns.previously: Artaxerxes I dies late in 424 BC, after some forty years as king.
paragraphs: Xerxes II had the best claim of all Artaxerxes's sons. He was the only one born to the queen, Damaspia. Nobody seems to have told his half-brothers. What little we know about him comes from Ctesias, a Greek doctor who worked at the Persian court a generation later and collected palace gossip.

According to Ctesias, the new king had his parents' bodies sent to Persia for burial and then, at a festival, drank himself to sleep. That night men loyal to his half-brother Sogdianus, among them a eunuch named Pharnacyas, crept in and killed him. He had been king for about 45 days. In Babylonia, where scribes dated every contract by the king's year, he barely left a mark.

claims.text: Xerxes II reigned only 45 days.
claims.note: The figure is Ctesias's. Diodorus gives him a year, and no Babylonian document dated to his reign is known.

claims.text: He was killed in his bed while drunk after a festival.
claims.note: Only Ctesias tells it, and his history survives only in a later summary by Photius.

reigns.hook: The killer, Sogdianus, is a son of a Babylonian concubine. He has the palace. But another half-brother, Ochus, governs a province, and he has an army.

reigns.tagline: He took the throne by murder and lost it in the ashes
reigns.previously: Xerxes II is murdered after just 45 days on the throne.
paragraphs: Sogdianus was the son of Artaxerxes I and a Babylonian woman named Alogyne. He had his half-brother killed and sat on the throne for about six months. Almost everything we know comes from Ctesias, the Greek court doctor, and his story is that Sogdianus made enemies fast. He put to death a respected eunuch of the old king and lost the army's trust.

His half-brother Ochus, governor of Hyrcania by the Caspian, saw his chance. The cavalry commander and the governor of Egypt joined Ochus, and the troops followed. Sogdianus was talked into surrendering on a sworn promise of safety. Ochus broke it. The fallen king was thrown into a room full of hot ash, a Persian punishment that killed without spilling royal blood.

claims.text: Sogdianus was executed by being smothered in ash.
claims.note: Ctesias tells it. The Roman writer Valerius Maximus describes the same punishment, but no Persian source mentions his death.

claims.text: He reigned six months and fifteen days.
claims.note: Ctesias's figure; Diodorus says seven months. Babylonian documents seem to skip him and go straight to Darius II.

reigns.hook: Ochus takes the throne name Darius. He owes his crown to his half-sister and wife, Parysatis, and she means to collect.

reigns.tagline: The bastard king whose queen held the purse strings
reigns.previously: Ochus overthrows Sogdianus and has him smothered in ash.
paragraphs: The Greeks called him Nothus, the bastard, because his mother was a concubine. He was married to his half-sister Parysatis, and she was the real force at court. When his full brother Arsites rebelled and gave himself up on a promise of mercy, she talked Darius into killing him. When Terituchmes, a noble married to the king's daughter, plotted to murder her, Parysatis wiped out his family. She spared only his sister Stateira, wife of her own eldest son.

Darius's big chance came from Athens's mistakes. After the Athenians lost a whole army in Sicily in 413 BC, his governors in Asia Minor began paying for Sparta's fleet. In 407 BC he sent his younger son Cyrus, still a teenager, to Sardis to run the war. Cyrus became close friends with the Spartan admiral Lysander, and Persian silver kept Sparta's oarsmen paid.
In 404 BC Athens surrendered. The same year Darius lay dying in Babylon. Parysatis wanted the throne for Cyrus, but the crown went to the eldest son, Arses.

claims.text: Persian money paid for the Spartan fleet that beat Athens.
claims.note: Thucydides and Xenophon describe the treaties and payments from Tissaphernes, Pharnabazus and later Cyrus.

claims.text: Parysatis argued Cyrus should be king because he was born after his father took the throne.
claims.note: Plutarch reports it. Herodotus tells the same argument about Xerxes, so it may be a borrowed story.

reigns.hook: Arses is crowned at Pasargadae as Artaxerxes II. Cyrus is at the ceremony too, and a priest whispers that he plans to kill his brother in the temple.

reigns.tagline: He survived his brother and ruled for over forty years
reigns.previously: Darius II dies in Babylon in 404 BC, as Athens surrenders.
paragraphs: Arses took the name Artaxerxes at his coronation, and the trouble started right there. His brother Cyrus was accused of planning to kill him in the temple and was saved only by their mother's pleading. Three years later Cyrus came back with an army of Greek mercenaries. At Cunaxa in 401 BC Artaxerxes was wounded, but Cyrus was killed. Parysatis took revenge on the men who boasted of killing her favourite.

Egypt broke away early in the reign and stayed free. The king learned to fight Greeks with money. His gold stirred up Sparta's enemies, and a Persian fleet under the Athenian Conon smashed the Spartan navy at Cnidus in 394 BC. In the King's Peace of 387/386 BC the Greeks accepted that the cities of Asia Minor belonged to him.

His long old age was poisoned by his sons. His heir, Darius, plotted against him and was executed. Another son, Ariaspes, was driven to suicide and a third, Arsames, was murdered. The man behind it all was a fourth son, Ochus. The old king died in 359 or 358 BC.

claims.text: Parysatis poisoned Queen Stateira with a knife greased on one side, carving a bird and eating the clean half herself.
claims.note: Plutarch, drawing on Ctesias, the court doctor. A great story from a writer who loved melodrama.

claims.text: Artaxerxes married two of his own daughters, Atossa and Amestris.
claims.note: Plutarch says so. Greek writers liked tales of Persian incest, and no Persian source confirms it.

claims.text: He lived to 94.
claims.note: Plutarch's figure. It would make him nearly 50 at his accession, and Plutarch's other numbers for the reign don't add up.

reigns.hook: Rewind to 401 BC. Cyrus never forgave the coronation. He is in Sardis with Spartan friends, a full treasury and over 10,000 Greek soldiers for hire.

reigns.tagline: The prince who marched 10,000 Greeks to Babylon
reigns.previously: Artaxerxes II dies very old, but in 401 BC his brother came for him.
paragraphs: Cyrus was his mother's favourite, sent to Sardis as a teenager with money to win the war for Sparta. Back home, Parysatis saved him from a charge of plotting murder at his brother's coronation. He returned west and quietly built an army. He hired Greek veterans, over 10,000 of them, telling them they were off to fight hill tribes. Only deep in Syria did they learn the real target: the Great King.

In 401 BC the armies met at Cunaxa, north of Babylon. The Greeks routed the troops facing them. Cyrus spotted his brother in the centre and charged with his bodyguard. He wounded Artaxerxes, then was struck down himself. His head and right hand were cut off. The Greeks had won their part of the battle and lost the war.

Their generals were lured to a meeting and seized. The young Athenian Xenophon helped lead the survivors north through hostile mountains and Armenian snow to the Black Sea. His book about it, the Anabasis, showed every Greek how far an army could march through the Persian Empire.

claims.text: Charging his brother, Cyrus shouted 'I see the man!'
claims.note: Xenophon reports it, but he was with the Greeks on the other wing and wrote years later.

claims.text: Cyrus was killed by a javelin to the head while wounding his brother.
claims.note: Plutarch's version, drawn from Ctesias, who treated the king's wound. Accounts of who struck the blow differ.

claims.text: When the Ten Thousand finally saw the Black Sea, they shouted 'The sea! The sea!'
claims.note: Xenophon was there and tells it himself, but his is the only account.

reigns.hook: Artaxerxes reigns another four decades. When he finally dies, the son still standing is Ochus, and he is not a man who leaves loose ends.

reigns.tagline: The ruthless old king who won Egypt back
reigns.reignEnded: Poisoned, said to be by Bagoas
reigns.previously: Artaxerxes II dies very old; his son Ochus is the one left standing.
paragraphs: Ochus took the name Artaxerxes and made sure nobody would challenge it. Later writers say he killed most of his relatives. He ordered the governors of Asia Minor to send away their private armies of mercenaries. One who refused, Artabazus, ended up a refugee at the court of Philip II of Macedon.

Egypt had been free for almost sixty years, and his first attack on it failed. Then Phoenicia rebelled. When the king's army reached Sidon around 345 BC, its own ruler betrayed it, and the people set fire to their city rather than surrender. Around 343 BC Artaxerxes marched on Egypt again with Greek mercenaries. The last native pharaoh, Nectanebo II, fled south. Egypt was Persian again, and its temples were looted.
The king leaned more and more on his chief minister, the eunuch Bagoas. In 338 BC, the year Philip of Macedon crushed the Greeks at Chaeronea, Bagoas had the king poisoned by his doctor.

claims.text: Artaxerxes III killed most of his relatives on taking the throne.
claims.note: Later Greek and Roman writers such as Justin say so; the numbers and details can't be checked.

claims.text: 40,000 people died when Sidon burned itself.
claims.note: Diodorus gives the figure three centuries later. A Babylonian tablet does mention prisoners from Sidon.

claims.text: Bagoas had him poisoned by his physician.
claims.note: Diodorus tells it, three centuries later. Some historians read a Babylonian tablet as pointing to a natural death.

reigns.hook: Bagoas picks the youngest son, Arses, and kills most of the others. A boy on a string, he thinks. Across the sea, Philip of Macedon is planning an invasion.

reigns.tagline: The puppet who tried to cut his strings
reigns.previously: Bagoas poisons Artaxerxes III in 338 BC.
paragraphs: Arses was the youngest son of Artaxerxes III, and he owed everything to his father's killer. Bagoas put him on the throne, where he took the name Artaxerxes, and got rid of nearly all his brothers. The minister expected an obedient boy. What he got was a king who soon started planning to punish him.

Bagoas moved first. In 336 BC, according to Diodorus, he poisoned Arses and wiped out his children too. That same spring Philip II of Macedon sent an advance army across the Hellespont under his generals Parmenion and Attalus. His excuse was revenge for the temples Xerxes had burned in Greece 144 years earlier. Persia faced it with a kingmaker in charge instead of a king.

claims.text: Bagoas poisoned Arses and all his children.
claims.note: Diodorus is the main source, writing three centuries later; Persian records are almost silent on the reign.

claims.text: Philip II said he was invading Persia to avenge Xerxes's burning of Greek temples.
claims.note: Diodorus and other Greek writers report it as the declared war aim of the League of Corinth.

reigns.hook: Bagoas needs a new puppet and picks a royal cousin who seems safe. He isn't. And in Macedon, Philip is murdered and his 20-year-old son Alexander is king.

reigns.tagline: The last Great King, chased across his own empire
reigns.cameToPower: Put on the throne by a poisoner
reigns.previously: Bagoas poisons Artaxerxes IV in 336 BC, his second royal victim.
paragraphs: Bagoas chose Darius III, a royal cousin, as a safe puppet. He wasn't. When Bagoas tried to poison him too, Darius made him drink the cup himself. But in 334 BC Alexander of Macedon crossed into Asia and beat the local Persian governors at the river Granicus.

Darius led the royal army himself at Issus in November 333 BC, and fled when the Macedonians broke through. He left behind his mother Sisygambis, his wife and his daughters. He offered land and a daughter's hand for peace, and Alexander said no. On 1 October 331 BC, at Gaugamela in northern Iraq, Darius fled again, and his empire went with him.

Babylon and Susa opened their gates. Darius fell back east to raise another army, but his own nobles had had enough. In July 330 BC Bessus, the satrap of Bactria, and his allies put the king in chains, stabbed him and left him dying in a wagon as Alexander's cavalry closed in.

claims.text: Darius forced Bagoas to drink the poison meant for him.
claims.note: Diodorus tells it, writing three centuries later. Neat, but Bagoas does disappear early in the reign.

claims.text: Alexander treated Darius's captive mother, wife and daughters with great honour.
claims.note: Arrian, Plutarch and others agree, but they were Alexander's admirers, writing centuries later.

claims.text: Alexander found Darius's body and covered it with his own cloak.
claims.note: Plutarch tells it. Other versions have Darius still alive, giving his last words to a Macedonian soldier.

reigns.hook: Darius gets a royal burial. Alexander now poses as his avenger and heir, while in Bactria the killer Bessus calls himself king. Iran has two would-be Great Kings, and one of them is Greek-speaking and 26.

reigns.tagline: He burned Persepolis, then dressed as a Persian king
reigns.previously: Darius III is stabbed by his own satrap and left to die in a wagon.
paragraphs: Alexander had been king of Macedon since he was 20. By spring 330 BC he held Persepolis, and before moving on he burned its palaces. After Darius died he hunted down Bessus, who had claimed the crown, and had him mutilated and executed. Then came years of hard fighting in Bactria and Sogdia, where in 327 BC he married Roxana, the daughter of a local noble.

To his Macedonians' disgust he started wearing Persian dress and asked Greeks to bow down to him in the Persian way, proskynesis. He pushed on into India, then led his army back through the Gedrosian desert, where thousands died. At Susa in 324 BC he held a mass wedding, taking Darius's daughter Stateira as a wife while his officers married Persian noblewomen.

In June 323 BC, in Babylon, he fell ill after a drinking party and died at 32. Iranians remembered him in two ways. Zoroastrian books call him 'the accursed Alexander', who burned the holy scriptures. Yet the Shahnameh makes him half Persian, a son of the Persian king Darab, so his conquest becomes a family affair.

claims.text: Persepolis was burned on a drunken whim, urged on by the Athenian courtesan Thaïs.
claims.note: Plutarch and Diodorus tell it. Arrian presents the burning as deliberate revenge for Xerxes burning Athens.

claims.text: Alexander was poisoned.
claims.note: Rumours spread fast, aimed at the family of his general Antipater. Most historians suspect illness, made worse by drink and old wounds. Even the day, 10 or 11 June, is disputed.

claims.text: Alexander was the son of the Persian king Darab and a Greek princess.
claims.note: Ferdowsi's Shahnameh, finished around 1010, borrowing from the Alexander Romance. It turns a foreign conqueror into a rightful Iranian heir.

reigns.hook: Alexander leaves no grown heir, and his generals fight over the empire for 11 years. Out of the wreck rises Seleucus, one of his officers, who makes Babylon his base.

reigns.tagline: The last of Alexander's men, and the luckiest
reigns.previously: Alexander's generals spend 11 years fighting over his empire.
paragraphs: Seleucus had marched all the way to India with Alexander and led his elite foot guards. At the mass wedding at Susa he married Apama, daughter of a Sogdian warlord, and unlike most of the officers he kept his Iranian wife. After Alexander died he became governor of Babylon, lost it to the rival general Antigonus and fled to Egypt with almost nothing.

In 312 BC he slipped back into Babylon with a small force and won it over. His followers counted the years from that moment, and the Seleucid Era stayed in use for centuries. He swept east across Iran, traded his Indian lands to Chandragupta Maurya for war elephants, and used them to crush Antigonus at Ipsus in 301 BC. He built Seleucia on the Tigris and Antioch in Syria.

In 281 BC, now in his seventies, he beat his old comrade Lysimachus at Corupedium, the last of Alexander's generals besides himself. He crossed into Europe to claim Macedon, his homeland. There Ptolemy Keraunos, an exiled Egyptian prince he had sheltered, stabbed him to death.

claims.text: Seleucus gave up his Indian provinces to Chandragupta Maurya for 500 war elephants.
claims.note: Strabo gives the number, nearly three centuries later. A treaty and a marriage deal are widely accepted; the exact figure is not.

claims.text: Seleucus handed his young wife Stratonice to his son Antiochus, after a doctor worked out the prince was sick with love for her.
claims.note: Plutarch and Appian tell it as a romance. The marriage happened; the lovesick prince and the clever doctor look like storytelling.

claims.text: The Seleucid Era, counted from 312 BC, outlived the dynasty by many centuries.
claims.note: Babylonian tablets use it from the start, and Syriac Christians and Jewish communities still dated by it in the Middle Ages.

reigns.hook: Seleucus dies in Thrace, far from the empire he built. His son Antiochus, half Macedonian and half Sogdian, has already been running the east for a decade. Now he gets the lot.

reigns.tagline: The half-Iranian king who saved Asia from the Gauls
reigns.previously: Ptolemy Keraunos stabs Seleucus I in Thrace, months after his win.
paragraphs: Antiochus was the son of Seleucus and his Sogdian wife Apama, so the second Seleucid king was half Iranian. His father made him co-king around 292 BC and sent him to rule the eastern provinces from Seleucia. When Seleucus was murdered, Antiochus had to rush west to hold the empire together.

Bands of Galatians, Celtic raiders, were looting Asia Minor. Around 275 BC Antiochus beat them, and the Greek cities hailed him as Soter, the saviour. He fought a long war with Ptolemy II of Egypt over southern Syria. In Babylonia he played the traditional king, rebuilding the temple of Nabu at Borsippa and recording it in Babylonian cuneiform on a clay cylinder that still survives.
His last years went badly. His eldest son Seleucus, his co-king, was executed for rebellion, and Eumenes of Pergamon beat him near Sardis. He died on 2 June 261 BC.

claims.text: Antiochus won his 'Elephant Victory' when 16 elephants panicked the Galatians' horses.
claims.note: Told by Lucian, writing four centuries later, as a story about luck. A victory over the Galatians is real; the details are not secure.

claims.text: He had a building inscription written in Babylonian cuneiform, calling himself a king in the old Mesopotamian style.
claims.note: The Antiochus Cylinder, found at Borsippa and now in the British Museum.

claims.text: He put his eldest son Seleucus to death for plotting against him.
claims.note: Known only from late, brief notices. The son vanishes from Babylonian records, which fits.

reigns.hook: His surviving son, another Antiochus, inherits the crown, an unfinished war with Egypt and a far east that is quietly starting to slip away.

reigns.tagline: Called a god, he left behind two wives and a war
reigns.previously: Antiochus I dies in 261 BC after a run of defeats.
paragraphs: The city of Miletus was so pleased when Antiochus II freed it from a local tyrant that it called him Theos, the god. He spent much of his reign fighting Ptolemy II for the coast of Syria and Asia Minor. The peace deal, around 253 BC, came with a bride: Ptolemy's daughter Berenice. To marry her, Antiochus put aside his first wife Laodice and her sons.

Meanwhile the far east began to drift away. Diodotus, governor of Bactria, started acting like a king of his own, and in Parthia the governor Andragoras did the same. Antiochus seems not to have noticed. In 246 BC he went back to Laodice at Ephesus and died there soon afterwards. Within weeks Berenice and her baby son had been murdered in Antioch.

claims.text: Laodice poisoned Antiochus once she was sure her son would be named heir.
claims.note: Appian and later writers say so. It suits Laodice's role as villain, and no contemporary confirms it.

claims.text: Miletus gave him the title Theos, 'god', for removing the tyrant Timarchus.
claims.note: Appian reports it, and the title is well attested on inscriptions and in later king lists.

claims.text: He left real power to drinking companions and favourites.
claims.note: Athenaeus, quoting the hostile historian Phylarchus. Ancient writers loved to call kings drunks.

reigns.hook: Laodice's son becomes Seleucus II. But murdered Berenice's brother has just become king of Egypt, and Ptolemy III is coming for revenge.

reigns.tagline: The 'Glorious Victor' who kept losing
reigns.reignEnded: Killed in a fall from his horse
reigns.previously: Antiochus II dies at Ephesus; Laodice has Berenice and her son killed.
paragraphs: Seleucus II was named Callinicus, the glorious victor, which was optimistic. In his first year Ptolemy III invaded to avenge his sister Berenice and marched deep into Seleucid land. Babylonian records show Egyptian troops fighting in Babylon itself. Seleucus won most of it back, but then his younger brother Antiochus, nicknamed Hierax, the Hawk, set himself up as king in Asia Minor.

The brothers fought for years, and Hierax, with Galatian mercenaries, beat Seleucus badly at Ancyra. In the east things got worse. A nomad chief, Arsaces, rode into Parthia and took it. Seleucus marched against him in the 230s BC and was driven back. He died in 225 BC after falling from his horse.

claims.text: Ptolemy III conquered everything as far as Bactria.
claims.note: His own victory inscription at Adulis says so. Royal boasts like this were standard, and nobody believes he got that far.

claims.text: The Parthians kept the day they beat Seleucus as the birthday of their freedom.
claims.note: Justin reports it. He wrote centuries later and summarised a lost history.

claims.text: Antiochus Hierax got his nickname because, like a hawk, he snatched what belonged to others.
claims.note: Justin's explanation. It may be no more than a later pun.

reigns.hook: His eldest son, another Seleucus, takes the throne. He is young, eager to win back Asia Minor and has a nickname to live up to: Ceraunus, the Thunderbolt.

reigns.tagline: The Thunderbolt who struck out in two years
reigns.previously: Seleucus II dies after falling from his horse.
paragraphs: He was born Alexander and took the name Seleucus when he became king. The soldiers called him Ceraunus, the Thunderbolt. His plan was to win back western Asia Minor, which Attalus of Pergamon had grabbed while the Seleucid brothers were busy fighting each other.

In 223 BC he crossed the Taurus mountains with his army. Somewhere in Phrygia two of his own officers, a Galatian called Apaturius and a man named Nicanor, murdered him. His cousin Achaeus, commanding the army, caught and killed the killers. The troops then begged Achaeus to be king himself. He said no, and kept the throne for the dead king's younger brother.

claims.text: Seleucus III was murdered by Apaturius the Galatian and Nicanor.
claims.note: Polybius names them. Why they did it is not known.

claims.text: 'Thunderbolt' was a joke, because he was sickly and short of money.
claims.note: A late chronicle tradition preserved via Eusebius says so. Polybius does not.

claims.text: Achaeus turned down the crown when the army offered it to him.
claims.note: Polybius reports it. He did call himself king a few years later.

reigns.hook: The crown goes to Seleucus's brother Antiochus, a teenager in Babylon. His governor in Media, Molon, is already thinking of making himself king.

reigns.tagline: He won back the East, then picked a fight with Rome
reigns.cameToPower: Hailed king after his brother's murder
reigns.reignEnded: Killed robbing a temple in Elymais
reigns.previously: Seleucus III is murdered by two of his own officers in Asia Minor.
paragraphs: Antiochus III started badly. Molon, his governor of Media, rebelled, and it took until 220 BC to beat him. In 217 BC Ptolemy IV crushed Antiochus at Raphia in southern Palestine, a battle with elephants on both sides. Then he set off on the great eastern march of 210 to 206 BC. In Parthia, Arsaces II submitted. Antiochus besieged Bactra for two years, made a deal with its king and crossed into India for elephants.

He came home 'the Great', the new Alexander. In 200 BC he beat Egypt at Panion and took Judea and southern Syria. Then he gave refuge to Rome's arch-enemy Hannibal and landed in Greece. Rome beat him at Thermopylae in 191 BC and at Magnesia in 190 BC.

The Peace of Apamea took away Asia Minor and his elephants, and demanded a huge war debt. His younger son Antiochus went to Rome as a hostage. Short of cash, in July 187 BC he raided a temple in Elymais, and the locals killed him.

claims.text: Antiochus was killed by locals while plundering a temple of Bel in Elymais.
claims.note: Diodorus, Strabo and Justin all report it, though the details differ.

claims.text: At Raphia, Ptolemy's African elephants panicked and fled from the bigger Indian elephants of Antiochus.
claims.note: Polybius describes it. Modern zoologists think Ptolemy's were small North African forest elephants.

claims.text: When Antiochus showed off his gilded army and asked if it was enough for the Romans, Hannibal said yes, however greedy they are.
claims.note: A joke told by Aulus Gellius centuries later.

reigns.hook: His son Seleucus IV inherits a smaller kingdom with a huge bill to pay Rome. His younger brother Antiochus is still a hostage there.

reigns.tagline: The quiet king who paid Rome's bill
reigns.previously: Antiochus III is killed raiding a temple in Elymais.
paragraphs: Seleucus IV had fought at Magnesia beside his father. As king he played it safe. Rome was owed a vast war debt, paid in instalments of 1,000 talents a year, and he paid. He kept out of wars, married his daughter Laodice to King Perseus of Macedon, and around 178 BC sent his own young son Demetrius to Rome as hostage, freeing his brother Antiochus.

Money was always short. Jewish tradition tells how his chief minister Heliodorus came to Jerusalem to seize the Temple treasury and was beaten back by a heavenly horseman. In September 175 BC Heliodorus murdered the king and tried to take the throne for himself.

claims.text: Heliodorus was attacked in the Temple by a horseman in golden armour and two young men, and gave up the treasure.
claims.note: 2 Maccabees, a religious history written to show God protecting the Temple.

claims.text: Heliodorus murdered Seleucus IV to take power.
claims.note: Appian says so, and a Babylonian king list dates the king's death to September 175 BC.

claims.text: Seleucus sent his son Demetrius to Rome in exchange for his brother Antiochus.
claims.note: Appian reports it. It explains why Demetrius later claimed he was robbed of the throne.

reigns.hook: Heliodorus holds Antioch, but the dead king's brother Antiochus is out of Rome and on his way with an army from Pergamon.

reigns.tagline: God made manifest, or the madman, depending who you ask
reigns.previously: Heliodorus murders Seleucus IV and tries to take the crown.
paragraphs: Antiochus IV had spent years as a hostage in Rome and loved Roman ways. His coins called him Epiphanes, god made manifest. His enemies called him Epimanes, the madman. He wandered Antioch chatting with craftsmen, gate-crashed parties and threw a festival at Daphne so lavish it was talked about for centuries.

In 168 BC he was about to take Alexandria when the Roman envoy Popillius Laenas drew a circle in the sand round him and told him to decide before he stepped out. Antiochus went home. In Judea he looted the Temple and banned Jewish practice, which set off the Maccabean revolt. Hanukkah celebrates the Temple's recapture in 164 BC.
Antiochus marched east to win back Iran from the rising Parthians and empty more temples. Turned away from one in Elymais, he fell ill and died in Persis late in 164 BC.

claims.text: Popillius drew a circle round Antiochus in the sand and made him answer Rome before leaving it.
claims.note: Polybius, a contemporary who knew people involved, tells it, and Livy follows him.

claims.text: People punned on his title Epiphanes and called him Epimanes, the madman.
claims.note: Polybius records the joke and his odd habits.

claims.text: He died raving, punished by the gods for robbing temples.
claims.note: Polybius blames the temple in Elymais. Jewish books blame the Temple in Jerusalem. Both read his death as divine justice.

reigns.hook: He leaves a nine-year-old son and a regent, Lysias. In Rome, his nephew Demetrius, the son of Seleucus IV, is watching for his chance.

reigns.tagline: A boy king with a regent, a war and Rome on his back
reigns.previously: Antiochus IV dies on campaign in Iran, raving, say the Greeks.
paragraphs: Antiochus V was about nine when his father died. The regent Lysias ruled for him, and called him Eupator, 'of a good father'. They marched into Judea against the Maccabees in 162 BC, won at Beth Zechariah, then made peace and gave the Jews back their religious freedom so they could hurry home to deal with a rival regent.

Rome took a close interest. Under the peace treaty the kingdom had no right to war elephants or a big fleet, and a Roman embassy led by Gnaeus Octavius had the elephants hamstrung and the ships burned. A furious local man murdered Octavius. Then the boy's cousin Demetrius escaped from Rome and landed in Syria. The army went over to him and handed over Antiochus and Lysias, who were killed.

claims.text: Roman envoys had the royal elephants hamstrung and the warships burned.
claims.note: Polybius and Appian both report it. It showed who really ran the kingdom.

claims.text: At Beth Zechariah the Jewish hero Eleazar stabbed the king's biggest elephant from below and was crushed when it fell.
claims.note: 1 Maccabees tells it as a hero's death. It may well have happened, but only one pro-Maccabee source records it.

claims.text: Demetrius said 'Do not show me their faces' and let the soldiers kill the boy.
claims.note: 1 Maccabees gives the line. Appian just says the boy was killed.

reigns.hook: Demetrius has the throne he says was always his. But in Media a rebel governor called Timarchus has crowned himself king.

reigns.tagline: He escaped from Rome to take back his throne
reigns.cameToPower: Escaped from Rome; the army joined him
reigns.previously: The army hands boy-king Antiochus V to Demetrius, who has him killed.
paragraphs: Demetrius had been a hostage in Rome since childhood. When his uncle died he asked the Senate to let him go home. They refused, because a boy king suited Rome better. So in 162 BC, with help from his friend the historian Polybius, he slipped out of Ostia on a Carthaginian ship and sailed for Syria.

The army joined him. He beat Timarchus, the rebel king of Media, around 160 BC, and the grateful Babylonians called him Soter, the saviour. His generals fought the Maccabees in Judea and killed Judas Maccabeus. But Demetrius made enemies everywhere: Egypt, Pergamon, Rome. People said he drank and hid in his palace. When a young man called Alexander Balas turned up claiming to be the son of Antiochus IV, they all backed him, and in 150 BC Demetrius was killed in battle.

claims.text: Polybius himself helped Demetrius plan his escape from Rome.
claims.note: Polybius tells the story in his own history, with some pride.

claims.text: Demetrius drank heavily and shut himself away from his people.
claims.note: Polybius and Josephus say so. Enemies at the time had good reason to spread it.

claims.text: In his last battle his horse stuck in a marsh and he fought on foot until he was cut down.
claims.note: Josephus and Justin tell versions of it. Details of the battle are thin.

reigns.hook: His sons are safe abroad. On the throne sits Alexander Balas, a man nobody can prove is the son of a king.

reigns.tagline: A pretender with friends in high places
reigns.previously: Demetrius I dies fighting Alexander Balas in 150 BC.
paragraphs: Alexander Balas said he was a son of Antiochus IV. Ancient writers said he was a nobody from Smyrna, groomed by Heraclides, a former minister with a grudge against Demetrius. It didn't matter. Pergamon, Egypt and the Roman Senate all wanted Demetrius gone, and they backed him. He made the Maccabee leader Jonathan high priest to win Judea's support. After he won, Ptolemy VI gave him his daughter Cleopatra Thea as his wife.

Balas left the work to his minister Ammonius and enjoyed being king. Around 148 BC the Parthian king Mithridates I took Media, the heart of western Iran. In 147 BC Demetrius's son, also called Demetrius, landed in Syria. Ptolemy VI switched sides and even gave Cleopatra Thea to the newcomer. Balas lost a battle on the Oenoparas river in 145 BC and fled to Arabia, where a local chief cut off his head.

claims.text: Alexander Balas was an impostor, not a son of Antiochus IV.
claims.note: Polybius, Diodorus and Justin call him a fake. Some modern historians think he may really have been a son, or that it hardly mattered.

claims.text: His head was sent to Ptolemy VI, who died of his own battle wounds days later.
claims.note: 1 Maccabees and Josephus say Ptolemy died on the third day after the battle; others agree he died of wounds.

claims.text: He made the Maccabee Jonathan high priest of Jerusalem.
claims.note: 1 Maccabees quotes his letter, and Josephus follows it.

reigns.hook: Demetrius II wins the throne and Balas's wife. But in the east, Mithridates of Parthia is eyeing the richest prize of all: Babylonia.

reigns.tagline: The king who lost Iran for good
reigns.cameToPower: Backed by Ptolemy VI against Balas
reigns.previously: Alexander Balas flees to Arabia and loses his head.
paragraphs: Demetrius II came home as a teenager with an army of Cretan mercenaries. He made a bad start. He sent the regular soldiers home without pay and kept the Cretans, and when Antioch rioted in 145 BC he used Jewish troops sent by Jonathan Maccabeus to crush it, burning much of the city.

A general called Diodotus Tryphon took Balas's little son, crowned him Antiochus VI and seized Antioch. Demetrius was stuck fighting for Syria while the east fell apart. Mithridates I of Parthia marched into Babylonia, and in 141 BC Seleucia on the Tigris, the great Greek city of the east, opened its gates to him. Seleucid rule in Iran was over.

claims.text: Demetrius used 3,000 Jewish soldiers to crush a riot in Antioch.
claims.note: 1 Maccabees gives the number and has them burning the city. It is a proud Jewish account; Diodorus tells of the revolt too.

claims.text: Babylonia was in Parthian hands by July 141 BC.
claims.note: Babylonian astronomical diaries and contract tablets start dating by the Parthian king that summer.

claims.text: He turned the Antiochenes against him by disbanding the army and keeping only his Cretans.
claims.note: Diodorus and Josephus agree on it.

reigns.hook: Babylon and Seleucia belong to Parthia now, and no Seleucid will rule Iran again. So who are these Parthians? To find out, go back a century to a steppe chief named Arsaces.

reigns.tagline: The nomad chief whose name became a royal title
reigns.previously: The Parthians take Seleucia. Their story began a century earlier.
paragraphs: The Parni were horsemen from the steppe east of the Caspian Sea, one of the nomad peoples the Greeks lumped together as the Dahae. Their chief was Arsaces. Around 238 BC, while the Seleucid kings were tied up in wars far to the west, he led his riders into Parthia, a Seleucid province in what is now north-eastern Iran and Turkmenistan. Its governor Andragoras had already started acting like a king himself. Arsaces killed him and took the land.

The newcomers took the province's name, and history has called them Parthians ever since. Arsaces grabbed neighbouring Hyrcania too and built forts against the comeback he knew was coming. When Seleucus II did march east to punish him, the Parthians held on, and Seleucus was soon dragged home by trouble elsewhere. Later Parthians counted their royal years from 247 BC, around the time Arsaces became chief.

Arsaces put his name on his coins in Greek, with an archer in a soft steppe cap on the back. Every Parthian king after him called himself Arsaces too, for more than four centuries, which is why historians still argue over who struck which coin. He died around 217 BC, leaving a small, tough kingdom on the Seleucid frontier.

claims.text: Arsaces killed the Seleucid governor Andragoras to take Parthia.
claims.note: Justin says so. Other writers tell it differently, and the dates given range over about a decade.

claims.text: The Parthians celebrated the day they beat Seleucus II as the birthday of their freedom.
claims.note: Only Justin's summary of the lost history of Pompeius Trogus says so. Seleucus may simply have been called away by revolts.

claims.text: The dynasty began when two brothers, Arsaces and Tiridates, killed a Seleucid official who had made a pass at Tiridates.
claims.note: From Arrian's lost history of Parthia, known only from a later summary. Tiridates may never have existed.

reigns.hook: Arsaces dies, and his son takes his name and his kingdom. Then the most ambitious Seleucid king in generations, Antiochus III, sets out east to take it all back.

reigns.tagline: He fought Antiochus the Great, then signed up as his ally
reigns.previously: Arsaces I dies, leaving a small, tough kingdom on the frontier.
paragraphs: Arsaces II had a dangerous neighbour. The young Seleucid king Antiochus III spent his first years crushing a rebel governor in Media and fighting Egypt. Then, in 209 BC, he turned east with a big army to win back everything his family had lost. Parthia was first in line.

Polybius tells the story. The Parthians spoiled the wells on the desert road, hoping the Seleucid army would never make it across. It did, and took Hecatompylos, the city of a hundred gates. Antiochus pushed on into Hyrcania, fighting tribesmen for the passes of Mount Labus, and laid siege to the town of Syrinx. Justin says Arsaces fought back hard, but in the end he made terms. He kept his throne as Antiochus's ally, and the Seleucid army moved on to Bactria and India.
It cost Arsaces his pride, not his kingdom. Antiochus soon turned west, towards a far bigger fight with Rome, and nobody came back to check on Parthia. Arsaces II died around 191 BC.

claims.text: Arsaces II fought Antiochus III and then became his ally.
claims.note: Justin says so. Polybius's detailed account of the campaign breaks off before the end, but an agreement is widely accepted.

claims.text: The Parthians tried to stop Antiochus by spoiling the desert wells.
claims.note: Polybius, Book 10, writing within living memory. He has the Seleucid cavalry racing ahead to stop it.

reigns.hook: Arsaces II dies, and the crown passes to a cousin, Phriapatius. The Seleucids, about to be thrashed by Rome, will have no time to watch the east.

reigns.tagline: A quiet king while Rome humbled the Seleucids
reigns.previously: Arsaces II dies. The Seleucids are heading for war with Rome.
paragraphs: Phriapatius, also spelled Priapatius, ruled for about fifteen years, and the histories give him barely a sentence. He was not Arsaces II's son. A pottery label from the royal wine stores at Nisa seems to make him the son of a nephew of Arsaces I, so he came from a side branch of the family.

His luck was in the timing. In 190 BC Rome smashed Antiochus III at Magnesia. The peace that followed took away the Seleucid war elephants and fleet and loaded the king with a huge debt. Antiochus died in 187 BC trying to rob a temple for cash, and his son Seleucus IV spent his reign paying Rome off. Nobody had money or men to spare for Parthia.
Phriapatius died around 176 BC. He left two sons, Phraates and Mithridates, and both would be king.

claims.text: Phriapatius was descended from a brother of Arsaces I, not from Arsaces II.
claims.note: Based on an ostracon, a wine-jar label from Nisa listing a king's ancestors. The reading is widely accepted but the wording is open to argument.

claims.text: He reigned for fifteen years and left two sons, Phraates and Mithridates.
claims.note: Justin gives the length and the sons. The exact years are modern estimates.

reigns.hook: His elder son Phraates takes the crown and goes after the Mardi, a tough hill people in the mountains south of the Caspian.

reigns.tagline: He passed over his own sons to crown his brother
reigns.previously: Phriapatius dies, leaving two sons who will both be king.
paragraphs: Phraates I had a short reign and used it well. His target was the Mardi, a warlike people of the mountains south of the Caspian Sea. Justin says he beat them. Then he moved them, settling them at a place called Charax near the Caspian Gates, the great pass on the road west into Media. That pushed Parthia's reach towards the Seleucids' rich western provinces.

The Seleucids were in a mess. In 175 BC Seleucus IV was murdered by his own minister Heliodorus, and his brother Antiochus IV took over. Then Phraates fell ill. He had sons, but Justin says he passed them over and named his brother Mithridates king, putting the good of the kingdom ahead of his family. It was one of the best choices any Parthian ever made.

claims.text: Phraates passed over his own sons and left the throne to his brother Mithridates.
claims.note: Justin says so plainly. It fits what came next: Mithridates took the throne without a fight.

claims.text: Phraates I died around 171 BC.
claims.note: That is the traditional date. Some scholars now place his reign around 168 to 165 BC, from the coins.

claims.text: He settled the conquered Mardi at Charax, near the Caspian Gates.
claims.note: Isidore of Charax mentions the town and Phraates' settlers in his Parthian Stations, written around the time of Augustus.

reigns.hook: Mithridates I takes his brother's crown. Within thirty years he will take far more: Media, Babylonia and the great Greek city of Seleucia.

reigns.tagline: The king who turned a border state into an empire
reigns.cameToPower: Chosen by his brother Phraates I
reigns.previously: Phraates I dies and leaves Parthia to his brother Mithridates.
paragraphs: Mithridates took over a frontier kingdom and left an empire. His brother Phraates had passed over his own sons to give him the crown, and he made it count. He fought the Greek kings of Bactria in the east, then turned west while the Seleucids were tearing themselves apart. Around 148 BC he took Media. In 141 BC he marched into Babylonia and took Seleucia on the Tigris, the great Greek city of the east.

He was a nomad's heir ruling Greeks and Babylonians, and he played it well. His coins called him Philhellene, friend of the Greeks, and he took up the old title Great King. When the Seleucid king Demetrius II came east to win it all back, the Parthians captured him in 138 BC. Mithridates treated him like an honoured guest, kept him in Hyrcania and gave him his daughter Rhodogune as a wife.
Mithridates died around 132 BC. His empire ran from Mesopotamia to the borders of Bactria, and his family would keep most of it for more than three and a half centuries.

claims.text: Mithridates married his daughter Rhodogune to his royal prisoner, Demetrius II.
claims.note: Appian and Justin both report it. Demetrius still tried to escape and was dragged back.

claims.text: He came to the throne around 171 BC.
claims.note: That is the traditional date. Some scholars argue for about 165 BC from the coins.

claims.text: He called himself Philhellene, friend of the Greeks.
claims.note: The word appears on his coins, aimed at the Greek cities he now ruled.

reigns.hook: Mithridates dies the master of Iran and Mesopotamia. His son Phraates inherits it all, and a Seleucid king is already marching east to take it back.

reigns.reignEnded: Killed in battle with the Saka
reigns.previously: Mithridates I dies, master of Iran and Mesopotamia.
paragraphs: Phraates II took over the empire his father had built. In 129 BC he defeated and killed the Seleucid king Antiochus VII, who had marched east to win back Mesopotamia.
He then turned to fight the nomadic Saka on the eastern frontier. The Greek prisoners he had forced into his army deserted in battle, and Phraates was killed.
reigns.hook: His uncle Artabanus takes over the war with the nomads.

reigns.previously: Phraates II is killed by the Saka.
paragraphs: Artabanus took the throne after his nephew's death, with nomad invaders still pressing on Parthia's eastern borders.
He fought the Tocharians and was mortally wounded, reportedly by a poisoned arrow in the arm, around 124 BC.
reigns.hook: His son Mithridates II will turn the empire around.

reigns.tagline: The first Parthian to call himself King of Kings
reigns.previously: Two Parthian kings in a row die fighting nomads from the steppe.
paragraphs: Mithridates II inherited a crisis. Nomads from Central Asia, the Saka among them, were pouring into the eastern provinces and had already killed two kings. He beat them back and won the east again. The Saka ended up in the south-east, in the land later named Sistan after them. He took Armenia's prince Tigranes as a hostage, then sent him home as a friendly king. On his coins he was the first Parthian to call himself King of Kings.

This was the age of the Silk Road. Envoys from Han China reached Parthia, which the Chinese called Anxi, and silk began to move west through Parthian hands. Then came the first meeting with Rome. Around 96 BC the king's envoy Orobazus met the Roman general Sulla on the Euphrates. Sulla set out three chairs and took the middle one, as if Rome were in charge. Back home, Orobazus paid for that with his life.

claims.text: The king had his envoy Orobazus executed for letting Sulla take the seat of honour.
claims.note: Plutarch is the only source, writing nearly two centuries later. The meeting is accepted; the execution can't be checked.

claims.text: The king of Anxi sent 20,000 horsemen to meet the first Han envoys at his eastern border.
claims.note: So says Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian. Which king it was, and the exact date, are argued over.

claims.text: He was the first Parthian king to use the title King of Kings.
claims.note: His coins carry it, an old Achaemenid title brought back to life.

reigns.hook: After him Parthia sinks into decades of rival kings, so murky that coin experts call it a dark age. First comes Gotarzes, a name known mostly from Babylonian clay tablets.

paragraphs: After Mithridates II, Parthian history goes murky for over thirty years, a period historians call the Parthian Dark Age. Gotarzes I is known mostly from Babylonian records and coins.
He may have ruled only Babylonia while rivals held other parts of the empire.
reigns.hook: Rivals now compete for the Parthian throne.

He was pushed out by Orodes I around 80 BC.

He reigned around seven years and died in about 69 BC, passing the crown to his son Phraates III.

reigns.tagline: Murdered by his own sons
reigns.previously: Sinatruces dies, and Rome is at war in Armenia.
paragraphs: Phraates III ruled while Rome fought Mithridates of Pontus and Tigranes of Armenia. He made a treaty with Pompey and kept Parthia out of the war, winning back some western lands.
In about 57 BC his sons Mithridates and Orodes murdered him, then fought each other for the throne.
reigns.hook: His sons Mithridates IV and Orodes II go to war over the crown.

reigns.tagline: Rome's richest man came east for glory and lost his head
reigns.cameToPower: Killed his father, then his brother
reigns.reignEnded: Murdered by his son Phraates IV
reigns.previously: Parthia's rival kings end with Phraates III murdered by his sons.
paragraphs: Orodes and his brother Mithridates killed their father together, then turned on each other. Mithridates fled to the Romans, came back with an army, was trapped in Babylon and executed in front of Orodes. Now Orodes had all of Parthia, and a Roman problem. Marcus Crassus, the richest man in Rome, wanted a war to match the glory of his partners Pompey and Caesar. In 53 BC he crossed the Euphrates.

At Carrhae, on the dry plains of northern Mesopotamia, the Parthian general Surena was waiting with horse archers and armoured lancers. Camels brought up fresh arrows so the archers never ran short. The legions could not catch them or get away. Crassus's son died in a charge, Crassus was killed at a parley, and around 20,000 Romans died. Rome's eagle standards went to Parthia as trophies.

Surena had done too well. Orodes, jealous, had him put to death. The king's son Pacorus raided deep into Roman Syria, but in 38 BC he was killed in battle. The grieving king made another son, Phraates, his heir. Phraates thanked him with murder.

claims.text: Crassus's severed head was used as a prop in a performance of Euripides's Bacchae at the Armenian court.
claims.note: Plutarch tells it in vivid detail, about 150 years later. No other source confirms it.

claims.text: The Parthians poured molten gold down Crassus's throat to mock his greed.
claims.note: Only Cassius Dio has it, around 250 years after the battle, and he hedges it with 'some say'.

claims.text: Phraates gave his sick father poison, and when it cured him instead, strangled him.
claims.note: Plutarch's neat twist makes historians wary. That Phraates killed Orodes is widely accepted.

reigns.hook: Rewind to 57 BC. Orodes didn't kill his father alone. His brother Mithridates was in it too, and he thinks the crown should be his.

paragraphs: Mithridates IV took the throne after he and his brother killed their father, but Orodes soon turned on him. Mithridates fled to the Romans in Syria and returned with their help.
Besieged in Seleucia, he surrendered in about 54 BC and was executed on his brother's orders.
reigns.hook: Orodes rules alone and crushes Crassus at Carrhae. Years later his son Phraates murders him, kills his brothers and waits for Mark Antony.

reigns.reignEnded: Poisoned by his queen, Josephus says
reigns.previously: Orodes II, grieving for his son Pacorus, is murdered by Phraates.
paragraphs: Phraates IV started with a purge. Justin says that after killing his father he killed about thirty brothers, then his own grown son, so nobody was left to replace him. Nobles fled, some to Mark Antony. In 36 BC Antony invaded with a huge army and besieged the Median royal city of Phraaspa, but Parthian riders destroyed his siege train. His winter retreat to Armenia cost him about 24,000 men, Plutarch says.

Phraates was cruel enough that his own people threw him out for a time. A rival, Tiridates II, held the throne until Phraates came back with nomad help. Tiridates fled to Augustus, taking a kidnapped son of Phraates with him. That gave Rome a lever. In 20 BC Phraates got the boy back and handed over the eagles and prisoners taken at Carrhae. Augustus treated it as a great victory and put it on the breastplate of his Prima Porta statue.

Augustus had sent another gift: an Italian slave girl named Musa. She became Phraates' favourite, then his queen. Around 10 BC he sent his four eldest sons to live in Rome, out of reach of plotters, and her own son became the heir. Around 2 BC Phraates died. Josephus says Musa poisoned him.

claims.text: Phraates IV killed some thirty of his brothers, and his own adult son.
claims.note: Justin reports it. The number may be inflated, but a bloody purge at his accession is widely accepted.

claims.text: Queen Musa poisoned Phraates IV to put her son on the throne.
claims.note: Josephus says so, about a century later. No other writer describes how Phraates died.

claims.text: The return of Crassus's standards is shown on the breastplate of the Prima Porta statue of Augustus.
claims.note: The statue, found in 1863 and now in the Vatican Museums, shows a Parthian handing a standard to a Roman.

reigns.hook: Musa's son, Phraataces, takes the throne as Phraates V. His mother rules at his side, and her face goes on the coins with his.

reigns.title: Phraates V and Musa
reigns.tagline: A mother and son on one coin, and a scandal at court
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son and widow of Phraates IV
reigns.previously: Phraates IV dies, poisoned by his queen Musa, Josephus says.
paragraphs: Phraataces, 'little Phraates', was Musa's son, and around 2 BC he became Phraates V. His mother did not step back. Coins from these years show his head on one side and hers on the other, crowned and named 'Queen Musa, the heavenly goddess'. No other Parthian queen is known to have had her portrait on the coins.

Rome was watching. Augustus sent his grandson Gaius Caesar east with an army to settle Armenia. In AD 1 the two young men met on an island in the Euphrates, with each army lined up on its own bank, and dined with each other in turn. Parthia agreed to keep its hands off Armenia. A Roman officer called Velleius Paterculus was there and later described the scene.

At home the nobles turned on them. Josephus says Musa married her own son, and that this disgusted the Parthians. Around AD 4 a revolt drove the pair from the throne. After that they disappear, and nobody knows for sure what became of them.

claims.text: Musa married her son Phraates V.
claims.note: Josephus says so, and makes it the reason for their fall. It may be hostile gossip.

claims.text: Musa's portrait appears on Parthian coins beside her son's.
claims.note: Silver drachms survive with his head on one side and hers, named in Greek, on the other.

claims.text: Phraataces met Augustus's grandson Gaius Caesar on an island in the Euphrates in AD 1.
claims.note: Velleius Paterculus served on Gaius's staff and describes it as an eyewitness.

reigns.hook: The nobles want a king with no Roman strings and no scandal. They pick an Arsacid named Orodes, and soon wish they hadn't.

reigns.tagline: Too savage even for the Parthian nobles
reigns.reignEnded: Killed at a feast or on a hunt
reigns.previously: The nobles drive out Musa and her son Phraates V.
paragraphs: With Musa and her son gone, the Parthian nobles needed a king from the royal family who owed nothing to Rome. They chose Orodes, an Arsacid whose exact place in the family tree nobody now knows. It went wrong fast.

Josephus, the only writer who says much about him, calls him harsh and violent, a man who flew into rages. Within about two years the nobles had had enough and killed him. Josephus heard two versions. Some said it happened at a feast and sacrifice, where Parthian men always wore their swords. Most said he was lured out on a hunt and cut down there.
That left the nobles stuck. The royal men they most wanted were living in Rome: the sons Phraates IV had sent there years before.

claims.text: Orodes III was so cruel that the nobles killed him.
claims.note: Josephus is the only real source, writing about 90 years later. He gives no examples of the cruelty.

claims.text: He was murdered either at a feast or while out hunting.
claims.note: Josephus gives both stories and says most people believed the hunting one.

reigns.hook: The Parthians send envoys to Rome to ask for Phraates IV's eldest son, Vonones. He has spent most of his life as a Roman, and it shows.

reigns.tagline: Raised in Rome, he came home a stranger
reigns.cameToPower: Sent for from Rome by the nobles
reigns.previously: Orodes III is murdered, and Parthia has no king.
paragraphs: Vonones had grown up as a hostage in Rome, one of the four sons Phraates IV sent there. When Parthian envoys came asking for a king, Augustus sent him, and he was welcomed home with joy. It did not last. Tacitus says the Parthians soon felt ashamed of him. He rode through cities in a litter, cared little for hunting or horses, kept Greek friends round him and was easy and friendly with everyone, which looked like weakness to his nobles.

They found another Arsacid, Artabanus, who had grown up among the Dahae nomads. Vonones won the first round, and struck coins boasting that he had beaten Artabanus. Then Artabanus came back and won. Vonones fled to Armenia, whose throne happened to be empty, and was made its king.

Artabanus leaned on Rome, and the Romans moved Vonones to Syria and then to Cilicia, under guard. In AD 19 he slipped away on a hunting trip and rode for the border. He was caught at a river and killed by Remmius, the Roman veteran who had been guarding him.

claims.text: The Parthians despised Vonones for his Roman habits: litters, Greek friends and no taste for hunting.
claims.note: Tacitus describes it a century later, and enjoys showing Romans as too civilised for Parthia. The basic story of his rejection is not in doubt.

claims.text: Vonones issued coins calling himself the victor over Artabanus.
claims.note: Drachms with a Greek legend naming his victory over Artabanus survive.

claims.text: His guard Remmius killed him to hide the fact that he had helped him escape.
claims.note: Tacitus says Remmius struck him 'as if in anger', and hints at the cover-up. It cannot be proved.

reigns.hook: Artabanus II has the throne. He's an Arsacid only through his mother, raised far from court, and Rome is already looking for someone to replace him.

reigns.tagline: The nomad-raised king who kept coming back
reigns.previously: Vonones, mocked for his Roman ways, is driven out by Artabanus.
paragraphs: Artabanus was an Arsacid only through his mother. He grew up far to the north-east among the Dahae, a nomad people of the steppe, and ruled Media Atropatene before he made his move. The Parthian nobles had grown sick of Vonones, and Artabanus beat him in battle and took the throne around AD 12. Vonones ran to Armenia and Rome.

Artabanus was tough, and he made enemies. Tacitus says he wrote boasting letters to Tiberius and claimed all the lands Cyrus and Alexander had ruled. Tiberius answered with rival kings. In 35 or 36 the Roman candidate Tiridates was crowned at Ctesiphon while Artabanus hid in the wilds of Hyrcania. Within months Artabanus came back with nomad horsemen, and Tiridates fled.

Meanwhile in Babylonia two Jewish brothers, Asinai and Anilai, ran a private robber state, and the king found it easier to make them allies than to crush them. Artabanus was overthrown at least once more and fought his way back. He died around 40, and his sons began fighting over the crown at once.

claims.text: Artabanus wrote to Tiberius claiming every land that Cyrus and Alexander had once ruled.
claims.note: Tacitus reports it. It may be Roman framing of Parthian ambitions; no Parthian source survives.

claims.text: Two Jewish brothers, Asinai and Anilai, ran a robber state in Babylonia with the king's blessing.
claims.note: Only Josephus tells the story, as a long dramatic tale. The broad outline is often accepted.

claims.text: A king of Adiabene, Izates, helped the deposed Artabanus win back his throne.
claims.note: Josephus again, in a story praising Izates, a convert to Judaism.

reigns.hook: Artabanus is dead. His son Vardanes is his chosen heir, but another son, Gotarzes, grabs the throne first. The brothers are ready for war.

reigns.tagline: The young king who rode 340 miles in two days
reigns.cameToPower: Raced in and drove out Gotarzes
reigns.previously: Artabanus II dies, and his sons fight over the crown.
paragraphs: Vardanes was young, daring and hungry for fame. When his brother Gotarzes seized the throne, the nobles sent for him. Tacitus says he covered 3,000 stadia, roughly 340 miles, in two days and caught Gotarzes completely off guard. Gotarzes fled east to Hyrcania. Vardanes then besieged Seleucia on the Tigris, the great Greek city that had defied the Parthian kings for seven years, and forced it to surrender around 42.

Gotarzes came back with an army. Then the two brothers found out the nobles were plotting against both of them, made peace at an altar and split the realm. Gotarzes went back to Hyrcania. Vardanes wanted Armenia next, but a Roman governor warned him off. When Gotarzes broke the truce, Vardanes beat him and chased him far to the east.
The nobles thought their young king was getting too proud. Around 46, while he was out hunting, they murdered him.

claims.text: Vardanes covered about 340 miles in two days to surprise his brother.
claims.note: Tacitus gives the figure of 3,000 stadia. It may be exaggerated, but fast Parthian riders were famous.

claims.text: The wandering sage Apollonius of Tyana visited Vardanes at Babylon and won his friendship.
claims.note: From Philostratus's Life of Apollonius, written about 150 years later and full of marvels.

claims.text: Vardanes was murdered by his own nobles while hunting.
claims.note: Tacitus says so plainly, and nobody contradicts him; the details are lost.

reigns.hook: Vardanes is dead in the hunting grounds. Gotarzes rides back from Hyrcania, and this time nobody stands in his way.

reigns.tagline: He took the throne twice and the rival's ears once
reigns.cameToPower: Seized it, lost it, took it back
reigns.previously: Nobles murder King Vardanes while he is out hunting.
paragraphs: Gotarzes was quick off the mark when Artabanus II died. Tacitus says he killed another brother, also called Artabanus, along with his wife and son. The nobles turned to Vardanes instead, and Gotarzes ended up in Hyrcania. He came back, made peace with Vardanes, broke it and lost again. Once Vardanes was murdered around 46, the throne was his.

He was not popular. Some nobles asked Rome for a new king, and in 49 the emperor Claudius sent Meherdates, a grandson of Phraates IV raised in Rome. His allies drifted away, and Gotarzes beat him. Instead of killing Meherdates he had his ears cut off, which made him unfit to be king, and let him live as a lesson.
A carving of Gotarzes on horseback, spearing an enemy, is cut into the rock at Behistun, close to Darius I's great relief. He died around 51.

claims.text: Gotarzes killed his brother Artabanus with his wife and son.
claims.note: Tacitus is the only source, and he writes as a hostile outsider.

claims.text: Gotarzes cut off the ears of the Roman candidate Meherdates.
claims.note: Tacitus tells it. Mutilation to bar a man from the throne was a known Iranian custom, which makes it believable.

claims.text: Gotarzes was really an adopted son of Artabanus.
claims.note: A Greek inscription at Behistun seems to call him son of Gew. Scholars still argue over how to read it.

reigns.hook: Gotarzes is dead. The nobles send for Vonones, the king of Media, an Arsacid who will barely have time to unpack.

reigns.tagline: King for a season, father of a dynasty
reigns.cameToPower: Called from Media by the nobles
reigns.previously: Gotarzes II dies, about AD 51, after a harsh reign.
paragraphs: Vonones II was already a king when the call came. He was king of Media Atropatene, the mountain kingdom in what is now north-western Iran, and he had the right blood. When Gotarzes died the nobles offered him the crown of Parthia.

It did him little good. Tacitus gives him a single sentence: a short reign, with nothing great or terrible to remember. He seems to have died within months. His real legacy was his sons. One of them, Vologases, would hold Parthia for almost thirty years, and the others would get kingdoms of their own.

claims.text: Vonones II reigned only a few months and did nothing worth recording.
claims.note: This is Tacitus's verdict. Some coins have been tied to him, but nothing else is known.

reigns.hook: Vonones is dead. His son Vologases, born to a Greek concubine, takes the throne with his brothers' blessing. He has plans for Armenia.

reigns.tagline: He made Rome crown his brother
reigns.previously: Vonones II dies after a few months on the throne.
paragraphs: Vologases was the son of a Greek concubine, says Tacitus, but his brothers let him have the throne. He paid them back with kingdoms. One brother, Pacorus, got Media. For the other, Tiridates, he wanted Armenia, and Rome claimed the right to choose Armenia's kings. Nero sent his best general, Corbulo, who burnt the capital Artaxata. Then in 62 a second Roman army surrendered to the Parthians at Rhandeia.

The deal was clever. Tiridates would rule Armenia, but take his crown from Nero. In 66 he crossed half the world to Rome, knelt to Nero, and was crowned in a splendid show. Vologases had won what he wanted. When the Roman world fell into civil war in 69 he offered Vespasian 40,000 horsemen, and kept the peace with Rome.
At home he built a new town, Vologasocerta, beside the Greek city of Seleucia. In 72 Alan raiders swept down from the Caucasus into Media and Armenia. He died around 78.

claims.text: Nero crowned Tiridates king of Armenia in Rome in AD 66.
claims.note: Suetonius and Cassius Dio both describe the ceremony.

claims.text: Tiridates, a Zoroastrian priest, went to Rome overland because he would not defile the sea.
claims.note: Pliny the Elder says so; he was alive at the time, but the religious reason may be his own explanation.

claims.text: An Arsacid king called Valakhsh ordered the scattered Avesta to be gathered and written down.
claims.note: A ninth-century Zoroastrian book, the Denkard, says so. Which Vologases is meant, if any, is unknown.

reigns.hook: Vologases is dead. His son Pacorus takes over, but two more Arsacids say they are king too, and one of them will shelter a man claiming to be Nero.

reigns.tagline: A false Nero, a Chinese envoy and a kingdom for sale
reigns.previously: Vologases I dies after nearly thirty years on the throne.
paragraphs: Pacorus took over young, and not alone. Two other Arsacids, Vologases II and Artabanus III, claimed the crown. Around 80 a man who looked like Nero turned up in the east, and Artabanus III took him in and talked of marching him to Rome. Pacorus won out over both rivals and ruled for about thirty years.

His reign had a moment of world history. In 97 a Chinese envoy, Gan Ying, reached the sea at the edge of Parthian lands on his way to Rome. Parthian sailors told him the voyage could take two years, and that men pined for home and many died. He turned back. China and Rome never met.
Pacorus also needed cash. He sold the little kingdom of Osroene, around Edessa, to its prince Abgar. In his last years the west slipped away from him to a rival, Osroes, and he died around 110.

claims.text: The Parthians sheltered a man claiming to be Nero.
claims.note: Cassius Dio says Artabanus III backed a fake Nero around 80. Suetonius mentions another one, supported by the Parthians, about 88.

claims.text: Parthian sailors frightened the Chinese envoy Gan Ying into turning back.
claims.note: This is the Chinese Book of the Later Han's account. Historians suspect the Parthians wanted to keep the silk trade to themselves.

claims.text: Pacorus sold Osroene to Abgar for a large sum.
claims.note: Cassius Dio says so, in a passage about Trajan. No eastern source confirms it.

reigns.hook: Pacorus is dead. His son Vologases holds the east, but Osroes sits in Ctesiphon. And in Rome, the soldier-emperor Trajan is looking for a war.
