reigns.tagline: He waited out Trajan from the far side of Iran
reigns.cameToPower: Took the east as Pacorus's heir
reigns.previously: Pacorus II dies, and his son and Osroes split the empire.
paragraphs: Vologases III spent his first twenty years ruling only half an empire. Osroes held Ctesiphon and the west. Vologases kept the eastern lands, far from Rome. So when Trajan smashed his way down the Tigris in 116, it was Osroes who lost his capital. Vologases sat it out.

Patience paid. Trajan died in 117 and Hadrian gave up the conquests. By about 129 Vologases had pushed Osroes out and held the whole kingdom. Another rival, Mithridates, still struck coins of his own for some years.

Then trouble came from the north. Around 135 the Alans, nomad horsemen, broke through the Caucasus and raided Media and Armenia. Cassius Dio blames the king of Iberia for letting them through. Vologases complained to Hadrian. He died around 147.

claims.text: The Alans were let through the Caucasus passes by Pharasmanes, king of Iberia.
claims.note: Cassius Dio says so. Only a summary of his account survives for these years.

claims.text: Antoninus Pius refused to give back Osroes's captured golden throne.
claims.note: The Historia Augusta says so, and it is a notoriously unreliable source.

reigns.hook: Vologases III is gone. The next king, another Vologases, is the son of the rival Mithridates. He has his eye on Armenia, and on Rome's eastern frontier.

reigns.tagline: Trajan took his capital, his daughter and his throne
reigns.previously: Pacorus II's grip slips, and a rival seizes western Parthia.
paragraphs: Osroes ruled from Ctesiphon, the western capital, while Pacorus and then Vologases III held the east. He made the mistake of meddling in Armenia. Around 113 he threw out its king and installed Parthamasiris, a son of Pacorus II, without asking Rome. Trajan marched east. In 114 Parthamasiris laid his crown at Trajan's feet, expecting it back. He did not get it, and was killed soon afterwards.

Trajan took Armenia and Mesopotamia, then sailed down the Tigris and took Ctesiphon in 116. Osroes escaped, but his daughter and his golden throne were captured. Trajan reached the Persian Gulf, watched a ship sail for India, and said he wished he were young enough to follow Alexander.
Revolts flared behind the Romans, and in 117 Trajan died. Osroes came home. Hadrian sent back his daughter. Around 129 Vologases III finally pushed him out, and he disappears.

claims.text: Trajan captured Osroes's daughter and his golden throne at Ctesiphon.
claims.note: Cassius Dio reports it, and the Historia Augusta mentions both the daughter and the throne.

claims.text: At the Gulf, Trajan said he would have gone on to India if he were younger.
claims.note: Cassius Dio tells it. It is the kind of Alexander comparison Romans loved, but may be authentic.

claims.text: Hadrian sent Osroes's daughter home.
claims.note: Only the Historia Augusta says so, and it is a notoriously unreliable source.

reigns.hook: Osroes has fled Ctesiphon. Trajan doesn't want to rule Parthia himself, so he looks for a Parthian who will do as he's told: Osroes's own son.

reigns.tagline: The king Rome gave to Parthia, and Parthia gave back
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Osroes I, it seems
reigns.previously: Trajan takes Ctesiphon, and Osroes flees.
paragraphs: Parthamaspates was an Arsacid prince, probably Osroes's own son, who had come over to the Romans. In 116, at Ctesiphon, Trajan called a great meeting of Romans and Parthians, put a crown on his head and declared him king. Rome even struck coins showing the scene, with the proud words REX PARTHIS DATUS: a king given to the Parthians.

The Parthians did not want him. As soon as Trajan headed home, sick, in 117, support for the puppet king collapsed and Osroes came back. Hadrian found Parthamaspates a smaller job: king of Osroene, the little Roman-backed kingdom around Edessa.

claims.text: Trajan crowned Parthamaspates himself at Ctesiphon.
claims.note: Cassius Dio describes it, and Roman coins with REX PARTHIS DATVS celebrate it.

claims.text: Parthamaspates was the son of Osroes.
claims.note: The late chronicler John Malalas says so; most historians accept it, but Cassius Dio does not say.

reigns.hook: Parthamaspates is gone and Osroes is back in Ctesiphon. But in the east Vologases III has been waiting, and he is ready to take it all.

reigns.tagline: He started a war with Rome and paid for it in fire
reigns.previously: Vologases III dies after reuniting Parthia.
paragraphs: Vologases IV began with a win at home. In 151 he marched on Characene, the rich kingdom at the head of the Gulf, and threw out its king. A bronze statue of Heracles, taken as loot and set up at Seleucia, still carries his inscription boasting of it.

In 161, as Marcus Aurelius came to power, he struck at Rome. He put his own man on the Armenian throne, and at Elegeia a Roman army was wiped out. Rome sent Lucius Verus. His generals took back Armenia, and in 165 Avidius Cassius sacked Seleucia and burnt the palace at Ctesiphon. Seleucia never recovered.
The soldiers marched home, and a deadly plague spread with them across the Roman world. Parthia lost northern Mesopotamia and the Euphrates city of Dura-Europos. Vologases ruled on until about 191.

claims.text: A Heracles statue from Seleucia records Vologases's victory over the king of Characene.
claims.note: The bronze, found in 1984, has a Greek and Parthian inscription dated 151. It is in the Iraq Museum.

claims.text: Verus's soldiers caught the Antonine Plague at Seleucia and spread it through the Empire.
claims.note: Roman writers made the link. The disease may already have been spreading, and what it was is uncertain.

claims.text: The Roman commander at Elegeia killed himself as his army was destroyed.
claims.note: Lucian mocks a historian's account of it in How to Write History. Cassius Dio has the army destroyed; details are thin.

reigns.hook: Vologases IV is dead. His son Vologases, king of Armenia, takes Parthia. In Rome a new emperor, Septimius Severus, is fighting for his throne.

reigns.tagline: Severus sacked his capital and took 100,000 captives
reigns.previously: Vologases IV dies after a war that cost Parthia dearly.
paragraphs: Vologases V had been king of Armenia before he became King of Kings. In Rome the throne was up for grabs too, and he backed Pescennius Niger, the general holding Syria, against Septimius Severus. He bet on the wrong man. Severus crushed Niger in 194 and came east for revenge.

Late in 197 Severus floated his army down the Euphrates and took Ctesiphon. Cassius Dio says he killed huge numbers, carried off 100,000 people as slaves and grabbed the treasury. Then he tried twice to take Hatra, a desert city loyal to the Parthians, and failed both times. Its walls and archers broke the Romans.
Severus kept northern Mesopotamia as a new province. Vologases ruled on until about 208, and his sons began to fight.

claims.text: Severus carried off 100,000 captives from Ctesiphon.
claims.note: Cassius Dio gives the figure. He lived through these years, but round ancient numbers are often inflated.

claims.text: Hatra beat off Severus twice.
claims.note: Cassius Dio and Herodian both describe the failed sieges.

reigns.hook: Vologases V is dead. His son Vologases VI takes the throne, but his brother Artabanus is not going to wait his turn.

reigns.tagline: He kept the capital while his brother took the empire
reigns.previously: Vologases V dies, and his sons are ready to fight.
paragraphs: Vologases VI had a few quiet years. Around 213 his younger brother Artabanus rose against him, and soon most of Iran, from Media eastward, answered to Artabanus. Vologases held on to Mesopotamia and Seleucia, the old money-making heart of the realm.

Rome noticed. The emperor Caracalla demanded that Vologases hand over two men who had fled to him, a prince called Tiridates and a Cynic philosopher called Antiochus, and he gave them up rather than face a war. It did not help. Caracalla turned his attention to Artabanus, and Vologases faded. His coins go on until about 228, but by around 222 he no longer held Seleucia.

claims.text: Vologases handed over two fugitives to avoid war with Caracalla.
claims.note: Cassius Dio says so; only a summary of his text survives for these years.

claims.text: Vologases VI kept striking coins until about 228, after Artabanus IV was dead.
claims.note: Dated coins show it. Where he ruled by then, and how he ended, is unknown.

reigns.hook: The real power now belongs to Artabanus IV. And Caracalla, the most dangerous emperor in years, wants to marry his daughter.

reigns.tagline: He beat Rome, then lost everything to a rebel
reigns.previously: Vologases VI loses most of the empire to his brother Artabanus.
paragraphs: Artabanus IV took most of Iran from his brother and faced Caracalla. The emperor asked for his daughter's hand. Herodian says Artabanus agreed and came out to greet the groom, and the Romans fell on the unarmed wedding party. Cassius Dio says the king refused and Caracalla invaded anyway. Either way, Romans dug up the royal tombs at Arbela and scattered the bones.

In 217 Caracalla was murdered near Carrhae. Artabanus caught his successor Macrinus at Nisibis, and after three days of battle Rome paid a huge sum to end the war. Cassius Dio says 200 million sesterces. It was Parthia's last great win.

The danger was a lord called Ardashir in Persis, who was swallowing his neighbours. Artabanus moved too late. Around 28 April 224 the armies met at Hormozdgan, Artabanus was killed, and the Arsacids, who had ruled for nearly 500 years, were finished.

claims.text: Caracalla massacred Artabanus's people at a wedding feast.
claims.note: Herodian tells it. Cassius Dio, who lived through it, says the marriage was refused and Caracalla simply attacked.

claims.text: Rome paid 200 million sesterces after the battle of Nisibis.
claims.note: The figure is Cassius Dio's; he was a senator then and close to events.

claims.text: Ardashir killed Artabanus with his own hand at Hormozdgan.
claims.note: Al-Tabari and Persian tradition say so, centuries later; they wanted a heroic founder.

reigns.hook: Ardashir rides away from Hormozdgan as master of Iran. Now he must show everyone that a new family, the Sasanians, rules by the will of the gods.

reigns.tagline: A lord from Persis topples Parthia and founds a dynasty
reigns.previously: Artabanus IV beats Rome, but a rebel lord rises in Persis.
paragraphs: Ardashir came from Istakhr in Persis, the old Persian heartland near the ruins of Persepolis. His grandfather Sasan, the story goes, served at the temple of the goddess Anahita there, and his father Papak made himself a local king. Ardashir conquered his neighbours one by one, then took on the Parthian king Artabanus IV. At Hormozdgan in 224 he killed him and became King of Kings of the Iranians.

He made sure everyone got the message. At Naqsh-e Rostam, below the tombs of the old Achaemenid kings, he had himself carved on horseback taking the ring of kingship from the god Ahura Mazda. Under his horse lies Artabanus. Under the god's horse lies Ahriman, the spirit of evil. Ardashir backed a Zoroastrian state church, and later tradition says the priest Tansar helped him build it.

Then he turned on Rome. He pushed into Roman Mesopotamia, and around 240 he took Hatra, the desert city that had beaten off two Roman emperors. By then he had made his son Shapur co-ruler. Around 242 Ardashir died, and Shapur had the throne to himself.

claims.text: Ardashir escaped the Parthian court with the king's slave girl, and a great ram, the spirit of royal glory, ran after him.
claims.note: From the Kar-namag i Ardashir, a Middle Persian romance written down centuries later. It reads like a folk tale.

claims.text: Sasan was Ardashir's grandfather.
claims.note: Shapur's inscription and al-Tabari say so. The Kar-namag makes Sasan his real father, with Papak as his mother's father.

claims.text: The priest Tansar wrote a letter defending Ardashir's new order.
claims.note: The letter survives only in a 13th-century Persian version of a lost Arabic translation. How much is Ardashir's era is argued over.

reigns.hook: Shapur inherits his father's war with Rome. Over the next twenty years three Roman emperors will face him: one dies, one pays, and one becomes his prisoner.

reigns.tagline: The King of Kings who took a Roman emperor prisoner
reigns.previously: Ardashir I topples the Parthians and makes his son Shapur co-ruler.
paragraphs: Shapur fought Rome three times and won three times, and he made sure nobody forgot. In 244 the young emperor Gordian III died after a battle at Misiche on the Euphrates. His successor, Philip the Arab, bought peace for 500,000 denarii. In 253 Shapur smashed a Roman army at Barbalissos and went on to sack Antioch, the great city of Roman Syria.

Then came the big one. In 260, near Edessa, the emperor Valerian was captured along with his officers. No Roman emperor had ever been taken by a foreign enemy before. Shapur had his triumphs carved into the cliffs at Naqsh-e Rostam and Bishapur, with Roman emperors at his horse's feet. On the Ka'ba-ye Zartosht he put up his own account of it all in Middle Persian, Parthian and Greek.

Thousands of Roman prisoners were settled in Iran, where they built new towns and, so it's said, the Band-e Kaisar dam at Shushtar. Shapur also welcomed the prophet Mani, whose new faith blended ideas from Zoroaster, the Buddha and Jesus. His last years were less glorious. Odaenathus of Palmyra, fighting on Rome's side, raided deep into Persian Mesopotamia. Shapur died around 270.

claims.text: Shapur used the captive Valerian as a mounting block, and had his skin stuffed and hung in a temple after he died.
claims.note: Told by Lactantius, a Christian writer who saw Valerian's fate as God punishing a persecutor. No Persian source mentions it.

claims.text: Gordian III was killed in battle against Shapur.
claims.note: Shapur's inscription says so. Roman writers say he died later, perhaps murdered by his own officers.

claims.text: Valerian's captured soldiers built the Band-e Kaisar, the 'Caesar's dam', at Shushtar.
claims.note: Later Persian and Arab tradition says so and the name fits, but nothing written at the time confirms it.

reigns.hook: Shapur dies around 270 and his chosen heir, Hormizd, takes the crown. The high priest Kartir is waiting at his side, and he has decided that Mani, the prophet Shapur protected, is a dangerous heretic.

reigns.tagline: The heir who barely had time to try on the crown
reigns.previously: Shapur I, the king who caught a Roman emperor, dies about 270.
paragraphs: Hormizd was the son Shapur trusted. While his father was alive he ruled Armenia as its Great King, Iran's most important frontier post, and he rode with the army in Shapur's wars against Rome. When the old king died around 270, Hormizd was the one waiting with the crown, ahead of his older brother Bahram.

He didn't get long. Hormizd kept his father's policies. The prophet Mani, who had travelled with Shapur's court, was allowed to keep preaching. At the same time Hormizd gave the priest Kartir a new cap and belt of rank and made him a chief priest, which turned out to matter far more. Later tradition also credits him with founding the city of Hormizd-Ardashir, today's Ahvaz. Then, about a year in, he died.

claims.text: Hormizd gave Kartir the cap and belt of high rank and the title of chief priest.
claims.note: Kartir says so himself in his inscriptions, which list the honours each king gave him.

claims.text: Hormizd founded the city of Hormizd-Ardashir, now Ahvaz.
claims.note: Later Arab and Persian writers say so, but some credit his grandfather Ardashir I, whose name the city also carries.

claims.text: Hormizd let Mani go on preaching and promised him the same protection Shapur had.
claims.note: This comes from Manichaean writings, which naturally remember him kindly. No Persian source mentions it.

reigns.hook: Hormizd is dead after a year. The crown passes to his elder brother Bahram, the son Shapur had skipped over, and Bahram owes his throne to Kartir.

reigns.tagline: The passed-over prince who let the priests have Mani
reigns.previously: Hormizd I dies after barely a year as King of Kings.
paragraphs: Bahram was Shapur's eldest son, but his father had made him king of Gilan by the Caspian and left it at that. When Hormizd died, Bahram got the crown after all, with the priest Kartir backing him. His youngest brother Narseh had a decent claim of his own. Bahram kept him sweet by making him king of Armenia.

Kartir wanted something in return. The prophet Mani had been protected by Shapur and Hormizd, and the Zoroastrian priests saw him as a dangerous heretic. Bahram summoned him to the royal city of Gundeshapur, berated him and had him thrown into chains. Mani died in prison some weeks later, in about 274 or a little after. His followers called it his crucifixion. Bahram himself died soon after, around 274.

claims.text: Mani died in chains after about 26 days in prison.
claims.note: Manichaean texts from Egypt describe his last days in detail. The year is disputed, anywhere from 274 to 277.

claims.text: Mani's body was flayed and his skin stuffed and hung over a city gate.
claims.note: Told by much later Muslim-era writers. Mani's own followers only say he died in chains.

claims.text: Bahram was passed over because his mother was a lesser wife.
claims.note: A common guess by historians. No source from the time explains why Shapur preferred Hormizd.

reigns.hook: Bahram dies and his son, another Bahram, is crowned in his teens. Behind the boy stands Kartir, about to become the most powerful priest in Iran.

reigns.tagline: The boy king who left the priest to rule his soul
reigns.previously: Bahram I hands Mani to the priests and dies around 274.
paragraphs: Bahram II was young when he was crowned, and the priest Kartir stood right beside him. Kartir carved his own inscriptions next to the kings' reliefs, something no priest had done before. In them he boasts of striking down Jews, Buddhists, Brahmins, Christians and Manichaeans, and of setting up sacred fires across the land. Bahram also put his own family in stone, with his queen and princes around him, more than any Sasanian king before him.

Trouble came from two sides. In the east a cousin, also named Hormizd, rose against him with help from the Sakas. In 283 the Roman emperor Carus marched down the Tigris and took Ctesiphon itself. Then Carus died suddenly, and his army went home. Bahram made peace with Diocletian in 287 and let a Roman-backed king take Armenia. He died around 293 after nearly twenty years on the throne.

claims.text: Kartir boasted of persecuting Jews, Buddhists, Brahmins, Christians and Manichaeans.
claims.note: His own inscriptions say so. How far the persecution really went beyond his boasts is hard to tell.

claims.text: The emperor Carus was killed by a bolt of lightning in his tent near Ctesiphon.
claims.note: Several Roman writers report it. Others suspected illness or murder by his own officers.

reigns.hook: Bahram II's son is crowned in 293. But Shapur I's last surviving son, Narseh, is still king of Armenia and thinks the crown should be his.

reigns.tagline: The king of four months whom everyone deserted
reigns.cameToPower: Put on the throne by a noble
reigns.previously: Bahram II dies after nearly twenty years with Kartir at his side.
paragraphs: Under his father, Bahram III had been king of the Sakas in Sistan, a training post for princes. When Bahram II died in 293 a powerful noble named Wahnam set the young man on the throne. Not everyone agreed. Many of the great families looked instead to Narseh, Shapur I's youngest son, an old hand who had spent years ruling Armenia.

Narseh marched south from Armenia. As he came, the nobles slipped away from Bahram's camp and went over to him. They met Narseh at Paikuli, in today's Iraqi Kurdistan, and hailed him as king. Wahnam was handed over and put to death. Bahram III had reigned about four months. What became of him nobody knows.

claims.text: The nobles abandoned Bahram III and met Narseh at Paikuli.
claims.note: Narseh's own inscription at Paikuli tells the story and lists the nobles who came over. It is the winner's version.

claims.text: Bahram III was killed after his fall.
claims.note: Often assumed, but no source says what happened to him.

reigns.hook: Narseh has the crown at last. Next he wants back the lands Rome took from Bahram II, and a Roman army under Galerius is waiting for him.

reigns.tagline: He won the crown, then lost his harem to Rome
reigns.cameToPower: Nobles deserted Bahram III for him
reigns.previously: The nobles desert Bahram III for his great-uncle Narseh.
paragraphs: Narseh was the last of Shapur I's sons, passed over again and again. Once he had the crown he made sure everyone knew he deserved it. On a tower at Paikuli he had his version carved in two languages, naming the nobles who had come over to him. At Bishapur he had Bahram I's name chiselled off a royal relief and his own put in its place.

Then he went after Rome. In 296 or 297 he beat the Roman Caesar Galerius in the plains of northern Mesopotamia. Galerius came back the next year through Armenia, caught Narseh off guard and routed him. Narseh escaped wounded, but his wives, his children and his treasure were taken.

To get his family back he signed the Peace of Nisibis in 299. Rome took five provinces beyond the Tigris and control of Armenia, and all trade had to pass through Nisibis. It was a humiliating deal. Narseh died in 302 or 303.

claims.text: Narseh told the story of his rise on a monument at Paikuli.
claims.note: The inscription survives in hundreds of blocks, in Middle Persian and Parthian, and has been pieced together by scholars.

claims.text: Galerius captured Narseh's wives, sisters and children and treated them honourably.
claims.note: Roman writers agree on the capture. The fine treatment is their claim, and it helped Rome bargain.

claims.text: Narseh gave up the throne to his son before he died.
claims.note: Some later sources say he abdicated. Others simply have him die as king.

reigns.hook: Narseh dies, and his son Hormizd inherits a crown dented by defeat. The great nobles have learned how much a king needs them.

reigns.tagline: A quiet reign that ended with a family bloodbath
reigns.previously: Narseh signs away land to Rome at Nisibis and dies about 303.
paragraphs: Hormizd II reigned for about six and a half years, and we know frustratingly little about them. He kept the peace with Rome that his father had paid for. He is said to have married a princess from the Kushan lands in the east, and a relief at Naqsh-e Rostam may show him knocking an enemy off his horse with a lance.

What matters is how it ended. When Hormizd died in 309 he left several grown sons, but the nobles and priests had other plans. They wanted no strong king who would bring them to heel. His eldest son Adur Narseh was crowned, and the knives were already out.

claims.text: Hormizd II was killed by Arab raiders while out hunting.
claims.note: Some later accounts say so. Others just say he died. The Arab raids that followed his death are better attested.

claims.text: The jousting relief at Naqsh-e Rostam shows Hormizd II.
claims.note: It has no inscription. Scholars identify the king from his crown, and some prefer another king.

reigns.hook: Hormizd II is dead. His eldest son Adur Narseh takes the crown, but the nobles don't plan to let him keep it.

reigns.tagline: Crowned, then cut down within months
reigns.previously: Hormizd II dies in 309, leaving several grown sons.
paragraphs: Adur Narseh lasted only a few months. Later writers said he was cruel, which may simply be how the winners explained what came next. The nobles and priests had him killed. Then they dealt with his brothers. One was blinded, which barred him from the throne. Another, called Hormizd like his father, was thrown into prison.

That Hormizd got out years later. His wife helped him escape, and he fled to the Roman emperor Constantine. He spent the rest of his life in Roman service and rode with the emperor Julian against Persia in 363. Back home the nobles picked a king who couldn't argue with them: a baby brother so young he may not yet have been born.

claims.text: Prince Hormizd escaped from prison and fled to the Romans.
claims.note: Roman historians, including Ammianus Marcellinus and Zosimus, mention the exiled prince and his later career.

claims.text: His wife smuggled him a file hidden inside a fish.
claims.note: Zosimus tells it in detail. It is a good story and impossible to check.

claims.text: Adur Narseh was murdered because he was cruel.
claims.note: Later Arab and Persian writers say so. The nobles who killed him had every reason to blacken his name.

reigns.hook: The nobles have their king, a baby called Shapur. They expect decades of easy power. They have no idea who they have crowned.

reigns.tagline: Crowned in the womb, king for seventy years
reigns.cameToPower: Nobles crowned him as a baby
reigns.previously: Nobles murder Adur Narseh months after his father Hormizd II dies.
paragraphs: The story goes that the nobles laid the crown on his pregnant mother's belly. True or not, Shapur II was a baby when he became king, and the great families ran Iran for him. They did a poor job. Arab raiders crossed the Gulf and plundered the coast. When Shapur grew up he hit back hard, raiding deep into Arabia, and Arab writers later gave him a grim nickname: the man of the shoulders.

Then Rome turned Christian, and Shapur began to see Persia's Christians as Rome's friends. From the 340s he squeezed them with double taxes and executions, and Syriac writers kept the memory of the martyrs. His wars with Rome dragged on for decades. In 359 he took the fortress of Amida after a long siege. A Roman officer, Ammianus Marcellinus, was inside, slipped out as it fell and wrote it all down.

In 363 the emperor Julian marched all the way to Ctesiphon, couldn't take it and turned back. He was killed in a skirmish on the retreat. His successor Jovian, stuck with a hungry army, handed back Nisibis and the lands Narseh had lost. Shapur also fought the Kushans and Huns in the east. When he died in 379, after about seventy years on the throne, Persia was stronger than it had been in generations.

claims.text: Shapur was crowned before he was born, the crown laid on his mother's belly.
claims.note: Agathias and al-Tabari tell it centuries later. He may simply have been a small baby when crowned.

claims.text: He pierced the shoulders of Arab captives and led them away on ropes, earning the name Dhu'l-Aktaf.
claims.note: This is al-Tabari's explanation. Other Arab writers explain the nickname differently.

claims.text: Ammianus Marcellinus was inside Amida in 359 and escaped when it fell.
claims.note: He tells the story himself, as an eyewitness, in Book 19 of his history.

reigns.hook: Shapur leaves a strong state and a son too young to rule. The nobles hand the crown to his old brother Ardashir, king of Adiabene, to keep it warm.

reigns.tagline: The old caretaker king who turned on his nobles
reigns.previously: Shapur II dies after about seventy years on the throne.
paragraphs: Ardashir was Shapur II's brother and had spent decades as vassal king of Adiabene, around Arbela in northern Iraq. There, in the 340s, he took part in Shapur's harsh persecution of Christians, and Syriac martyr stories remember his name. When Shapur died in 379, the nobles put the ageing Ardashir on the throne.

He made himself unpopular fast. Armenia, which Shapur had fought so hard for, kept slipping out of Persian hands. Worse for him, Ardashir went after the great families themselves and had a number of them put to death. In 383 they removed him. Nobody recorded what became of him.

He did leave a fine memorial. At Taq-e Bostan he is carved receiving the ring of kingship from a crowned figure, either the god Ahura Mazda or his brother Shapur II, with the god Mithra behind him and a fallen enemy under their feet.

claims.text: Ardashir II was deposed because he had many nobles killed.
claims.note: Al-Tabari says so. It is one-sided, but it fits the pattern of the time.

claims.text: The fallen man at Taq-e Bostan is the Roman emperor Julian.
claims.note: A common identification, since Julian died invading Persia in 363. The relief has no label.

claims.text: As king of Adiabene, Ardashir oversaw the killing of Christians.
claims.note: Syriac acts of the Persian martyrs name him. Martyr stories exaggerate, but the persecution is real.

reigns.hook: The nobles have thrown out Ardashir. Now they turn to Shapur II's son, also called Shapur, and hope he will be easier to handle.

reigns.tagline: He split Armenia with Rome, then his tent fell in
reigns.previously: The nobles depose Ardashir II for killing too many of them.
paragraphs: Shapur III was the great Shapur's son, and he made sure people saw it. At Taq-e Bostan he had a small cave carved out of the rock, with figures of himself and his father standing side by side and inscriptions naming them both. It was a family portrait meant to say that he was the rightful heir.

His main achievement was ending the long fight over Armenia. Around 387 Persia and Rome agreed to split it. Persia got the larger eastern part and Rome a strip in the west, and the old Armenian kingdom never recovered. But the nobles who had made Shapur king turned against him too. In 388 they cut the ropes of the great tent where he was sitting, and it came down and killed him.

claims.text: Shapur III and Shapur II are carved together in the small grotto at Taq-e Bostan.
claims.note: Middle Persian inscriptions beside the figures name both kings.

claims.text: The nobles killed Shapur III by cutting the ropes of his tent.
claims.note: Al-Tabari tells it. It may be a tidy story for a quiet murder, but no source gives another cause.

claims.text: Armenia was divided between Persia and Rome in 387.
claims.note: The split certainly happened, but the year is uncertain; historians suggest dates from 384 to 391.

reigns.hook: Shapur III dies under his tent. His son Bahram, governor of Kerman, takes the crown, and out on the steppe the Huns are on the move.

reigns.tagline: The governor of Kerman who met the Huns
reigns.previously: Shapur III dies when nobles bring his tent down on him.
paragraphs: Before he was king, Bahram ruled Kerman in the south-east, and he kept the title Kermanshah for life. Later tradition even says he gave his name to the city of Kermanshah in the west. As king he tightened his grip on Persian Armenia, removing its Armenian king and putting the man's brother in his place.

In 395 a new terror arrived. Hunnic horsemen poured through the passes of the Caucasus and raided far into Roman Syria and Persian Mesopotamia, getting close to Ctesiphon before they were driven off. Bahram survived the Huns but not his own army. In 399 his troops mutinied and killed him.

claims.text: Bahram IV founded the city of Kermanshah and named it after his title.
claims.note: Later Persian and Arab writers say so. The link between the city and the title may simply be a guess from the names.

claims.text: Bahram IV was killed by his own soldiers in 399.
claims.note: Al-Tabari says his troops rose against him and killed him. Few details are known.

claims.text: The Huns raided deep into both empires in 395.
claims.note: Roman writers, among them the poet Claudian and Saint Jerome, describe the raid.

reigns.hook: Bahram IV is dead and the crown goes to Shapur III's son Yazdegerd. He will make peace with Rome and with Christians, and the priests will never forgive him.

reigns.tagline: The king the priests called the Sinner
reigns.cameToPower: Took the throne after Bahram IV's murder
reigns.previously: Bahram IV is killed by his own mutinous troops in 399.
paragraphs: After three murdered or deposed kings in twenty years, Yazdegerd I brought calm. He made peace with Rome and kept it for his whole reign. He also did something no Sasanian king had done before: he let Christians organise openly. In 410 the bishops of his empire met in council at Seleucia-Ctesiphon with his blessing, and the Church of the East took shape as a church with its own head.

Jews did well under him too, and later Jewish tradition remembered him kindly. The Zoroastrian priests and the great noble families saw things differently. To them he was a king who ignored their advice and favoured outsiders, and they called him the Sinner. Late in his reign a Christian priest burned down a fire temple, and Yazdegerd turned on the Christians, but his reputation with the priests was already fixed.

He died in 420, far from the capital in the north-east of his empire. The priests told a pointed story about it. A splendid horse rose out of a spring, let no one but the king near it, kicked him dead and vanished back into the water. Whatever really happened, the nobles were determined that none of his sons would follow him.

claims.text: Yazdegerd was killed by a magical horse that rose from a spring and vanished.
claims.note: Al-Tabari and the Shahnameh tell it. Many historians suspect the nobles had him murdered.

claims.text: The emperor Arcadius made Yazdegerd guardian of his little son Theodosius II.
claims.note: Procopius tells it over a century later. Earlier Roman writers say nothing about it.

claims.text: In 410 a council of bishops at Seleucia-Ctesiphon organised the Church of the East with the king's approval.
claims.note: The council's acts survive in the Syriac collection of the church's synods.

reigns.hook: Yazdegerd's son Shapur is king of Armenia. He races to Ctesiphon to claim his father's crown, straight into the arms of nobles who want none of the family.

reigns.tagline: King of Armenia, then king of kings for a few weeks
reigns.previously: Yazdegerd I dies, by a magic horse if you believe the priests.
paragraphs: Around 415 Yazdegerd I put his son Shapur on the throne of Armenia, the mountain kingdom Persia and Rome had split between them. The Persian half had lost its own king, and Yazdegerd wanted it in safe hands. Armenian writers remembered Shapur as an unwelcome outsider. He tried to win over the Armenian lords with hunts and feasts, and they stayed cool.

When news came in 420 that his father was dead, Shapur left Armenia and hurried to Ctesiphon to take the crown. He did not last. The great nobles had hated Yazdegerd and did not want any of his sons on the throne. Shapur was murdered soon after he arrived, and the throne was empty again.

claims.text: Shapur was murdered by the nobles at court soon after reaching Ctesiphon.
claims.note: Armenian historians and al-Tabari agree on the murder, but give few details and no exact date.

claims.text: Shapur reigned in Armenia from about 415 to 420.
claims.note: Armenian writers give these years. They are hard to square exactly with other sources.

reigns.hook: With Shapur dead, the nobles look past Yazdegerd's other sons and pick a distant royal cousin named Khosrow. But another son, Bahram, is coming with an Arab army.

reigns.tagline: The stand-in king who wouldn't fight the lions
reigns.previously: Shapur IV races home to claim the crown and is murdered.
paragraphs: The nobles who had hated Yazdegerd I wanted none of his sons. So they reached past them to a distant Sasanian, a man named Khosrow, and crowned him. It looked safe. But Yazdegerd had another son, Bahram, who had grown up at the court of the Arab kings of al-Hira on the edge of the desert. The Arab king al-Mundhir gave him an army, and Bahram marched on Ctesiphon.

The famous story of what happened next comes from al-Tabari and the Shahnameh. To avoid a war, Bahram offered a test. The crown would be laid between two hungry lions, and whoever took it would be king. Khosrow said the claimant should go first. Bahram walked in, killed both lions and put on the crown. Khosrow and the nobles accepted him. Nothing much is heard of Khosrow after that.

claims.text: The crown was placed between two lions, and Bahram killed them to take it.
claims.note: Al-Tabari and the Shahnameh tell it centuries later. It is a story about courage, not a record.

claims.text: The nobles passed over Yazdegerd's sons because they had hated their father.
claims.note: Al-Tabari says so plainly. The nobles' fear of Bahram's upbringing among the Arabs is part of his account.

reigns.hook: Bahram has the crown, a taste for the hunt and a heap of stories already gathering around him. Persia's poets are about to find their favourite king.

reigns.tagline: The hunter king the poets never forgot
reigns.cameToPower: Won the crown with an Arab army
reigns.previously: The nobles crown a distant cousin, Khosrow, to shut Bahram out.
paragraphs: Bahram was raised in the desert court of al-Hira, where the Arab kings taught him to ride, shoot and hunt. He loved hunting the onager, the wild ass, which in Persian is gur, and so he became Bahram Gur. He won his crown in 420 against the nobles' candidate Khosrow, with an Arab army behind him. A short war with Rome followed, ended by a peace in 422.

Then came real danger. Nomads from the east, Kidarites or early Hephthalites, broke into Khorasan. Bahram let them think he was off hunting, crept up with a small force and routed them. In 428 he ended the old royal line in Armenia and sent a Persian governor to rule it instead. At home, later writers said, he lightened taxes and brought musicians from India to entertain his people.

Above all, Bahram became a hero of story. Poets told of the harp girl Azadeh who rode on his camel, and Nizami's great poem The Seven Beauties is built around him. Around 438 he went hunting and never came back. The legend says he rode into a swamp or a deep pit and was swallowed up.

claims.text: Bahram had his harp girl Azadeh trampled under his camel when she mocked his archery.
claims.note: The Shahnameh tells it, and Sasanian-style plates and later bowls show the scene.

claims.text: Bahram brought thousands of musicians from India to play for the common people.
claims.note: The Shahnameh and other later writers tell it. Some link these musicians to the origin of the Roma, which is not proven.

claims.text: Bahram vanished into a swamp or pit while hunting.
claims.note: Al-Tabari and the Shahnameh give versions. The real cause of his death is unknown.

reigns.hook: Bahram's son Yazdegerd II inherits a kingdom at peace with Rome. He sets out to make sure every lord in it, including the Christians of Armenia, worships his way.

reigns.tagline: The king who fought Armenia's Christians at Avarayr
reigns.previously: Bahram Gur vanishes on a hunt, swallowed by a swamp or a pit.
paragraphs: Yazdegerd II began with a short war against Rome in 440, which ended quickly in a deal. His real worry lay east. The Kidarites, nomad lords in what is now Afghanistan, pressed on Khorasan, and Yazdegerd spent years campaigning against them from bases in the north-east, far from Ctesiphon.

He wanted his empire united behind one faith. In Armenia, Christian for well over a century, he ordered the nobles to accept Zoroastrianism. Many refused, and in 451 they took up arms under Vardan Mamikonian. At Avarayr the Persian army won and Vardan was killed, but the Armenians kept fighting a guerrilla war and kept their church. The Armenian Church still honours Vardan and his comrades as saints.

At home he leaned harder on Christians in Mesopotamia and, Jewish sources say, on Jews too. He died in 457. He left two grown sons, Hormizd and Peroz, and no settled rule on which of them should be king.

claims.text: Armenian rebels led by Vardan Mamikonian fought the Persians at Avarayr in 451, and Vardan was killed.
claims.note: The Armenian historians Elishe and Ghazar Parpetsi describe the battle and the rising in detail.

claims.text: Yazdegerd ordered the Armenian nobles to convert to Zoroastrianism.
claims.note: Elishe quotes his edict, but Elishe wrote as a passionate Christian partisan and may have shaped the text.

reigns.hook: Yazdegerd's sons Hormizd and Peroz both want the crown. Hormizd gets it first, but Peroz slips away east to find himself an army.

reigns.tagline: Two years on the throne, then his brother came
reigns.cameToPower: Took the throne on his father's death
reigns.previously: Yazdegerd II dies in 457, leaving two sons and one crown.
paragraphs: When Yazdegerd II died in 457, his son Hormizd was in the north at Ray and took the crown. In the capital, their mother Denag kept the government running for a while. Hormizd's brother Peroz did not accept him. He fled east and found allies among the Hephthalites, the White Huns, who were becoming the great power beyond the frontier.

Peroz also had the backing of a powerful noble, Raham of the House of Mihran. Their army came west in 459, beat Hormizd and captured him. Hormizd was put to death, and Peroz became king. The war between the brothers had invited the Hephthalites into Persian affairs, and they would not leave.

claims.text: Hormizd was the elder brother, and Peroz rebelled against the rightful heir.
claims.note: Sources disagree. Some say Yazdegerd preferred Peroz, others make Hormizd the older and favoured son.

claims.text: Queen Denag ruled from Ctesiphon while her sons fought.
claims.note: Al-Tabari says she governed for a time. Little else is known of her rule.

reigns.hook: Peroz has his brother's crown and owes the Hephthalites a debt. Soon he will be fighting them instead.

reigns.tagline: He kept going back to fight the Huns, once too often
reigns.previously: Peroz beats his brother Hormizd III with Hephthalite help.
paragraphs: Peroz began well. In the east he finished off the Kidarites and for a while struck his own coins at Balkh. Then a long drought struck Iran. Al-Tabari says it lasted seven years and that Peroz cut taxes and handed out grain so well that hardly anyone starved. Armenia and Georgia rose against him in the 480s and were not crushed.

His real enemy was the Hephthalites, who had helped him to his throne. He went to war with them and was captured, and he had to pay a huge ransom. His son Kavad stayed behind as a hostage until it was paid. Still Peroz went back. In 484 he marched east again against the Hephthalite king, and this time he and most of his army were killed, along with several of his sons.
Persia now had to pay tribute to the Huns. It was the worst defeat a Sasanian king had suffered.

claims.text: The Persian cavalry charged into a hidden trench the Hephthalites had dug and covered.
claims.note: Procopius tells it. He wrote decades later and had it from Persian informants.

claims.text: Before he fell, Peroz threw away his great pearl earring so no one else would wear it.
claims.note: Procopius tells it, with a fairy tale about how the pearl was first found.

claims.text: Peroz's young son Kavad was left with the Hephthalites as a hostage.
claims.note: Procopius and al-Tabari both say so, though details of when and how long vary.

reigns.hook: Peroz is dead and the Huns want tribute. His brother Balash takes the throne for four hard years, while Peroz's son Kavad waits among the Huns who raised him.

reigns.tagline: The mild king who was blinded
reigns.cameToPower: Chosen after Peroz died in battle
reigns.previously: Peroz I is killed by the Hephthalites.
paragraphs: Balash came to the throne after his brother Peroz was killed fighting the Hephthalites, leaving Iran paying them tribute. He made peace in Armenia by allowing Christians to practise freely.
With the treasury empty, he could not pay the army, and the Zoroastrian priests turned against him. In 488 the nobles deposed and blinded him and made his nephew Kavad king.
reigns.hook: Kavad I, Peroz's son, takes the throne.

reigns.tagline: The king who got out of jail in his wife's clothes
reigns.previously: Peroz falls to the White Huns. His brother Balash is deposed.
paragraphs: Kavad grew up as a hostage among the White Huns, and in 488, after his uncle Balash was thrown out and blinded, he took the throne with their help. The treasury was empty and the country was still reeling from famine. Kavad backed a radical preacher called Mazdak, who said the world's goods should be shared out. Poor people liked the idea. The great families and the priests did not.

In 496 they deposed him, gave the crown to his brother Jamasp and locked Kavad in the Castle of Oblivion, a prison so feared that, Procopius says, you weren't allowed to mention who was in it. His wife came to visit, swapped clothes with him, and he walked out. He fled to the Huns and came back with an army in 498 or 499. Jamasp stepped aside.

Kavad needed money to pay the Huns, so he went to war with Rome and took Amida in 503. Late in life he turned on the Mazdakites, and his son Khosrow led the slaughter. In 530 a young Roman general named Belisarius beat a Persian army at Dara. Kavad died in September 531, having picked Khosrow over his older sons.

claims.text: Kavad escaped prison by swapping clothes with his wife.
claims.note: Procopius tells it. Other sources say he escaped with help from friends.

claims.text: Mazdak preached that women, as well as property, should be shared.
claims.note: Only his enemies say so: Zoroastrian priests and later Muslim writers. No Mazdakite writings survive.

claims.text: Khosrow had the Mazdakites buried upside down, a garden of human trees.
claims.note: This grim scene comes from the Shahnameh, written about 500 years later.

reigns.hook: Rewind to 496. Kavad has backed Mazdak, a preacher who says wealth should be shared. The nobles and priests have had enough, and Kavad has a brother.

reigns.previously: Kavad I backs the Mazdakite reformers, and the nobles strike back.
paragraphs: When Kavad I supported Mazdak's movement, which preached sharing out wealth, the nobles and priests deposed and imprisoned him and crowned his brother Jamasp.
Kavad escaped to the Hephthalites and came back with an army in 498. Jamasp stepped down without a fight and was spared.

reigns.tagline: The model just king, who also sacked Antioch
reigns.previously: Kavad I dies, passing over his older sons for Khosrow.
paragraphs: Later Persians and Arabs remembered Khosrow as the perfect just king, Anushirvan, of the immortal soul. He began by clearing out rival brothers. In 532 he made an Eternal Peace with Justinian, and the Romans paid a fortune in gold for it. Eight years later he broke it, sacked Antioch and marched its people home. He built them a new city near Ctesiphon and called it Khosrow's Better Antioch.

At home he rebuilt the state. Land was surveyed and taxed at fixed rates, and cavalrymen got pay and kit from the crown, so the king leaned less on the great lords. Greek philosophers pushed out of Athens came to his court hoping for a philosopher king. They went home disappointed. Chess arrived from India, and the story goes that his vizier Bozorgmehr answered it by inventing backgammon.

Around 560 he joined forces with the Turks and destroyed the White Huns, who had killed his grandfather. About 570 he sent a force to Yemen and drove out its Ethiopian rulers. The great brick arch at Ctesiphon, the Taq Kasra, still carries his name. He died about 579, and the crown passed to his son Hormizd IV.

claims.text: Khosrow's vizier Bozorgmehr invented backgammon to answer India's gift of chess.
claims.note: A Middle Persian text and the Shahnameh tell it. Bozorgmehr himself may be legendary.

claims.text: The Taq Kasra, the great arch at Ctesiphon, was built by Khosrow I.
claims.note: Tradition says so, but some scholars date it to Shapur I, three centuries earlier.

claims.text: The Greek philosophers found his court a letdown and went home.
claims.note: Agathias, a Greek writer with little love for Khosrow, is the source.

reigns.hook: Hormizd IV falls out with the nobles, then insults Bahram Chobin, the general who has just saved his empire. A general with an army doesn't take insults quietly.

reigns.tagline: The king who humbled the nobles
reigns.previously: Khosrow I dies, the greatest of the Sasanians.
paragraphs: Hormizd IV protected the common people against the nobles and priests, and had many great nobles executed. His long war with Byzantium went badly.
When he insulted his best general, Bahram Chobin, Bahram rebelled. Palace nobles deposed and blinded Hormizd in 590 and soon killed him, crowning his son Khosrow II.
reigns.hook: Khosrow II is crowned, but Bahram Chobin is marching on the capital.

reigns.tagline: He came close to beating Rome, then lost it all
reigns.reignEnded: Overthrown and killed by his son
reigns.previously: Hormizd IV has fallen out with his nobles and his best general.
paragraphs: In 590 a palace coup tied to Khosrow's uncles blinded his father and then killed him. Khosrow got the crown but couldn't keep it. The general Bahram Chobin marched on Ctesiphon and made himself king, and Khosrow ran to the Roman emperor Maurice. In 591 he came back with a Roman army, beat Bahram and took his throne back.

Khosrow loved luxury. He and his black horse Shabdiz are carved in the rock grotto at Taq-e Bostan. Poets made a love story of his Christian wife Shirin and Farhad, the sculptor who cut through a mountain for her. When the usurper Phocas murdered Maurice in 602, Khosrow invaded Roman lands as the dead emperor's avenger, and kept going for twenty years.

His armies took Antioch in 613 and Jerusalem in 614, carrying off the True Cross. Egypt fell in 619. In 626 a Persian army camped across the water from Constantinople while the Avars attacked it. Then the emperor Heraclius struck deep into Iran, won at Nineveh in December 627 and sacked Khosrow's palace at Dastagird. In February 628 Khosrow's son Kavad II overthrew him, and he was killed days later.

claims.text: The sculptor Farhad carved through a mountain for love of Shirin.
claims.note: Shirin was real. Farhad's story grows in later poems, above all Nizami's Khosrow and Shirin (12th century).

claims.text: Khosrow tore up a letter from the Prophet Muhammad inviting him to Islam.
claims.note: Islamic tradition tells it. No Persian or Roman source of the time mentions the letter.

claims.text: The Taq-e Bostan carvings show Khosrow II on his horse Shabdiz.
claims.note: The great grotto is usually dated to his reign. A few scholars have argued for another king.

reigns.hook: Rewind to 590. Khosrow's throne is barely warm when Bahram Chobin takes Ctesiphon and crowns himself. The young shah runs to the Romans for help.

reigns.tagline: The general who took the crown
reigns.reignEnded: Beaten by Khosrow II and Byzantium
reigns.previously: Hormizd IV is dead, and his general wants the throne.
paragraphs: Bahram Chobin, a famous general from a great noble family, rebelled against Hormizd IV, took Ctesiphon and crowned himself as Bahram VI. The young Khosrow II fled to the Byzantines.
In 591 Khosrow returned with a Byzantine army and beat him. Bahram fled to the Turks and was murdered there; he became the hero of Persian legends.
reigns.hook: Back to 628: Khosrow has lost his war with Rome, and his own son Kavad leads the nobles against him. A beaten king has few friends.

reigns.tagline: He took his father's crown and lasted months
reigns.previously: Khosrow II has lost his war with Rome and his son turns on him.
paragraphs: Khosrow II's long war had ended in disaster, with the emperor Heraclius sacking his palace. In February 628 a group of nobles freed Kavad, known as Sheroe, from prison and made him king. Khosrow was caught, held for a few days and then killed. Kavad wanted no rivals, so he had his brothers killed too, including Mardanshah, the son Khosrow had wanted as his heir.

Then he made peace. Kavad wrote to Heraclius, agreed to give back Roman lands and prisoners, and pulled Persia out of a war it could no longer fight. But a terrible plague swept through Mesopotamia that year, killing huge numbers in the capital region. Later writers called it the plague of Sheroe. By the autumn of 628 it had killed Kavad too, after about seven months as king.

claims.text: Kavad had seventeen or eighteen of his brothers killed.
claims.note: Later sources give these numbers. That he wiped out his brothers is widely reported.

claims.text: Shirin, Khosrow's widow, killed herself on her husband's tomb rather than marry Kavad.
claims.note: This comes from the Shahnameh and later romance. Earlier sources do not tell it.

claims.text: Kavad died of the plague.
claims.note: Most sources say so. A few hint at other causes, and the exact month is uncertain.

reigns.hook: Kavad's heir is a boy of about seven, Ardashir. Out west sits Khosrow's greatest general, Shahrbaraz, with an army and Roman friends.

reigns.tagline: A seven-year-old king in a city full of wolves
reigns.previously: Kavad II dies of plague after a few months on the throne.
paragraphs: Ardashir III was about seven when his father died, and the real power lay with his guardian, the steward Mah-Adur Gushnasp. The court was split between noble factions. The plague was still about, and the empire had just lost a long war. The one man with a strong army was the general Shahrbaraz, who had not been asked his opinion about the new king.

Shahrbaraz did a deal with his old enemy Heraclius in 629. He would pull his troops out of Roman lands, and the Romans would back his bid for power. Then he marched on Ctesiphon. The city fell to him, and on 27 April 630 the boy king was killed on his orders, along with his guardian and leading nobles.

claims.text: Shahrbaraz agreed his bid for the throne with Heraclius in 629.
claims.note: Roman and Armenian sources record their meeting at Arabissos in July 629. What exactly was promised is less clear.

claims.text: Ardashir was about seven years old when he became king.
claims.note: Al-Tabari gives his age. Other sources do not, and his birth date is only an estimate.

reigns.hook: For the first time in four centuries, a man with no royal blood sits on the Sasanian throne. The nobles give him about forty days.

reigns.tagline: The great general who grabbed the crown for forty days
reigns.reignEnded: Killed by nobles after forty days
reigns.previously: Shahrbaraz has the boy king Ardashir III killed in April 630.
paragraphs: Shahrbaraz, the Boar of the Empire, was Khosrow II's star general. His troops took Jerusalem in 614 and Egypt soon after. In 626 he camped across the water from Constantinople while the Avars besieged the city. But Khosrow grew to distrust him, and by the late 620s Shahrbaraz sat in Syria with his army, keeping out of the war Heraclius was winning.

In 629 he and Heraclius came to terms. Persian troops left Roman lands, and in March 630 the True Cross was back in Jerusalem. Shahrbaraz then marched on Ctesiphon, killed the boy king Ardashir III and took the crown himself. No one outside the royal family had done that since the dynasty began. On 9 June 630, after about forty days, nobles killed him during a parade, and his body was dragged through the streets.

claims.text: Khosrow sent orders to kill Shahrbaraz, and Heraclius intercepted them and showed them to the general.
claims.note: Later Byzantine and Arab writers tell versions of this. It may explain his switch rather than record it.

claims.text: Shahrbaraz returned the True Cross to Heraclius.
claims.note: The Cross did return to Jerusalem in 630, but sources differ on how and when he handed it over.

claims.text: Nobles killed him during a public parade.
claims.note: Al-Tabari gives the details. Other sources, including the Armenian Sebeos, agree he was murdered.

reigns.hook: The nobles need a royal to crown, and few are left. They turn to Khosrow II's daughter Boran, the first woman to rule Iran in her own right.

reigns.tagline: The first woman to rule Iran in her own right
reigns.previously: Shahrbaraz, the usurping general, is killed after about forty days.
paragraphs: With the men of the royal house dead or murdered, the great families turned to Khosrow II's daughter Boran. Her backer was Farrukh Hormizd, a warlord of the Parthian clans from Khorasan. No woman had ever ruled Iran in her own name. Boran did it with confidence, striking silver coins that showed her own crowned face.

She wanted calm above all. She sent the head of the Church of the East, Ishoyahb II, to the emperor Heraclius to settle the peace. Al-Tabari says she cut taxes and promised to rule with justice. But the court was split between the Parthian clans and the Persian nobles of the south-west, and in 630 or 631 the Persian side pushed her aside for rival rulers.

Farrukh Hormizd's son Rostam brought her back in 631, with himself as the real power behind the throne. A year later she was dead. Some said she was strangled, others that she simply died. Other names flicker through these months too, such as Khosrow III in Khorasan and Farrukhzad Khosrow, each gone almost as soon as he appeared.

claims.text: Boran was the first woman to rule Iran in her own right, and her coins show her portrait.
claims.note: Her silver drachms survive in museum collections, with her name and a crowned female bust.

claims.text: Boran sent the Catholicos Ishoyahb II to Heraclius to make peace.
claims.note: Syriac Christian chronicles record the embassy. What exactly was agreed is less clear.

claims.text: Boran was strangled.
claims.note: Some later Persian and Arab accounts say so, naming different killers. Others record only her death.

reigns.hook: Boran's first fall leaves the throne empty for anyone with soldiers. First in line is Shapur, son of the dead usurper Shahrbaraz and a nephew of Khosrow II.

reigns.tagline: The usurper's son who thought royal blood was enough
reigns.previously: Boran is pushed aside by the Persian nobles of the south-west.
paragraphs: Shapur had a claim of sorts. His father was Shahrbaraz, the general who had murdered the boy king Ardashir III and sat on the throne for forty days. His mother was a sister of Khosrow II, so he had royal blood on one side at least. In the chaos of 630 that was enough to get him crowned for a moment.

It was not enough to keep the crown. The powerful Persian faction of the south-west, led by Piruz Khosrow, would not accept the son of a usurper. They threw him out within weeks, or perhaps months. After that Shapur drops out of the record. Nobody knows what happened to him.

claims.text: Shapur V was the son of Shahrbaraz and a sister of Khosrow II.
claims.note: Al-Tabari and other Arab historians give his parents; modern historians accept it.

claims.text: Shapur V ruled between Boran's two reigns.
claims.note: The order of the kings of 630 to 632 is a puzzle. Different sources line them up differently, and coins only help a little.

reigns.hook: The nobles want someone of pure Sasanian blood. They dig out Peroz, a distant cousin who descends from the great Khosrow I through his mother.

reigns.tagline: He complained the crown was too tight. It was fatal
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Distant cousin of the royal line
reigns.cameToPower: Picked by nobles for his bloodline
reigns.previously: Shapur V, the usurper's son, is thrown out by the Persian nobles.
paragraphs: By 630 the royal family had been hacked down to almost nothing, so the nobles went looking for any prince with the right blood. They found Peroz, a great-great-grandson of Khosrow I through his mother. He seems to have been crowned in the same feverish year as Boran, Shapur V and Azarmidokht.

Al-Tabari tells a grim little story. When the crown was set on his head, Peroz said it felt tight. The nobles took this as a terrible omen and killed him on the spot. Whether or not that is how it went, Peroz did not last. He left almost no trace except the story and a name on the king lists.

claims.text: Peroz was killed because he said his crown was too tight.
claims.note: Al-Tabari tells it, writing nearly 300 years later. It reads like a moral tale about an unlucky king.

claims.text: The dates and order of Peroz II's reign are uncertain.
claims.note: Some lists put him in 630, others later. No coins can be pinned on him with certainty.

reigns.hook: The crown goes back to Khosrow II's own family: his daughter Azarmidokht, Boran's sister. The most powerful general in Iran has his eye on her.

reigns.tagline: The queen who said no to a warlord, and paid for it
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Sister of Boran, daughter of Khosrow II
reigns.previously: Peroz II is killed by the nobles who crowned him.
paragraphs: Azarmidokht was Khosrow II's daughter and Boran's sister, and she was the Persian faction's choice. That put her up against Farrukh Hormizd, the Parthian warlord who had backed Boran. He came to court and asked to marry her, which would have made him master of Iran. A queen does not marry, she is said to have replied.

The story goes on that she invited him to come to her by night, then had him killed by a guard waiting in the dark. It was a bold move and a deadly one. Farrukh Hormizd's son Rostam, commander in Khorasan, marched on Ctesiphon to avenge him. He took the capital, had Azarmidokht blinded and killed, and put Boran back on the throne.

claims.text: Azarmidokht had Farrukh Hormizd murdered when he asked to marry her.
claims.note: Al-Tabari and the Shahnameh tell it with dramatic details. Historians accept the killing but not every line of the story.

claims.text: Rostam Farrokhzad blinded and killed her to avenge his father.
claims.note: Later Arab and Persian histories say so. No source from the time survives.

claims.text: Coins were struck in Azarmidokht's name.
claims.note: Silver drachms with her name are known, though which coins are hers has been argued over.

reigns.hook: Boran is back, with Rostam behind her. But another king's coins are turning up in these same months, struck for a Hormizd.

reigns.tagline: A king known almost only from his coins
reigns.relationToPredecessor: A rival of Khosrow II's daughters
reigns.cameToPower: Struck coins as a rival king
reigns.previously: Rostam kills Azarmidokht and brings Boran back to the throne.
paragraphs: For about two years, from 630 to 632, silver coins were struck for a king called Hormizd. They are real, so somebody with mints and soldiers was calling himself King of Kings while Boran and her sister ruled at Ctesiphon. But the histories barely mention him, and nobody is sure who he was.

One modern theory says he was Farrukh Hormizd himself, the Parthian warlord who backed Boran and then wooed Azarmidokht. Others make him a minor prince of the royal house whose base is unknown. Either way he shows how far the empire had split. By 632 three or four men and women could claim the crown at once, and Arab raiders were already testing the Iraq frontier.

claims.text: Coins in the name of a King Hormizd were struck from about 630 to 632.
claims.note: The coins survive and are dated by the regnal years on them.

claims.text: Hormizd VI and the warlord Farrukh Hormizd were the same man.
claims.note: Proposed by Parvaneh Pourshariati from the coins and the timing. Other scholars are not convinced.

reigns.hook: Boran dies, rival kings fall, and the nobles finally agree on someone: Yazdegerd, a boy grandson of Khosrow II, found at Istakhr.

reigns.tagline: The last King of Kings, running for his life
reigns.previously: Boran is dead, rival kings fall, and the nobles find a boy king.
paragraphs: Yazdegerd was a boy, and his generals ran the war. It came fast. The caliph Umar sent Arab armies into Iraq, and at al-Qadisiyyah, in 636 or 637, the Persian commander Rostam Farrokhzad was killed and the royal banner was captured. Ctesiphon fell soon after. The Arabs found a vast garden carpet woven with gold and jewels, the Spring of Khosrow, and cut it up to share out.

Yazdegerd fled up onto the Iranian plateau. A last big army gathered at Nahavand in 642, and the Arabs called their win there the victory of victories. After that Persia had no field army left. The king moved from city to city, always further east, with a shrinking court and a dwindling treasure.

In 651 he reached Merv, where the local governor turned against him. The best-known story says he hid in a mill and the miller killed him for his fine clothes. His son Peroz fled all the way to Tang China and asked the emperor for help. It never came. More than four centuries of Sasanian rule were over.

claims.text: Yazdegerd was killed by a miller who wanted his rich clothes.
claims.note: Al-Tabari gives this and other versions. Some blame the governor of Merv.

claims.text: The Arabs cut up the jewelled Spring of Khosrow carpet and shared out the pieces.
claims.note: Al-Tabari describes it. The size and splendour may have grown in the telling.

claims.text: Yazdegerd's son Peroz asked the Tang emperor for help.
claims.note: Chinese records note his embassies and his stay at the Tang court.

reigns.hook: Iran now belongs to the caliphs in Medina. Within ten years the caliphate itself splits, and a family based in Damascus takes it over.

reigns.title: Under the Caliphs
reigns.tagline: Iran gets new masters, and a new faith, slowly
reigns.reignEnded: Umayyads beaten on the Great Zab
reigns.previously: Yazdegerd III, last of the Sasanians, is murdered near Merv.
paragraphs: Iran was now a province of someone else's empire, ruled from Medina and then, from 661, by the Umayyad caliphs in Damascus. Zoroastrians kept their fire temples but paid the jizya, a tax on protected non-Muslims. Most Iranians stayed Zoroastrian for generations. Some left. One group sailed to Gujarat in India, and their descendants are the Parsis.

Converts found that Islam came with fine print. Persian Muslims, called mawali, were often treated as second class by their Arab masters. Around 700 the tax offices switched from Persian to Arabic. Far to the west, in 680, the Prophet's grandson Husayn was killed at Karbala, a death Shi'a Muslims still mourn every year. Iran would one day become the great Shi'a land, but not for eight centuries.

Anger boiled over in Khorasan, in the north-east. In 747 a shadowy organiser called Abu Muslim raised black banners there for the Abbasids, a family descended from the Prophet's uncle. Khorasani armies swept west, and in January 750 they smashed the last Umayyad caliph's army on the Great Zab river in Iraq.

claims.text: Zoroastrian refugees landed in Gujarat and were let in on conditions set by a local Hindu king.
claims.note: The tale comes from the Qissa-i Sanjan, written around 1600, long after the events.

claims.text: Most Iranians converted to Islam only in the 9th and 10th centuries.
claims.note: Richard Bulliet argued this from Muslim name lists. Other historians question his method.

claims.text: The tax offices in Iran switched from Persian to Arabic around 700.
claims.note: Arab historians tie the change to the governor al-Hajjaj. The year varies by province.

reigns.hook: The Abbasids have won with Persian swords. Now Abu Muslim, the man who won it for them, looks a little too powerful.

reigns.title: Persians at the Caliph's Court
reigns.tagline: The caliphs move east and start to rule like shahs
reigns.previously: The Umayyads are beaten on the Great Zab. The Abbasids take over.
paragraphs: The new caliphs owed everything to Khorasan, and they didn't trust it. In 755 the caliph al-Mansur summoned Abu Muslim and had him cut down. Then he built a new capital. Baghdad, founded in 762, rose on the Tigris not far from the ruins of Ctesiphon, and its court soon looked a lot like a Sasanian one, full of ceremony, viziers and Persian officials.

The greatest of those officials were the Barmakids, a family from Balkh whose ancestors had run a Buddhist monastery. They ran the empire for Harun al-Rashid, the caliph of the Thousand and One Nights. In 803 Harun turned on them overnight. The vizier Ja'far was beheaded and the rest were locked up. Nobody is quite sure why. Harun died at Tus in Khorasan in 809.

His sons fought over the throne. Al-Ma'mun, whose mother was Persian, ruled from Merv, and his general Tahir beat his brother's army and took Baghdad in 813. Al-Ma'mun named the Shi'a Imam Ali al-Rida his heir, but the Imam died suddenly at Tus in 818. His tomb grew into the holy city of Mashhad. In 821 Tahir became governor of Khorasan, and his family held on to it like a crown.

claims.text: Al-Mansur had Abu Muslim murdered in 755.
claims.note: All the main Arabic histories, al-Tabari's included, describe the killing.

claims.text: Harun destroyed the Barmakids because Ja'far secretly married Harun's sister Abbasa.
claims.note: One of several explanations in al-Tabari and later writers. Historians suspect plain fear of their power.

claims.text: Imam Ali al-Rida was poisoned on al-Ma'mun's orders.
claims.note: Shi'a tradition says so. Sunni sources say he died of illness, some say from eating grapes.

reigns.hook: Tahir's family rule Khorasan as kings in all but name. Others will soon go further, and Persian will become a language of poetry again.

reigns.title: Persian Revival
reigns.tagline: The caliph's grip slips, and Persian finds its voice again
reigns.previously: Tahir gets Khorasan, and his family keep it like a kingdom.
paragraphs: On paper the caliph in Baghdad still ruled Iran. In practice it was slipping away, province by province. Tahir's family ran Khorasan. In Sistan a tough upstart called Ya'qub ibn al-Layth, nicknamed the Coppersmith, carved out a kingdom with his sword and marched to within striking distance of Baghdad. Then the Samanids, ruling from Bukhara, built the brightest court in the east.

Under the Samanids something huge happened. Persian came back as a written language, now in Arabic letters, and poets like Rudaki wrote verse in it. In the west the Buyids, Shi'a soldiers from the mountains of Daylam, took Baghdad itself in 945 and kept the caliph as a figurehead. In the east the Turkish sultan Mahmud of Ghazni got rich raiding India.

It was an age of genius. Ferdowsi finished the Shahnameh, the giant epic of Iran's kings and heroes, around 1010. Avicenna wrote his Canon of Medicine, which doctors used for centuries. But on the steppe a new Turkish clan was on the move. In 1040 the Seljuks beat Mahmud's son Mas'ud at Dandanaqan, and Khorasan was theirs.

claims.text: Mahmud promised Ferdowsi gold for the Shahnameh, paid him in silver, and the insulted poet gave the money away.
claims.note: First told by Nizami Aruzi more than a century later, who says Ferdowsi split the silver between a bath attendant and a drinks seller.

claims.text: Ya'qub ibn al-Layth started out as a coppersmith.
claims.note: His nickname al-Saffar means coppersmith, and Arab historians say he worked the trade as a young man. Little else is known of his early life.

claims.text: The Samanid court made Persian a language of books again.
claims.note: Rudaki's surviving poems and the Persian version of al-Tabari's history made for a Samanid vizier, Bal'ami, are early proof.

reigns.hook: On the steppe a new Turkish clan is on the move. Its chief, Tughril Beg, has just crushed the Ghaznavids at Dandanaqan, and he has his eye on Baghdad.

reigns.tagline: The nomad chief the caliph crowned sultan
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Grandson of the clan founder Seljuk
reigns.previously: Mahmud of Ghazni's son Mas'ud is routed by the Seljuks at Dandanaqan.
paragraphs: Tughril and his brother Chaghri led Turkmen herders who had drifted south from the steppe looking for grazing. In 1040, at Dandanaqan in the desert near Merv, they smashed the Ghaznavid army of Mas'ud. Khorasan was theirs. Chaghri stayed to hold the east, and Tughril rode west, taking Rey and then Isfahan.

In 1055 he entered Baghdad and pushed out the Shi'a Buyids. The grateful Abbasid caliph al-Qa'im named him sultan, the protector of Sunni Islam. A Turkish general, al-Basasiri, rose against him and had the Friday prayer said for the rival Fatimid caliph of Cairo. Tughril came back, restored al-Qa'im and had al-Basasiri hunted down and killed in 1060.
He even forced the reluctant caliph to give him a daughter in marriage. But Tughril had no son. He died at Rey in September 1063, at about 70, master of an empire from Khorasan to Iraq.

claims.text: The caliph al-Qa'im named Tughril sultan and King of East and West.
claims.note: Arab chroniclers record the ceremony in Baghdad. Tughril's coins also use grand royal titles.

claims.text: Tughril forced the caliph to give him his daughter in marriage.
claims.note: Ibn al-Athir and others describe the caliph's long resistance. The marriage happened late in 1062 or in 1063, months before Tughril died.

claims.text: The tower at Rey called the Toghrol Tower is Tughril's tomb.
claims.note: Local tradition says so, but the tower is usually dated to the next century.

reigns.hook: Tughril has no son. His vizier crowns one nephew, but another nephew, Chaghri's son Alp Arslan, has the bigger army.

reigns.tagline: The lion who caught an emperor at Manzikert
reigns.previously: Tughril Beg dies at Rey with no son to follow him.
paragraphs: His name meant heroic lion, and he lived up to it. Alp Arslan, son of Chaghri, beat his brother Suleiman, crowned by Tughril's vizier, and his cousin Kutalmish to take the whole empire. His vizier was a brilliant Persian, Nizam al-Mulk, who ran the government while the sultan went to war. In 1064 he stormed Ani, the Armenian capital, a famous prize.

In August 1071 a big Byzantine army under the emperor Romanos IV met him at Manzikert, north of Lake Van. Part of the Byzantine force melted away, and Romanos was captured. Alp Arslan treated him well and let him go for a ransom and a treaty. Turkish bands soon poured into Anatolia.

The sultan died in a stupid way. On campaign beyond the Oxus in 1072, he had a captured fortress commander brought before him. The man drew a knife and lunged. Alp Arslan, sure of his bow, waved the guards back, missed his shot and was stabbed. He died days later.

claims.text: Romanos IV told Alp Arslan he would have whipped him had he won, and the sultan let him go anyway.
claims.note: A famous exchange in Ibn al-Athir and other later chroniclers. It may be polished, but the gentle treatment is real.

claims.text: Alp Arslan was stabbed by a captured commander after waving his guards away.
claims.note: Several chroniclers tell it in much the same way, though they differ on names and details.

reigns.hook: The dying sultan names his teenage son Malik-Shah. Before the boy can rule, he must deal with an uncle who thinks the throne should be his.

reigns.tagline: The golden age sultan whose vizier ran everything
reigns.cameToPower: Named heir by his dying father
reigns.reignEnded: Died in Baghdad weeks after Nizam
reigns.previously: Alp Arslan is stabbed by a prisoner and names Malik-Shah his heir.
paragraphs: Malik-Shah was about 17. His uncle Qavurt, ruler of Kerman, came for the throne, and was beaten and strangled with a bowstring. After that the young sultan left most of the work to his father's vizier, Nizam al-Mulk. Nizam ran the treasury, the army payroll and a chain of colleges, the Nizamiyyas, and wrote a book on how kings should rule.

The court settled at Isfahan, where the two great domes of the Friday Mosque went up. In 1079 astronomers including Omar Khayyam made a new solar calendar, the Jalali, named for the sultan. Iran's calendar today descends from it. Malik-Shah's armies reached from Syria to Samarkand, the biggest the Seljuk empire ever got.

Then it went wrong. In 1090 Hasan-i Sabbah took the castle of Alamut. Sultan and vizier fell out. In October 1092 Nizam al-Mulk was stabbed, by a killer dressed as a Sufi. Weeks later, on 19 November, Malik-Shah died in Baghdad at about 37.

claims.text: Omar Khayyam was one of the astronomers on Malik-Shah's calendar reform.
claims.note: Medieval writers name him among the team. The Jalali calendar dates from 1079.

claims.text: Malik-Shah was poisoned.
claims.note: Rumour said so at once, pointing at the caliph or at Nizam's people. Chroniclers also say he fell ill after hunting.

claims.text: Nizam al-Mulk was murdered by the Assassins.
claims.note: His killer was said to be an Ismaili, and the Ismailis later claimed it. Some suspect rivals at court.

reigns.hook: Malik-Shah is dead with no named heir. His widow Terken Khatun moves first, and her candidate is four years old.

reigns.tagline: A four-year-old sultan and his formidable mother
reigns.previously: Malik-Shah dies in Baghdad weeks after Nizam al-Mulk is murdered.
paragraphs: The real ruler was his mother, Terken Khatun, a Qarakhanid princess with money, troops and a plan. She kept Malik-Shah's death quiet long enough to get her little son proclaimed in Baghdad, leaning hard on the caliph to agree. Her ally was the vizier Taj al-Mulk, Nizam al-Mulk's great rival.

Nizam's people, the officers and slave soldiers he had trained, would not have it. They backed Malik-Shah's eldest son, Barkiyaruq, a boy of 12 or 13. Terken's army lost to them near Borujerd early in 1093, and Taj al-Mulk was caught and killed by Nizam's men. Terken held on in Isfahan, bargaining with anyone who might help.
It ended in 1094. Terken died, and little Mahmud died too, of smallpox or by murder. While the princes fought, the governors began to run their own provinces.

claims.text: Terken Khatun hid Malik-Shah's death to win the throne for her son.
claims.note: The chroniclers describe her keeping the news quiet and pushing the caliph to accept Mahmud.

claims.text: Mahmud died of smallpox.
claims.note: Some chroniclers say so. With a rival waiting and his protectors gone, others suspected murder.

reigns.hook: With Mahmud dead, Barkiyaruq has the throne alone. But two uncles and a half-brother are already sharpening their swords.

reigns.tagline: A boy sultan who spent his whole reign at war
reigns.previously: Malik-Shah dies with no heir named, and his sons' backers draw swords.
paragraphs: Barkiyaruq never got a quiet year. He was about 13 when Nizam al-Mulk's people made him sultan against his little half-brother Mahmud. Then his uncle Tutush came out of Syria to take the throne. In 1095 Barkiyaruq beat him near Rey, and Tutush was killed in the battle.

From 1098 his half-brother Muhammad Tapar rose against him, backed by their brother Sanjar in Khorasan. They fought five battles. Cities changed hands, viziers were killed, and Baghdad's Friday prayer flipped from one name to the other. In 1104 the brothers agreed to share the empire out.
All this time the Seljuks were too busy fighting each other to look west. Crusaders took Antioch in 1098 and Jerusalem in 1099. Barkiyaruq fell ill and died at about 25, leaving a small son.

claims.text: The First Crusade took Antioch and Jerusalem while the Seljuk princes fought each other.
claims.note: Both cities fell in 1098 and 1099, and no Great Seljuk army came. Historians link the two.

claims.text: Barkiyaruq and Muhammad Tapar fought five battles.
claims.note: Ibn al-Athir and other chroniclers list them, with the cities each one won or lost.

reigns.hook: Barkiyaruq's men proclaim his small son Malik-Shah as sultan in Baghdad. Uncle Muhammad Tapar is on his way.
