reigns.tagline: A boy sultan for a few months
reigns.previously: Barkiyaruq dies young, leaving a small son and an ambitious brother.
paragraphs: Malik-Shah II was a small boy when his father died. Barkiyaruq's commander, the emir Ayaz, had him proclaimed sultan in Baghdad, and for a few weeks the Friday prayer was said in his name. But the 1104 deal had given half the empire to his uncle Muhammad Tapar, and Muhammad wanted all of it.

Muhammad marched on Baghdad. Ayaz chose to make terms, and was murdered soon after on Muhammad's orders. The boy sultan was simply set aside, and Muhammad was sole ruler of the western lands. What happened to Malik-Shah II afterwards is unclear. Some say he was blinded, which would bar him from the throne for ever.

claims.text: Malik-Shah II was blinded by his uncle.
claims.note: Some later accounts say so. The chronicles are thin on what happened to the boy.

claims.text: Muhammad Tapar had the emir Ayaz killed after Ayaz had submitted to him.
claims.note: Ibn al-Athir reports the killing, soon after the boy was set aside.

reigns.hook: Muhammad Tapar is sole sultan in the west at last. His first target is a nest of Assassins on a mountain right above his capital, Isfahan.

reigns.tagline: The brother who won the civil war and hunted the Assassins
reigns.previously: Muhammad Tapar shoves aside his baby nephew Malik-Shah II.
paragraphs: Muhammad was a younger son of Malik-Shah, and he spent his twenties fighting his half-brother Barkiyaruq for the empire. They clashed again and again until, in 1104, a sick and weary Barkiyaruq agreed to split it. Within months Barkiyaruq was dead. His little son was proclaimed in Baghdad, but Muhammad brushed the boy aside and took the lot.

He set out to finish the Ismailis, the sect the Seljuks called the Assassins. In 1107 his army took Shahdiz, their fortress on a hill right above his capital, Isfahan. In Iraq he crushed the Arab prince Sadaqa, and he sent armies west against the crusaders. Year after year his men besieged Alamut, the Assassins' eagle's nest in the mountains.

He never got to see it fall. In April 1118 Muhammad died at Isfahan, still in his thirties. The army camped below Alamut packed up and went home when the news came. His full brother Sanjar, ruler of Khorasan for twenty years, was now the senior Seljuk.

claims.text: When Shahdiz fell, its commander Ahmad ibn Attash was paraded through Isfahan and put to death.
claims.note: Ibn al-Athir and other chroniclers tell it, and some say he was flayed. Ismaili sources give their own version.

claims.text: The army besieging Alamut gave up as soon as it heard Muhammad was dead.
claims.note: The Seljuk chroniclers and later Ismaili histories agree the siege collapsed in 1118.

reigns.hook: Muhammad's son Mahmud is only 14. In the east sits his uncle Sanjar, with an army, war elephants and very firm ideas about who the real sultan is.

reigns.tagline: Forty years as top sultan, then three as a nomad's prisoner
reigns.cameToPower: Senior sultan on his brother's death
reigns.previously: Muhammad Tapar dies at Isfahan, and the siege of Alamut falls apart.
paragraphs: Sanjar had run Khorasan from Merv since he was a boy, and when his brother died he decided he outranked everyone. In 1119 he marched west and beat his nephew Mahmud at Saveh, helped by a charge of war elephants. Mahmud kept western Iran as his junior partner. For decades the sultans of the west came and went, while Sanjar sat at Merv as head of the family.

His court was famous, full of poets and scholars. But in 1141 a new power came out of the east: the Qara Khitai, refugees from northern China. On the steppe of Qatwan near Samarkand they destroyed his army. Sanjar escaped with a handful of men, but his wife was captured and Transoxiana was lost for good.

Worse came in 1153. Oghuz nomads, angry about taxes, beat him in battle and took him prisoner. They looted Merv and Nishapur and kept the old sultan with them for about three years. He finally got away in 1156, a broken man, and died at Merv the next spring. His great domed tomb still stands there.

claims.text: News of Qatwan reached Europe and helped start the legend of Prester John, a Christian king in the east.
claims.note: Otto of Freising wrote in 1145 that a priest-king John had beaten the Persian kings. Many historians link this to Qatwan.

claims.text: The Oghuz set Sanjar on his throne by day and shut him in a cage at night.
claims.note: A story told by medieval chroniclers. Accounts of how he was treated in captivity differ.

claims.text: Sanjar lost the Battle of Qatwan in September 1141.
claims.note: Muslim chroniclers and Chinese sources both record the Qara Khitai victory.

reigns.hook: Rewind to 1118. While Sanjar ruled from Merv, the west needed a sultan of its own: Muhammad's son Mahmud, aged 14. He was about to find out who was boss.

reigns.tagline: A teenage sultan beaten by his uncle's war elephants
reigns.previously: Sanjar rules the east for 39 years. Back to 1118 in the west.
paragraphs: Mahmud was 14 when his father died, and his officers ran the government for him. His uncle Sanjar sent a list of demands. In 1119 the two armies met at Saveh. Mahmud's side was bigger, but Sanjar's war elephants terrified his horses and he lost. Sanjar made him his junior partner and heir, and gave him a daughter as his bride.

Mahmud ruled western Iran and Iraq from Isfahan and Hamadan. His brother Mas'ud rebelled and was forgiven. The caliph al-Mustarshid in Baghdad wanted his own army, so Mahmud marched on Baghdad in 1126 and made him back down. He made a hard Turkish emir named Zengi governor of Mosul, a choice that would matter to the crusaders.
He did not live long. Mahmud died in 1131, still in his twenties. He left several young sons, three ambitious brothers and an uncle in Merv who meant to choose the next sultan himself.

claims.text: Sanjar's war elephants won the Battle of Saveh.
claims.note: The Seljuk chroniclers say the elephants panicked Mahmud's cavalry. Historians accept it, though numbers are uncertain.

claims.text: Mahmud's men had the emir al-Bursuqi of Mosul murdered by Assassins in 1126.
claims.note: Assassins killed al-Bursuqi in a mosque at Mosul. Some chroniclers say the sultan was behind it; nothing proves it.

reigns.hook: Mahmud's son Dawud is proclaimed sultan at Hamadan. But two of Mahmud's brothers want the throne, and Sanjar is already marching west.

reigns.tagline: The boy sultan pushed aside by two uncles
reigns.previously: Mahmud II dies in his twenties, leaving a family fight.
paragraphs: When Mahmud died, his vizier and emirs proclaimed his son Dawud sultan at Hamadan. They did not ask Sanjar. Two of Dawud's uncles, Mas'ud and Tughril, also wanted the crown, and Sanjar favoured Tughril, who had been living at his court.

In 1132 Sanjar came west with his army and beat Mas'ud's side near Dinavar. He made Tughril sultan and went home. Tughril then beat Dawud too, and the young man's reign was over almost before it began. He kept a power base in Azerbaijan, around Tabriz, and for years he stayed in the game, backing whoever offered him the most.
In 1143 Dawud was murdered at Tabriz. The killers were said to be Assassins, and rumour named the man who sent them.

claims.text: Dawud was killed by Assassins sent by Zengi, the lord of Mosul.
claims.note: Ibn al-Athir reports the rumour that Zengi was behind it. Zengi denied it, and nobody proved it either way.

reigns.hook: Tughril II has his uncle's blessing and the crown. But Sanjar has gone home to Khorasan, and Mas'ud is still out there with an army.

reigns.tagline: Sanjar's favourite nephew, sultan for a couple of years
reigns.reignEnded: Fell ill and died at Hamadan
reigns.previously: Dawud is proclaimed sultan, but his uncles want the throne.
paragraphs: Tughril was a son of Muhammad Tapar who had fallen out with his brother Mahmud and found shelter with Sanjar. In 1132 his uncle brought him west at the head of an army, beat his rivals near Dinavar and put him on the throne at Hamadan.

Then Sanjar had to rush back east to deal with trouble from the Khwarazmshah, and Tughril was on his own. His brother Mas'ud beat him in 1133 and took Hamadan. Tughril spent the winter as a refugee with a local prince in Mazandaran, by the Caspian. In 1134 he came back, retook Hamadan, fell ill and died there that autumn.
He left a widow and a small son, Arslan. Mas'ud married the widow to one of his Turkish officers, Eldiguz. Nobody could have guessed what that marriage would lead to.

claims.text: Tughril II died of illness at Hamadan just after retaking it in 1134.
claims.note: Chroniclers agree he fell sick on his return. The exact date is given as October or November 1134.

claims.text: Tughril's widow was married off to the emir Eldiguz, who later ruled in her son's name.
claims.note: Ibn al-Athir and the Seljuk histories record the marriage. Eldiguz became the power behind her son's throne.

reigns.hook: Mas'ud is finally sultan of the west. His next problem is the caliph in Baghdad, who has raised an army of his own.

reigns.tagline: He captured a caliph, then Assassins killed his prisoner
reigns.previously: Tughril II retakes Hamadan and dies there of illness.
paragraphs: Mas'ud was the toughest of Muhammad Tapar's sons. He had first rebelled against his brother Mahmud at about 12. He took Hamadan in 1133, and after Tughril's death he was sultan of the west. His big problem was the caliph al-Mustarshid, who wanted to rule Iraq himself and had raised his own army.

In June 1135 the two sides met at Daymarg near Hamadan. The caliph's troops deserted, and Mas'ud took him prisoner. Weeks later a band of Assassins got into the camp and murdered al-Mustarshid in his tent. The next caliph, al-Rashid, fought too, so in 1136 Mas'ud took Baghdad and had him deposed.

Yet Mas'ud never fully ruled his own lands. Big emirs called atabegs held whole provinces and fought him when they liked. He beat a coalition of them in 1147 and survived another. He died at Hamadan in 1152, the last strong Seljuk sultan in the west.

claims.text: Mas'ud or Sanjar sent the Assassins who killed the captive caliph.
claims.note: Some chroniclers accused the sultans, since the murder happened in Mas'ud's camp. Others blame the Ismailis alone.

claims.text: Mas'ud captured the caliph al-Mustarshid at Daymarg in 1135.
claims.note: Recorded by Ibn al-Athir and the Seljuk chroniclers. A caliph taken prisoner in battle shocked the Muslim world.

reigns.hook: Mas'ud is gone. The emirs crown his nephew Malik-Shah, and then watch to see if he'll take orders.

reigns.tagline: Crowned, then locked in a tower for not doing his job
reigns.previously: Mas'ud dies at Hamadan, the last strong sultan of the west.
paragraphs: Malik-Shah was Mahmud II's son, and Mas'ud had made him his son-in-law. When Mas'ud died in 1152 the emirs put him on the throne at Hamadan. The real power was with Khass Beg, the late sultan's favourite emir, who expected the young man to do as he was told.

Within a few months the emirs had had enough. They arrested him and locked him up. They then sent to Khuzistan for his brother Muhammad. Malik-Shah later got free and kept trying to win back the throne, without success. He died at Isfahan in 1160.

claims.text: The emirs deposed Malik-Shah because he cared for nothing but drinking and fun.
claims.note: That is the chroniclers' version. It also suited emirs who wanted a sultan they could control.

claims.text: Malik-Shah III was poisoned in 1160.
claims.note: Some sources report poison. Sudden deaths of royal rivals were often put down to it.

reigns.hook: His brother Muhammad takes the crown. He has a bigger plan than the emirs think: he wants Baghdad back.

reigns.tagline: He laid siege to the caliph, and the caliph held
reigns.previously: The emirs lock up Malik-Shah III after a few months on the throne.
paragraphs: Muhammad was another son of Mahmud II. The emirs brought him from Khuzistan to replace his brother in 1153. He soon showed he was nobody's puppet and got rid of the emirs who thought they ran him. When his great-uncle Sanjar died in 1157, Muhammad was the most senior Seljuk left.

His target was Baghdad. The caliph al-Muqtafi had built up his own army and stopped taking orders from the sultans. Early in 1157 Muhammad besieged the city for weeks. The walls held, and when news came that rivals had seized Hamadan behind him, he gave up and went home.
That failure marked a turning point. From then on the caliphs ran Iraq for themselves. Muhammad fell ill and died in 1159, still young.

claims.text: Muhammad's siege of Baghdad in 1157 failed.
claims.note: Ibn al-Athir and Baghdad writers describe the siege and its collapse.

claims.text: After al-Muqtafi, the caliphs ruled Iraq again without the sultans.
claims.note: Historians date the Abbasid revival to his reign. The later caliph al-Nasir built on it.

reigns.hook: The emirs need a new sultan fast. They pick Muhammad Tapar's last surviving son, a man who spent years at Sanjar's court and then as a prisoner.

reigns.tagline: Sanjar's old heir wins a throne, then loses it and his life
reigns.previously: Muhammad II falls ill and dies, still young.
paragraphs: Suleiman-Shah was the youngest son of Muhammad Tapar. He grew up at Sanjar's court in Merv, and the old sultan named him heir. When the Oghuz captured Sanjar in 1153, Suleiman-Shah tried to lead the Khorasan army and failed. He drifted west, was proclaimed sultan in Baghdad by the caliph, was beaten, and ended up a prisoner of the lord of Mosul.

When Muhammad II died, the emirs asked Mosul to send him to Hamadan as their new sultan. Troops flocked to him. But he soon fell out with the men who had made him. In 1160 his own army arrested him at the gates of Hamadan. He was killed in captivity a few months later.

claims.text: Suleiman-Shah lost the throne because he was a drunkard who insulted the emirs.
claims.note: The chroniclers say so. They also wrote for the side that won.

claims.text: Sanjar named Suleiman-Shah as his heir.
claims.note: His name was read after Sanjar's in the Friday prayers in Khorasan, the usual sign of an heir.

reigns.hook: The kingmaker now is Eldiguz, the Turkish emir who married Tughril II's widow. He has a stepson of royal blood ready: Arslan-Shah.

reigns.tagline: A sultan in name while his stepfather ran Iran
reigns.cameToPower: Put on the throne by Eldiguz
reigns.previously: The emirs arrest Suleiman-Shah at the gates of Hamadan.
paragraphs: Arslan-Shah was Tughril II's son. His mother had been married to the emir Eldiguz, so the man who put him on the throne was also his stepfather. Eldiguz took the title of Great Atabeg and ran the army, the treasury and the provinces. Arslan-Shah lived at Hamadan, with his name on the coins and very little else.

Eldiguz was good at it. He fought the kings of Georgia and other atabegs and held most of western Iran together. His sons by Arslan-Shah's mother, Pahlavan and Qizil Arslan, were the sultan's half-brothers and the real heirs to power. When Eldiguz died around 1175, Arslan-Shah tried to break free. He raised troops against Pahlavan but died suddenly at Zanjan in 1176.

claims.text: Pahlavan had his half-brother the sultan poisoned.
claims.note: Some chroniclers suggest it because the death came so conveniently. There is no proof.

claims.text: Eldiguz, not the sultan, held real power.
claims.note: All the sources agree. Historians call this period the age of the atabegs.

reigns.hook: Pahlavan puts the dead sultan's son on the throne. Tughril III is seven years old.

reigns.tagline: The last Seljuk sultan of Iran went down swinging
reigns.cameToPower: Put on the throne by Pahlavan
reigns.previously: Arslan-Shah dies suddenly at Zanjan, perhaps poisoned.
paragraphs: Tughril III became sultan as a little boy, with his uncle Pahlavan in charge. Pahlavan treated him well. When Pahlavan died in 1186, his brother Qizil Arslan took over, and he was much harsher. Tughril grew up wanting to rule for real. He joined Qizil Arslan's enemies, and in 1190 Qizil Arslan locked him in a castle and planned to make himself sultan.

Qizil Arslan was murdered in 1191 before he could enjoy it. Tughril got free, raised an army and fought his way back to power at Hamadan. He was brave and loved poetry. The historian Rawandi, a calligrapher at his court, later wrote the story of the Seljuks.

But one of Pahlavan's sons, Qutlugh Inanch, called in the Khwarazmshah Tekish from the east. In 1194 their armies met near Rey. Tughril fought hard and was killed. More than 150 years of Seljuk sultans in Iran were over.

claims.text: Tughril rode into his last battle reciting verses from the Shahnameh.
claims.note: Told in later Persian histories. A fitting end for a poet-sultan, but impossible to check.

claims.text: Tekish sent Tughril's head to the caliph in Baghdad.
claims.note: Chroniclers including Ibn al-Athir report it. The details differ between accounts.

claims.text: Qizil Arslan locked Tughril up and claimed the sultanate for himself.
claims.note: Recorded by Ibn al-Athir and Rawandi. Qizil Arslan was murdered soon after.

reigns.hook: Tekish's son Muhammad builds a huge empire from the Aral Sea to the Gulf. In 1218 his governor at Otrar kills a caravan of Mongol merchants.

reigns.title: The Mongol Conquest
reigns.tagline: Genghis Khan's storm, then decades of Mongol governors
reigns.reignEnded: Hulagu came to rule in person
reigns.previously: Tekish kills the last Seljuk sultan, and Khwarazm rules Iran.
paragraphs: The Khwarazmshah Muhammad II ruled a big new empire, and he made a fatal mistake. In 1218 his governor at Otrar killed the merchants of a Mongol trade caravan, and when Genghis Khan sent envoys to complain they were killed or humiliated. In 1219 the Mongols came. Muhammad fled west across Iran and died on an island in the Caspian Sea.

The Mongols showed no mercy to cities that resisted. In 1221 Merv and Nishapur were destroyed by Genghis's son Tolui and their people massacred. The chroniclers' death tolls run into the hundreds of thousands. Historians think those figures are inflated, but the killing was real, and Khorasan took generations to recover. Muhammad's son Jalal al-Din fought on for ten years, until he was killed in the Kurdish mountains in 1231.

For the next quarter of a century Iran had no khan of its own. Governors sent by the Great Khans in Mongolia counted people and squeezed taxes out of Khorasan, while the general Baiju held the north-west and beat the Seljuks of Anatolia at Köse Dağ in 1243. Then in 1253 the Great Khan Möngke gave his brother Hulagu an army and a mission in the west.

claims.text: The governor of Otrar massacred a Mongol caravan of about 450 merchants.
claims.note: The figure comes from Juzjani and other Muslim chroniclers. The killing itself is in every account; the size of the caravan isn't certain.

claims.text: Hundreds of thousands, even more than a million, died at Merv and Nishapur.
claims.note: The figures come from chroniclers such as Ibn al-Athir and Juvaini. Modern historians think the real numbers were far lower, though still terrible.

claims.text: Jalal al-Din escaped Genghis by riding his horse off a cliff into the Indus, and Genghis told his sons to admire him.
claims.note: Juvaini, writing for the Mongols a generation later, tells it. A great scene, impossible to check.

reigns.hook: Hulagu, Genghis's grandson, is on his way with siege engineers from China. His first targets are the Assassins in their mountain castles. After them, the caliph in Baghdad.

reigns.tagline: He burned Alamut, then trampled the caliph
reigns.cameToPower: Sent west by his brother Möngke
reigns.previously: Möngke sends his brother Hulagu west to finish the job.
paragraphs: Hulagu was a son of Tolui, Genghis Khan's youngest son, and his mother Sorghaghtani was a Christian. In 1256 his army reached the Ismaili castles in the Elburz mountains. Their imam Rukn al-Din Khurshah surrendered, Alamut followed, and the Assassins were finished. The historian Juvaini, riding with the Mongols, saved some of Alamut's books before the library burned.

Then he turned on Baghdad. The caliph al-Musta'sim refused to submit, and in February 1258 the city fell. Its people were massacred for days and the caliph was put to death. In 1260 Hulagu took Aleppo and Damascus. When news came that Möngke had died, he marched most of his army home, and the force he left behind under Kitbuqa was beaten by the Mamluks of Egypt at Ain Jalut.

Hulagu stayed in Iran and took the title Ilkhan, a khan below the Great Khan. He gave the astronomer Nasir al-Din Tusi a great observatory at Maragheh. His cousin Berke of the Golden Horde, a Muslim, went to war with him over the Caucasus. Hulagu died near Maragheh in February 1265 and was buried on an island in Lake Urmia.

claims.text: The caliph was rolled in a carpet and trampled to death by horses.
claims.note: Several sources say so, explaining it by a Mongol taboo against spilling royal blood. Other accounts give him different deaths.

claims.text: Hulagu showed the caliph his own gold and told him to eat it, then left him to starve.
claims.note: The story reached Europe through Marco Polo and others. It is a moral tale about greed, not an eyewitness report.

claims.text: Young women were buried alive with Hulagu in his tomb.
claims.note: Rashid al-Din reports it as part of the old Mongol rites. No one has found the tomb to check.

reigns.hook: Hulagu is dead, and his widow Doquz Khatun soon follows him. His eldest son Abaqa, a Buddhist, takes the throne and faces enemies on three sides.

images.alt: Medieval Syriac manuscript painting of a royal couple, identified as Hulagu and Doquz Khatun

reigns.tagline: A Buddhist khan writing to the Pope for help
reigns.cameToPower: Chosen by the princes and emirs
reigns.reignEnded: Died at Hamadan after a drinking bout
reigns.previously: Hulagu dies near Maragheh and is buried on an island in Lake Urmia.
paragraphs: Abaqa made Tabriz his capital and married Maria, a daughter of the Byzantine emperor Michael VIII. She had been sent east as a bride for his father. He was a Buddhist, and his realm was boxed in by enemies: the Golden Horde in the Caucasus, his Chagatai cousins in Central Asia, and the Mamluks in Syria. In 1270 he crushed the Chagatai khan Baraq near Herat.

The Mamluks were harder. Abaqa wrote to the Pope and to the kings of Europe proposing a joint war on Egypt, and his envoys turned up at the Council of Lyon in 1274. Nothing came of it. In 1277 the Mamluk sultan Baybars smashed a Mongol army at Elbistan in Anatolia, and in 1281 Abaqa's brother Möngke Temür lost a huge battle at Homs.

At home the Persian brothers Juvaini ran things: Shams al-Din as chief minister, Ata-Malik as governor of Baghdad. Abaqa planned revenge for Homs, but in April 1282 he died at Hamadan after heavy drinking. The princes and emirs met to choose a successor, and they were split.

claims.text: Abaqa wrote to Pope Clement IV and later popes proposing an alliance against the Mamluks.
claims.note: Letters and replies survive, and his envoys at the Council of Lyon in 1274 are recorded by European writers.

claims.text: Abaqa wept when he saw the dead of Elbistan on the battlefield.
claims.note: Told by later chroniclers. It may be true, but it is the kind of scene historians like to add.

claims.text: Abaqa drank himself to death.
claims.note: Rashid al-Din says he died after a bout of heavy drinking at Hamadan. Arghun later accused the vizier Shams al-Din Juvaini of poisoning him.

reigns.hook: Abaqa's son Arghun expects the crown. The emirs instead pick his uncle Tekuder, a Muslim convert who wants peace with Egypt.

reigns.tagline: The first Muslim Ilkhan, killed without bloodshed
reigns.cameToPower: Chosen by the princes and emirs
reigns.previously: Abaqa drinks himself to death at Hamadan, and the emirs are split.
paragraphs: Tekuder was one of Hulagu's younger sons. He had been baptised as a boy, then became a Muslim and took the name Ahmad. Once in power he called himself sultan and wrote to the Mamluk sultan Qalawun offering peace and friendship. The Mamluks did not trust him, and many Mongol emirs thought he was betraying the old ways.

His nephew Arghun, Abaqa's son, believed the throne was his and suspected Tekuder's ministers of poisoning his father. In 1284 Arghun rebelled. At first Tekuder won and caught him, but emirs led by Buqa freed Arghun and changed sides. Tekuder fled and was taken. In August 1284 he was executed in the Mongol way for princes, with his back broken so no royal blood was spilled.

claims.text: Tekuder was killed by having his back broken, the bloodless death for Mongol princes.
claims.note: Rashid al-Din, writing for Arghun's son Ghazan, describes it. The custom of not shedding royal blood is well attested.

claims.text: Tekuder's mother Qutui Khatun was the real power behind him.
claims.note: Rashid al-Din blames her and the Juvaini brothers. He wrote for the rival branch of the family and had reason to blacken them.

reigns.hook: Arghun is khan at last. He is a Buddhist, he hates the Mamluks, and he is about to send a Christian monk from China all the way to Rome and Paris.

reigns.tagline: He sent a monk from China to the kings of Europe
reigns.reignEnded: Died after drinking a life elixir
reigns.previously: The emirs turn on Tekuder, and he is put to death without bloodshed.
paragraphs: Arghun was a Buddhist who kept monks at court, and he wanted the Mamluks crushed. In 1287 he sent Rabban Bar Sauma, a Christian monk born near Beijing, on a mission west. Bar Sauma met Philip IV of France in Paris, Edward I of England in Gascony, and Pope Nicholas IV in Rome. Everyone was polite. Nobody sent an army.

At home Arghun killed the vizier Shams al-Din Juvaini in 1284 and later put a Jewish physician, Sa'd al-Dawla, in charge of the finances. He was clever and hated by the emirs. When Arghun's favourite wife Bolghana died, he asked the Great Khan Kublai for a bride from her tribe, and a girl named Kököchin set off from China by sea.

Arghun did not live to meet her. He fell ill in 1291 after taking a medicine that was supposed to give long life. As he lay dying, the emirs killed Sa'd al-Dawla and his men. His young son Ghazan was far away in Khorasan.

claims.text: Arghun's letter of 1289 to Philip IV of France survives in the French archives.
claims.note: The scroll, in Mongolian in the Uyghur script and stamped with Chinese-style seals, is in the Archives nationales in Paris.

claims.text: Marco Polo was one of the escorts who brought Kököchin from China to Iran.
claims.note: Polo says so himself. A Chinese record names three envoys who match the ones he names, which makes the story more believable.

claims.text: Arghun was killed by an elixir of long life made by a holy man from India.
claims.note: Rashid al-Din says the medicine, thought to contain sulphur and mercury, ruined his health. Others blamed poison or plain illness.

reigns.hook: The emirs pass over the boy Ghazan and choose Arghun's brother Gaykhatu, a man who loves wine, parties and big new ideas about money.

images.caption: Part of Arghun's 1289 letter to Philip IV of France, in Mongolian with a red Chinese-style seal. The letter survives in Paris.
images.alt: A section of a long parchment scroll written in vertical Mongolian script with a square red seal

reigns.tagline: The khan whose paper money shut the bazaars
reigns.previously: Arghun dies after taking an elixir meant to give him long life.
paragraphs: Gaykhatu had governed Anatolia for his brother, and the emirs chose him over Arghun's son Ghazan. He took a Tibetan Buddhist name, Irinchin Dorji, and spent freely. The treasury was soon empty, and his vizier Sadr al-Din Zanjani had an idea from China: paper money.

In 1294 Tabriz got banknotes called chao, printed with Chinese and Arabic writing. Using coins was banned. Merchants refused the paper, shops closed and trade stopped. Within a couple of months the scheme was dropped. Gaykhatu's cousin Baydu, a grandson of Hulagu, had his own grudge, and in 1295 the emirs went over to him. Gaykhatu was caught and strangled with a bowstring.

claims.text: Gaykhatu's paper money brought trade in Tabriz to a standstill and was withdrawn within months.
claims.note: Rashid al-Din and other Persian historians describe the closed bazaars. The notes copied Kublai's Chinese paper money.

claims.text: Gaykhatu once had Baydu beaten at a drunken party, and Baydu never forgave him.
claims.note: The story appears in the Persian histories. It explains the feud neatly, which is a reason to be careful.

claims.text: Gaykhatu spent his time on drink and debauchery.
claims.note: The chroniclers say so, but they wrote for Ghazan, whose branch of the family took over. He also had defenders who praised his generosity.

reigns.hook: Baydu has the throne, but Arghun's son Ghazan is coming from Khorasan with an army, and an emir named Nawruz has a plan for him.

reigns.tagline: A khan for one summer, outplayed by a convert
reigns.previously: Gaykhatu's emirs desert him and he is strangled with a bowstring.
paragraphs: Baydu was a grandson of Hulagu through his son Taraghai. He held the throne for only a few months in 1295, and his enemies said he favoured Christians. Arghun's son Ghazan, who had spent years fighting rebels in Khorasan, refused to accept him and marched west.

Ghazan's ally, the emir Nawruz, was a Muslim, and he told Ghazan that most of the army and the people were Muslim too. In June 1295 Ghazan became a Muslim. It worked. Baydu's emirs went over to him one after another. Baydu ran towards Georgia, was caught near Nakhchivan and taken to Tabriz, and was put to death in October 1295.

claims.text: Ghazan converted to Islam on Nawruz's advice to win the throne.
claims.note: Rashid al-Din describes the conversion in 1295 and Nawruz's part in it. Whether Ghazan's faith was sincere is still argued over.

claims.text: Baydu was a secret Christian.
claims.note: Christian writers of the time hoped so, and Muslim chroniclers accused him of it. He seems to have favoured Christians without converting.

reigns.hook: Ghazan is khan. A Mongol prince is now a Muslim sultan with a new name, Mahmud, and the first thing he does is tear down the Buddhist temples.

reigns.tagline: The Mongol who became a Muslim reformer
reigns.previously: Ghazan turns Muslim, the emirs desert Baydu, and he is executed.
paragraphs: Ghazan made Islam the faith of the Mongol state in Iran. His followers wrecked Buddhist temples, churches and synagogues in the first months. Nawruz, who had helped him win, grew too powerful and was killed in 1297. Then Ghazan and his Persian vizier Rashid al-Din set about mending a country squeezed dry. They reformed taxes, standardised the coinage and weights, and cut back on soldiers grabbing what they liked.

Ghazan still fought the Mamluks. In December 1299 he beat them near Homs and his army held Damascus, but not its citadel, for a few weeks. In April 1303 his army was badly beaten at Marj al-Saffar, south of Damascus. He ordered Rashid al-Din to write the history of the Mongols, which grew into a history of the known world.
He built a tomb and a whole suburb, Shanb-e Ghazan, outside Tabriz. In May 1304 he died near Qazvin at about 32, leaving no son. The throne went to his younger brother.

claims.text: Ghazan ordered Rashid al-Din's Compendium of Chronicles, a history of the world.
claims.note: Rashid's own preface says so. Copies made in Tabriz in his lifetime survive.

claims.text: Ghazan was short and strikingly plain to look at.
claims.note: Mamluk and European writers say he was short and ugly. They were enemies or outsiders, and none of them saw him up close.

reigns.hook: Ghazan's brother becomes Öljaitü. Baptised as a boy, then Sunni, he will change religion again, and build a city with one of the greatest domes on earth.

reigns.tagline: Christian, Sunni, then Shi'a: the khan of the dome
reigns.previously: Ghazan dies near Qazvin with no son of his own.
paragraphs: Öljaitü's mother was a Christian and he was baptised as a child with the name Nicholas. Later he became a Sunni Muslim and took the name Khodabandeh, 'servant of God'. In about 1310 he turned to Shi'a Islam, the first Mongol khan to do so. His Sunni critics mocked his name as Kharbanda, 'donkey driver'.

His great project was a new capital, Soltaniyeh, on the plains west of Qazvin. His tomb there, finished in about 1313, has a huge double-shelled brick dome that still stands. Rashid al-Din stayed on as vizier but had to share the job with a rival, Taj al-Din Ali Shah. Öljaitü wrote to Philip IV of France proposing friendship, and in 1312 he failed to take the Mamluk fortress of Rahba on the Euphrates.
He died at Soltaniyeh in December 1316, in his thirties. His son and heir was still a boy.

claims.text: Öljaitü was baptised as a child, then became a Sunni and later a Shi'a Muslim.
claims.note: Christian and Muslim sources agree on the baptism, and Shi'a names and phrases appear on his coins from about 1310.

claims.text: He turned Shi'a in disgust after Hanafi and Shafi'i scholars insulted each other's schools in front of him.
claims.note: Later historians tell the story of an angry debate at court. Others point to his Shi'a advisers, such as the scholar Allama al-Hilli.

claims.text: His tomb at Soltaniyeh has one of the largest brick domes in the world.
claims.note: The building still stands and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

reigns.hook: The new khan, Abu Sa'id, is about twelve. The real power belongs to the emir Chupan, who has a beautiful daughter named Baghdad.

reigns.tagline: The poet khan who died and left no one
reigns.previously: Öljaitü dies at Soltaniyeh, and his heir is still a boy.
paragraphs: Abu Sa'id was a child, so the emir Chupan ran the empire. In 1318 the great vizier Rashid al-Din was accused of poisoning Öljaitü and put to death. In 1323 Abu Sa'id's government made peace with the Mamluks, ending more than sixty years of war. The young khan wrote poetry and music, and his court may have made the Great Mongol Shahnameh, one of the finest Persian books ever painted.

He fell for Chupan's daughter Baghdad Khatun, who was married to the emir Hasan Buzurg. Chupan refused to hand her over. In 1327 Abu Sa'id struck: Chupan's son Dimashq Khwaja was hunted down and killed at court, and Chupan, fleeing east, was killed at Herat. Abu Sa'id then married Baghdad Khatun.

Later he took a new wife, Dilshad, Baghdad's niece. In late 1335, marching to fight the Golden Horde in the Caucasus, he died suddenly aged about 30, with no son. People whispered that a jealous Baghdad Khatun had poisoned him.

claims.text: Abu Sa'id forced Chupan's daughter Baghdad Khatun to divorce her husband and marry him.
claims.note: The Persian histories agree on the outline: the khan's passion, Chupan's refusal and the fall of Chupan's family.

claims.text: Baghdad Khatun poisoned Abu Sa'id out of jealousy.
claims.note: The rumour was enough to get her killed soon after. Some historians suspect illness, perhaps even plague.

claims.text: Rashid al-Din poisoned Öljaitü.
claims.note: The charge was brought by his enemies at court. Most historians think it was a pretext to get rid of him.

reigns.hook: With no son to succeed, the vizier Ghiyath al-Din, Rashid al-Din's son, picks a distant cousin, Arpa, and races to put him on the throne.

reigns.tagline: The last real Ilkhan, gone in five months
reigns.cameToPower: Chosen by the vizier Ghiyath al-Din
reigns.previously: Abu Sa'id dies on campaign with no son, and Baghdad Khatun is blamed.
paragraphs: Arpa came from the family of Ariq Böke, Kublai's brother, not from Hulagu's line. He was raised to the throne in the army camp by the vizier Ghiyath al-Din, and married Abu Sa'id's sister Sati Beg. He was a hard man. He had Baghdad Khatun put to death on the charge that she had poisoned Abu Sa'id and was plotting with the Golden Horde.

Özbeg Khan of the Golden Horde invaded through the Caucasus, and Arpa drove him back. But many emirs refused a khan from outside Hulagu's family. Ali Padshah, the Oirat governor of Baghdad, crowned a rival, Musa, a grandson of Baydu. In April 1336 they met in battle near Maragheh and Arpa lost. He was captured and executed, and Ghiyath al-Din was killed too.

claims.text: Arpa had Baghdad Khatun killed for poisoning Abu Sa'id.
claims.note: The Persian histories agree she was put to death soon after Abu Sa'id's death. Whether she was guilty is another matter.

claims.text: Arpa married Abu Sa'id's sister Sati Beg to give himself a link to Hulagu's family.
claims.note: The marriage is recorded in the Persian histories. The motive is the obvious reading, not something the sources spell out.

reigns.hook: No khan will unite Iran again. The generals start crowning puppets of their own, and the country breaks into pieces.

reigns.title: After the Ilkhans
reigns.tagline: Puppet khans, warlords and the poet of Shiraz
reigns.previously: Arpa Ke'un, the last real Ilkhan, is defeated and executed.
paragraphs: With no strong khan left, the generals ran the show. Each faction found a descendant of Genghis and crowned him. Hasan Buzurg of the Jalayirids had his puppets, and the Chobanid family had theirs, including Abu Sa'id's sister Sati Beg. The Chobanid Hasan Kuchak was murdered by his own wife in 1343. His brother Malek Ashraf ruled Tabriz by terror until the Golden Horde took the city and had him executed.

In the south, Shiraz had the poet Hafez. His patron Abu Ishaq Inju lost the city in 1353 to the Muzaffarid Mubariz al-Din, a stern man who shut the taverns and later had Abu Ishaq executed. His own sons blinded him in 1358. One of them, Shah Shuja, ruled Shiraz for over 25 years while Hafez wrote the love poems Iranians still quote today.

In Khorasan a rebellion at Sabzevar in 1337 created the Sarbadars, a state run by a string of local leaders. They murdered the last khan recognised there, Togha Temür, in 1353. The Kartid kings held Herat. None of them could unite Iran, and across the Oxus a lame Turkic emir was watching.

claims.text: The name Sarbadar means 'head on the gallows': its rebels said they would rather hang than live in shame.
claims.note: The meaning of the word is clear. The defiant motto comes from later Persian chroniclers and may be a story built around it.

claims.text: Hasan Kuchak's wife killed him, fearing he had found out about her lover.
claims.note: Persian histories of the period tell it, with lurid details; there are no independent witnesses.

claims.text: Hafez mocked Mubariz al-Din as the 'muhtasib', the morals officer who closed the wine taverns.
claims.note: Several of Hafez's poems attack a hypocritical muhtasib, and readers have long linked them to Mubariz; Hafez never names him.

reigns.hook: Timur, lord of Samarkand, has spent ten years building his power north of the Oxus. In 1381 he crosses the river and takes Herat. Iran is next.

reigns.tagline: The lame emir who built towers of skulls
reigns.reignEnded: Died at Otrar, bound for China
reigns.previously: Timur crosses the Oxus in 1381 and takes Herat. Iran is next.
paragraphs: Timur was born around 1336 near Kesh, south of Samarkand, into the Barlas, a Turkic-speaking tribe of Mongol origin. Wounds taken in his youth left him lame in the right leg and stiff in the right arm, so Persians called him Timur-e Lang, Timur the Lame, and Europeans turned that into Tamerlane. He never called himself khan. He ruled as an emir behind puppet khans of Genghis's line, and married a Genghisid princess for the prestige.

By 1370 he was master of Samarkand. In 1381 he took Herat, and for the next twenty years his armies swept across Iran again and again. Cities that opened their gates paid ransom. Cities that resisted were wrecked. When Isfahan rose in 1387 and killed his tax collectors, his soldiers were ordered to bring in heads, which were piled into towers outside the walls. Delhi in 1398 and Baghdad in 1401 saw massacres too.

In 1402 he smashed the Ottoman army at Ankara and took Sultan Bayezid I prisoner. Bayezid died in captivity months later. Timur, now nearly seventy, went home to Samarkand and set out to conquer Ming China. He got as far as Otrar on the Syr Darya, fell ill in a bitter winter and died on 18 February 1405. Soviet scientists opened his tomb in 1941 and found the damaged leg and arm the chroniclers had described.

claims.text: Timur's soldiers stacked 70,000 heads in towers outside Isfahan.
claims.note: The figure comes from Timur's own court historians, who wrote to glorify him. Nobody counted, but the massacre itself is not in doubt.

claims.text: Timur scolded Hafez for offering Samarkand and Bukhara for a beauty's mole, and the poet joked that such generosity was why he was so poor.
claims.note: A much-loved story that first appears long after both men were dead. Timur did take Shiraz in 1387, while Hafez was alive.

claims.text: Opening Timur's tomb unleashed a curse: Germany invaded the Soviet Union within days.
claims.note: The tomb was opened in June 1941, just before the invasion, but the invasion had been planned for months. The curse story grew up afterwards.

reigns.hook: Timur named his grandson Pir Muhammad as heir. Nobody listened. Within weeks his sons and grandsons were fighting, and his quiet youngest son, Shah Rukh, was waiting in Herat.

reigns.tagline: Timur's gentle son, ruling from Herat
reigns.cameToPower: Won the war among Timur's heirs
reigns.previously: Timur dies at Otrar in 1405, on his way to invade China.
paragraphs: Shah Rukh was Timur's fourth and youngest son, and his father had made him governor of Khorasan. When Timur died, the empire split at once. A grandson, Khalil Sultan, grabbed Samarkand and the treasury. Shah Rukh sat tight in Herat, won the emirs over one by one, and took Samarkand in 1409. He handed it to his teenage son Ulugh Beg and kept Herat as his own capital.

He was everything his father was not: pious, careful and happiest at peace. He swapped embassies with the Ming emperor Yongle. His wife Gawhar Shad built the great mosque beside the shrine of Imam Reza at Mashhad, finished in 1418. Their son Baysunghur ran a workshop of calligraphers and painters in Herat that made some of the finest Persian books ever produced.

The west was harder. The Black Sheep Turkmen held Tabriz, and Shah Rukh marched against them three times in the 1420s and 1430s. He won battles but could not hold Azerbaijan, so he left it to a Turkmen prince who promised loyalty, Jahan Shah. In 1447, at about 69, he rode west once more to put down a rebel grandson, and died in camp near Rey in March.

claims.text: Gawhar Shad built the great mosque at Mashhad in 1418.
claims.note: The mosque's dated inscription, written out by her son Baysunghur, names her as its founder.

claims.text: A man stabbed Shah Rukh in the main mosque of Herat in 1427, and he survived.
claims.note: Timurid chroniclers record the attack. The attacker was linked to the Hurufis, a mystical sect, and their followers were hunted down afterwards.

claims.text: His envoys' diary of a trip to the Ming court still survives.
claims.note: The painter Ghiyath al-Din Naqqash kept a record of the embassy of 1419 to 1422, and the historian Hafiz-i Abru copied it into his chronicle.

reigns.hook: With Shah Rukh gone, the Timurid princes turn on each other. Ulugh Beg will be killed on his own son's orders within three years. In Tabriz, Jahan Shah stops pretending to be anyone's vassal.

reigns.tagline: The Black Sheep poet-king of Tabriz
reigns.cameToPower: Seized the west as Timurids fought
reigns.previously: Shah Rukh dies near Rey in 1447, and his heirs turn on each other.
paragraphs: The Qara Qoyunlu, the Black Sheep, were a league of Turkmen tribes from the country around Lake Van. Jahan Shah was a son of their great chief Qara Yusuf. He got Tabriz in the 1430s by siding with Shah Rukh against his own brother Iskandar. As long as the old Timurid lived, Jahan Shah behaved himself. When Shah Rukh died in 1447, he moved fast.

Within a few years he held most of western and central Iran, including Isfahan, Fars and Kerman. In 1458 he even took Herat, the Timurid capital, but a revolt by his own son back home forced him to give it up within months. In Tabriz he built the Blue Mosque, finished in 1465 and famous for its deep blue tiles. He also wrote poetry in Turkic and Persian under the pen name Haqiqi.

His great rival was the White Sheep chief Uzun Hasan, based at Diyarbakir. In 1467 Jahan Shah marched against him with a large army. In November, in eastern Anatolia, Uzun Hasan's horsemen caught him off guard, and the old king was cut down as he tried to escape. His sons could not hold his lands together.

claims.text: Jahan Shah wrote poems under the name Haqiqi.
claims.note: A collection of his Turkic and Persian verse survives in manuscript and was studied by the orientalist Vladimir Minorsky.

claims.text: He was a heavy drinker who cared nothing for religious law.
claims.note: So say chroniclers who worked for his enemies. He built mosques, and some historians think the charge partly reflects suspicion of his religious views.

claims.text: He was caught because he had sent most of his army off to winter quarters.
claims.note: This is how the White Sheep side explained the surprise. The accounts differ on the details.

reigns.hook: Uzun Hasan now has the Black Sheep lands. The Timurid sultan Abu Sa'id thinks the Turkmen upstart is easy prey, and marches west with a great army.

reigns.tagline: The tall Turkmen who took on the Ottomans
reigns.relationToPredecessor: White Sheep rival of Jahan Shah
reigns.previously: Uzun Hasan's horsemen surprise and kill Jahan Shah in 1467.
paragraphs: Uzun Hasan means Hasan the Tall. He led the Aq Qoyunlu, the White Sheep, a Turkmen league based at Diyarbakir, after pushing his brother aside in 1453. Killing Jahan Shah gave him the Black Sheep lands. Then the Timurid Abu Sa'id invaded, got stuck in Karabakh in winter with his army starving, and was captured in 1469. Uzun Hasan handed him to a Timurid rival, who had him executed.

He made Tabriz his capital and ruled most of Iran from there. His wife was a Christian, Theodora Komnene, a princess of Trebizond, known in Iran as Despina Khatun. After the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II swallowed Trebizond in 1461, Uzun Hasan was the man Europe pinned its hopes on. Venice sent envoys, and two of them, Giosafat Barbaro and Ambrogio Contarini, left lively accounts of his court.

In 1473 he finally faced Mehmed head on. At Otlukbeli in eastern Anatolia, Ottoman cannon and Janissary guns broke his horsemen. He kept his throne but never threatened the Ottomans again. He died in Tabriz on 6 January 1478. One of his daughters had married Haydar, head of the Safavid Sufi order of Ardabil, and that match would matter enormously.

claims.text: Uzun Hasan's queen was Theodora Komnene, daughter of the emperor of Trebizond.
claims.note: Greek and Venetian writers record the marriage, and the Venetian envoys met her at his court, where she kept her Christian faith.

claims.text: His tax rules outlived him: the Ottomans kept 'Hasan Padishah's laws' in eastern Anatolia.
claims.note: Ottoman law codes for Diyarbakir and nearby provinces in the 16th century refer to his regulations by name.

claims.text: Shah Ismail I's mother was Uzun Hasan's daughter by Despina Khatun.
claims.note: Safavid-era histories and European accounts agree on it, so the founder of Safavid Iran had a Greek Christian grandmother.

reigns.hook: Uzun Hasan is dead. His eldest son Khalil takes the throne, but a younger son, Ya'qub, barely in his teens, has powerful emirs behind him.

reigns.tagline: Poets, painters and a dead Safavid sheikh
reigns.cameToPower: Beat his brother Khalil in battle
reigns.previously: Uzun Hasan dies in Tabriz in January 1478.
paragraphs: Uzun Hasan's eldest son, Khalil, lasted about six months. Emirs who backed his young half-brother Ya'qub rose against him, and Khalil was killed in battle in the summer of 1478. Ya'qub was about 14. At first the emirs ran things, but he grew into the job, and in 1480 his army beat an invading Mamluk force from Egypt near Urfa.

Ya'qub's Tabriz was a city of books. The great poet Jami, far away in Herat, dedicated a poem to him. His painters worked in a bold, colourful Turkmen style, and many of their pages are now in the Topkapi Palace in Istanbul. His secretary Fazlallah Khunji wrote a glowing history of the reign.

There was trouble at Ardabil. The Safavid sheikh Haydar, married to Ya'qub's sister, was turning his devotees into an army in red caps. In 1488 Haydar raided into the Caucasus, and Ya'qub sent troops to help the shah of Shirvan. Haydar was killed, and his three young sons, Ismail among them, were locked up in a castle in Fars. In December 1490 Ya'qub died suddenly, aged about 26.

claims.text: Ya'qub was poisoned by his wife, who was made to drink from the same cup.
claims.note: Some chroniclers tell this story. Others say he died of plague or illness, and there is no way to check.

claims.text: Haydar invented the red cap with twelve folds, one for each Imam, that gave the Qizilbash their name.
claims.note: Safavid tradition credits Haydar and says the design came to him in a dream. Exactly when the cap appeared is debated.

reigns.hook: Ya'qub's son Baysunghur is a small boy. The emirs crown him and start fighting over who will rule in his name.

reigns.tagline: The boy sultan the emirs fought over
reigns.previously: Ya'qub dies suddenly in December 1490, leaving a little boy.
paragraphs: Baysunghur was a young boy, and nobody expected him to rule. The emir Sufi Khalil of the Mawsillu clan took charge in his name and fought off rival princes of the family. Within a year he was overthrown and killed by another emir, Sulayman Beg Bijan, who became the new power behind the throne. The state Uzun Hasan built was coming apart in feuds between Turkmen clans.

In May 1492 rival emirs brought a cousin, Rustam, out of prison and crowned him at Tabriz. Baysunghur fled north to Shirvan, where his mother's family ruled, and came back with an army. Rustam played a dangerous card. He freed the young Safavid brothers and set their red-capped followers on Baysunghur. In 1493 the boy was beaten and killed.

claims.text: Rustam freed the Safavid brothers so their followers would fight Baysunghur for him.
claims.note: Both the Safavid chronicles and historians of the White Sheep tell it. It was the Safavids' first step back to power.

claims.text: The White Sheep collapsed because their Turkmen clans would not stop feuding.
claims.note: John Woods traces how clans such as the Bayandur, Mawsillu and Purnak made and unmade sultans after 1490.

reigns.hook: Rustam has won, thanks to the red caps. But their young leader, Sultan Ali, is growing too strong, and Rustam starts to think freeing him was a mistake.

reigns.tagline: The sultan who let the Safavids out
reigns.previously: Baysunghur is beaten and killed by Rustam's Safavid allies in 1493.
paragraphs: Rustam was a grandson of Uzun Hasan through his son Maqsud. Emirs who were tired of the boy Baysunghur's regents fetched him out of prison and crowned him at Tabriz in May 1492. To beat Baysunghur he set loose the three Safavid brothers and their Qizilbash followers, and it worked. Then he looked at the eldest brother, Sultan Ali, and saw a rival.

In 1494 Rustam's troops went after the brothers. Sultan Ali was killed in a fight near Ardabil, but first, the story goes, he named his little brother Ismail as head of the order. Loyal followers smuggled Ismail to Lahijan in Gilan, near the Caspian, where the local ruler hid him for five years. Rustam's men searched and never found him.

Rustam's own emirs were the bigger danger. In 1497 his cousin Ahmad, a grandson of Uzun Hasan who had grown up in Ottoman lands, came east with Ottoman support. Rustam's army melted away. He fled, tried to fight his way back, and was caught and put to death.

claims.text: Sultan Ali named Ismail his heir just before his last battle.
claims.note: Safavid chronicles tell it this way. They were written after Ismail became shah and had every reason to show him chosen.

claims.text: Ismail hid in Gilan for about five years while White Sheep agents hunted for him.
claims.note: Safavid histories describe his years at Lahijan under its ruler, Karkiya Mirza Ali, and the dates fit the Aq Qoyunlu record.

reigns.hook: Ahmad has the throne. He means to tame the Turkmen emirs who have been making and breaking sultans. They have other ideas.

reigns.tagline: The Ottoman sultan's grandson lasts a few months
reigns.previously: Rustam is overthrown by his cousin Ahmad in 1497 and put to death.
paragraphs: Ahmad's father, Ughurlu Muhammad, was a son of Uzun Hasan who rebelled, fled to the Ottomans and married a daughter of Mehmed II. So Ahmad was a grandson of both the White Sheep's greatest chief and the conqueror of Constantinople. He grew up in Ottoman lands, and when he took Tabriz in 1497 he brought Ottoman ideas about how a state should be run.

He tried to rein in the great emirs, scrap unjust taxes and take back land grants that had been handed out. The emirs who had let him in saw a threat to everything they had grabbed since Ya'qub's death. They rose against him, and in December 1497, only months into his reign, Ahmad was killed in battle against them.

claims.text: Ahmad's mother was a daughter of the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II.
claims.note: Ottoman and White Sheep sources agree on the marriage of his father, Ughurlu Muhammad, to Mehmed's daughter.

claims.text: His reforms, modelled on Ottoman practice, are what turned the emirs against him.
claims.note: This is the reading of modern historians such as John Woods, based on the reforms the chronicles describe. The emirs' own motives are not recorded.

reigns.hook: With Ahmad dead, rival grandsons of Uzun Hasan fight over what is left. One of them, Alvand, grabs Tabriz.

reigns.tagline: The last White Sheep in Tabriz
reigns.cameToPower: Won Tabriz in a cousins' war
reigns.previously: Ahmad is killed fighting his own emirs, months into his reign.
paragraphs: Alvand was yet another grandson of Uzun Hasan, a son of his son Yusuf. After Ahmad's death he and his cousins Muhammadi and Murad fought for the throne for two years. In 1500 Alvand and Murad agreed to split the realm. Alvand kept Azerbaijan and the old White Sheep lands around Diyarbakir, and Murad took central Iran. Neither was strong.

Meanwhile Ismail had come out of hiding in Gilan. In 1499, aged about 12, he raised his father's banner and the Qizilbash flocked to him. In 1500 he took revenge on Shirvan, whose shah had helped kill his father. In 1501 Alvand met him at Sharur, near Nakhchivan, with a much bigger army, and was routed.

Ismail rode into Tabriz and was crowned shah. Alvand fled west, still calling himself sultan, and died around 1504. Murad was beaten by Ismail near Hamadan in 1503. The White Sheep, who had once ruled from the Euphrates to the Gulf, were finished, and Uzun Hasan's own grandson had taken their place.

claims.text: At Sharur about 7,000 Qizilbash beat a White Sheep army of some 30,000.
claims.note: The figures come from Safavid chroniclers, who liked to make Ismail's victories look miraculous. Alvand's army was clearly larger, but nobody knows by how much.

claims.text: Ismail's men killed the shah of Shirvan, Farrukh Yasar, in 1500 to avenge Haydar.
claims.note: Safavid and other chronicles agree that Farrukh Yasar died in battle against Ismail that year.

reigns.hook: In the summer of 1501 a boy of about 14 is crowned shah in Tabriz. His red-capped followers think he is more than human, and he is about to change the religion of Iran.

reigns.tagline: The boy saint-king who made Iran Shi'a
reigns.previously: Ismail routs Alvand, the last White Sheep sultan, at Sharur.
paragraphs: Ismail's father and eldest brother, leaders of the Safavid Sufi order, were both killed in battle, and the small boy was hidden away in Gilan by the Caspian. His followers were Turkmen tribesmen called the Qizilbash, the red heads, for their red caps with twelve folds, one for each Shi'a Imam. They saw him as more than human. In 1501 they beat the White Sheep and crowned him at Tabriz.

Then Ismail did something enormous. He made Twelver Shi'ism the religion of the state and forced it on his subjects, violently where they resisted. Most Iranians were Sunni then; within a few generations most were Shi'a, and they still are. In 1510 he beat the Uzbek khan Muhammad Shaybani near Merv. He also wrote poems in Azeri Turkish under the pen name Khata'i.

His aura of invincibility died at Chaldiran on 23 August 1514. The Ottoman sultan Selim I had cannon and Janissaries with guns, and the Qizilbash horsemen were cut to pieces. Tabriz was briefly occupied. Ismail never led an army into battle again. He died in 1524, aged 36, and left the throne to a ten-year-old son.

claims.text: Ismail turned Shaybani Khan's skull into a gold-covered drinking cup.
claims.note: Chroniclers writing at the time report it, and trophy skulls were not unknown on the steppe. No cup survives.

claims.text: His followers believed he was divine.
claims.note: His own poems as Khata'i present him as a holy figure close to God, and visitors to Iran reported the devotion of the Qizilbash.

claims.text: After Chaldiran he gave up on government and took to drink.
claims.note: Safavid chroniclers describe him hunting and drinking in his last years. Some historians think the story of a broken man is overdone.

reigns.hook: The new shah, Tahmasp, is ten years old. The Qizilbash chiefs who are supposed to guard him are already reaching for their swords.

reigns.tagline: Fifty-two years on a throne he got at ten
reigns.previously: Ismail I dies at 36. His heir is a boy of ten.
paragraphs: For his first ten years Tahmasp was a pawn. Qizilbash chiefs fought each other for control of the boy, and the country slid into civil war. The Ottoman sultan Suleiman the Magnificent invaded again and again, and Tabriz changed hands. Tahmasp learned to survive by playing the chiefs off against each other, and he moved his capital away from the border to Qazvin.

In 1544 an unexpected guest arrived: Humayun, the Mughal emperor, driven out of India. Tahmasp sheltered him and lent him troops to win his throne back. In 1555 the Peace of Amasya, the first formal peace with the Ottomans, settled the border for a generation. As a young man Tahmasp loved painting, and his workshop made one of the most lavish Shahnamehs ever, with 258 paintings.

Then he turned pious. He gave up wine, lost interest in art and closed the taverns. In 1562 he handed the runaway Ottoman prince Bayezid and his sons over to Ottoman executioners, in return for gold. He reigned 52 years, longer than any other Safavid. When he died in 1576 he had not settled the succession, and his sons went for each other's throats.

claims.text: Tahmasp was poisoned.
claims.note: Rumours of poison went round the court, as they often did. The chroniclers disagree, and he was over 60.

claims.text: His great Shahnameh was broken up and sold page by page.
claims.note: The American collector Arthur Houghton split it up from the 1970s. In 1994 Iran swapped a de Kooning painting for the pages he still had.

claims.text: He banned wine and painting at his court in a fit of repentance.
claims.note: Tahmasp describes his repentance in his own memoir. How strictly the bans worked outside the palace is unclear.

reigns.hook: His son Ismail II kills most of his brothers and dies within a year, perhaps poisoned. The next shah is half blind and losing land on every side.

reigns.tagline: The prince who left prison to kill his family
reigns.cameToPower: Released from prison to take the throne
reigns.previously: Tahmasp I dies after 52 years.
paragraphs: Ismail had spent almost twenty years locked in a fortress by his father. After Tahmasp died he was brought out and crowned, and he immediately had most of the male royal family killed or blinded.
He leaned towards Sunni Islam, which alarmed his Shia court. He died suddenly in 1577, probably poisoned with drugs by his sister and court women.
reigns.hook: His half-blind brother Mohammad becomes shah.

reigns.tagline: The nearly blind shah
reigns.previously: Ismail II dies suddenly.
paragraphs: Mohammad was almost blind, so had been passed over before. As shah he left power to others: first his wife Khayr al-Nisa Begum, who was murdered by the Qizilbash chiefs, then to rival factions.
The Ottomans and Uzbeks took large parts of Iran. In 1588 his teenage son Abbas, backed by the Qizilbash, marched on Qazvin and took the throne.
reigns.hook: Abbas I takes over and rebuilds the empire.

reigns.tagline: He built half the world and blinded his own sons
reigns.cameToPower: Put on the throne by a coup
reigns.previously: Half-blind Mohammad Khodabanda is losing land on every side.
paragraphs: Abbas was 17 when Qizilbash chiefs pushed his father aside and made him shah. He trusted none of them. First he bought time, giving the Ottomans a big slice of land in 1590 so he could deal with the Uzbeks. Then he built his own army of ghulams, slave soldiers drawn from Georgian, Armenian and Circassian converts, loyal only to him, plus musketeers and cannon.

In 1598 he made Isfahan his capital and rebuilt it around a vast square, Naqsh-e Jahan, lined with the Shah Mosque and the Ali Qapu palace. In 1605 he moved Armenian merchants from Julfa into a new suburb, New Julfa, to run his silk trade. He won back Tabriz, took Hormuz from the Portuguese with the help of English ships in 1622 and seized Baghdad in 1623.

He was also terrifyingly cruel. His campaigns in Georgia killed and deported people in huge numbers. Fearing plots, he had his eldest son Mohammad Baqer killed in 1615 and other sons blinded. When he died in 1629 there was no grown son left fit to rule. The throne went to his grandson Safi.

claims.text: The English brothers Anthony and Robert Shirley modernised his army.
claims.note: The Shirleys and their friends said so. Historians think Abbas's reforms were already under way and the brothers' role was small.

claims.text: The saying 'Isfahan is half the world' comes from his time.
claims.note: It rhymes in Persian and is usually linked to his new capital, but no one knows who first said it.

claims.text: Abbas walked the bazaars in disguise to see how his people lived.
claims.note: A favourite folk tale, told about many Persian rulers.

reigns.hook: Safi is a teenager who grew up behind harem walls. From now on Safavid princes are raised locked away, far from armies and provinces.

images.alt: Painted portrait of Shah Abbas I

reigns.tagline: The harem boy who purged his family and lost Baghdad
reigns.cameToPower: Chosen as heir by Abbas I
reigns.reignEnded: Died at Kashan, after hard drinking
reigns.previously: Shah Abbas dies, and the throne goes to his grandson Safi.
paragraphs: He was born Sam Mirza, son of the crown prince Abbas I had ordered killed in 1615. The boy grew up shut inside the harem, which suited his grandfather fine: a prince who never left the palace could never lead a revolt. When Abbas died in January 1629 the teenager was brought out, crowned, and given the name Safi. He had never run a province or led a soldier.

He made up for it with fear. In 1632 he turned on his own family and his grandfather's great men. Princes were blinded or killed, and Imam-Quli Khan, the governor of Fars who had won Hormuz, was put to death with his sons. Two years later the grand vizier went too. Real power drifted to a new vizier, the eunuch Saru Taqi.

The borders sagged. In 1638 the governor of Kandahar handed the city to the Mughals, and the Ottoman sultan Murad IV took Baghdad. The Treaty of Zuhab in 1639 gave Baghdad up for good and fixed a border close to today's line between Iran and Iraq. Safi died at Kashan in May 1642, about 31, worn out by drink. His heir was a boy of nine.

claims.text: Safi had a whole generation of royal princes and great nobles killed or blinded in 1632.
claims.note: Persian court chronicles and European visitors both record the purge; the exact number of victims differs between accounts.

claims.text: Heavy drinking killed him.
claims.note: Chroniclers and visitors blame wine (some add opium). Nobody examined the body, so it rests on his reputation.

claims.text: The Treaty of Zuhab drew a border that still roughly divides Iran and Iraq.
claims.note: Later Ottoman–Persian treaties kept returning to the Zuhab line, and the modern frontier broadly follows it.

reigns.hook: Safi's son is only nine, and Saru Taqi plans to keep running Iran in his name. The vizier is about to learn how fast a boy shah can grow up.

reigns.tagline: The boy shah who won back Kandahar and built in style
reigns.cameToPower: Crowned at Kashan as a child
reigns.previously: Safi drinks himself to death at Kashan in 1642.
paragraphs: Abbas II was crowned at nine, and for three years the vizier Saru Taqi ran the country. In 1645 a group of courtiers murdered the vizier, and the young shah took the reins himself. He turned out to be clever, hard-working and keen to be seen as a fair judge. He watched his officials closely and liked to hear complaints in person.

In 1648 he marched east, and early in 1649 Kandahar fell back into Persian hands. The Mughals came to take it again, twice under their prince Aurangzeb and once under his brother Dara Shikoh, and failed every time. At home Isfahan got the Chehel Sotoun, a garden palace with a tall wooden porch mirrored in a long pool, and the Khaju bridge across the Zayandeh river.

He also loved wine, and his drinking parties were famous among European visitors. He died in 1666, still in his mid-thirties, after a long illness. His eldest son, Sam Mirza, had been kept hidden away in the harem, so hidden that some courtiers were not even sure he was alive.

claims.text: The Chehel Sotoun is called 'forty columns' though it has only twenty.
claims.note: The porch has twenty wooden columns. The usual explanation is their reflection in the pool, though 'forty' can also just mean 'many' in Persian.

claims.text: Drink killed Abbas II.
claims.note: European visitors stressed his drinking. Other accounts blame disease, and some suggest syphilis or a throat illness.

reigns.hook: The court eunuchs fetch a young man nobody outside the harem has ever seen. He takes the throne as Safi II, and almost at once things start going wrong.

reigns.tagline: The shah crowned twice, who then vanished into the harem
reigns.previously: Abbas II dies in 1666, still in his thirties.
paragraphs: He was born Sam Mirza and spent his whole youth inside the harem. In 1666 the court brought him out and crowned him Safi II. The new reign started badly. He fell ill, plague and an earthquake struck, and the Cossack raider Stenka Razin began plundering the Caspian coast. The astrologers decided the coronation had been held at an unlucky hour.

So on Nowruz, the Persian New Year, in 1668 they crowned him again, this time as Suleiman. The French jeweller Jean Chardin, who sold gems at the court, saw it all and wrote it up in loving detail. The empire was at peace, with no big wars on any border, and Isfahan was rich and glittering.

Suleiman lost interest in ruling. He spent years in the harem, drinking, and left decisions to his eunuchs, his women and a small inner council. Grand viziers came and went, the army was let run down and the treasury emptied. He died on 29 July 1694. The choice of the next shah fell to the people who had run his court: the harem eunuchs.

claims.text: Suleiman was crowned twice, under two different names.
claims.note: Persian court chroniclers and Chardin both describe the second coronation and the astrologers' advice behind it.

claims.text: On his deathbed he said: choose Hoseyn for a quiet life, his brother for glory.
claims.note: Told by later European writers, including the Jesuit Krusinski. It fits the story of the decline too neatly to trust.

claims.text: Under Suleiman the harem and its eunuchs ran Iran.
claims.note: Chardin and other visitors say so. Some historians think they overstated it and that viziers still did much of the work.

reigns.hook: The eunuchs pick Suleiman's gentle, pious son Soltan Hoseyn. Far to the east, in Kandahar, the Afghan tribes are growing restless.

images.caption: An Isfahan portrait painted in his lifetime, inscribed with his name; now in the Louvre.

reigns.tagline: The gentle shah who lost Isfahan to hunger and Afghans
reigns.previously: Suleiman dies after a reign spent mostly in the harem.
paragraphs: Soltan Hoseyn was kind, devout and easy to talk round. The powerful cleric Mohammad-Baqer Majlesi had his ear, and pressure grew on Sunnis, Sufis and non-Muslims. That mattered, because the empire's eastern frontier was full of Sunni Afghans with grievances. Meanwhile the army was underpaid and the treasury was running dry.

In 1709 Mir Wais Hotak, a chief of the Ghilzai Afghans, killed the Persian governor of Kandahar and took the city. In 1722 his son Mahmud marched across the desert with a small army and on 8 March routed a much bigger Safavid force at Gulnabad, just outside Isfahan. Then he surrounded the capital.

The siege dragged on from March to October. Food ran out, and people ate leather, bark and worse. Huge numbers starved. In October 1722 Soltan Hoseyn rode out and surrendered. He lived on as a prisoner until the Afghans killed him a few years later. But one of his sons, Tahmasp, had slipped out of the city before the end, and he claimed the throne.

claims.text: Courtiers nicknamed him 'Very Well' because he agreed to everything.
claims.note: Said to come from his stock answer to any request. It appears in later writers and suits his reputation a bit too neatly.

claims.text: Soltan Hoseyn placed the crown on Mahmud's head with his own hands.
claims.note: Told by the Polish Jesuit Krusinski, who was in Isfahan, and by later chroniclers. The details differ between accounts.

claims.text: Tens of thousands died in the siege of Isfahan.
claims.note: Eyewitnesses describe mass starvation, but estimates of the dead vary widely and none is reliable.

reigns.hook: Isfahan has starved for six months. The shah rides out and hands his crown to the Afghan chief who besieged it.

reigns.tagline: The Afghan who took Isfahan
reigns.previously: Soltan Hoseyn surrenders Isfahan to Afghan rebels.
paragraphs: Mahmud, chief of the Afghan Ghilzai tribe, marched on Isfahan in 1722 and starved it into surrender after a six-month siege. Soltan Hoseyn handed him the crown.
He controlled little beyond the capital. Growing paranoid, he had many Safavid princes killed in 1725, and was soon overthrown and killed by his cousin Ashraf.
reigns.hook: Ashraf Hotak takes over, and Tahmasp II still holds out in the north.

reigns.previously: Mahmud Hotak is overthrown.
paragraphs: Ashraf beat back an Ottoman army and won recognition from the Ottoman sultan as shah. He had the captive Soltan Hoseyn executed.
In 1729 Nader Khan, general of Tahmasp II, crushed the Afghans in three battles. Ashraf fled towards Kandahar and was killed on the way.
reigns.hook: Tahmasp II is back in Isfahan, with Nader behind him.

reigns.tagline: The shah propped up by Nader
reigns.previously: Isfahan falls, and a Safavid prince escapes.
paragraphs: Tahmasp escaped Isfahan before it fell and proclaimed himself shah in the north. He had no real power until the general Nader Khan joined him and drove out the Afghans.
He lost a war with the Ottomans in 1731 and signed away the land Nader had won. Nader deposed him in 1732 and put his baby son on the throne.
reigns.hook: Nader rules in the name of an infant.

reigns.cameToPower: Put on the throne by Nader
reigns.previously: Nader deposes Tahmasp II.
paragraphs: Abbas III was a few months old when Nader made him shah. Nader ruled as regent and kept fighting the Ottomans and Afghans.
In 1736 Nader called a great assembly on the Mughan plain and had himself proclaimed shah. The child was sent away and later killed.
reigns.hook: Nader Shah rules Iran in his own name.

reigns.tagline: The nobody who looted Delhi and was killed in his tent
reigns.previously: The baby shah Abbas III is set aside, and Nader stops pretending.
paragraphs: Nader came from the Afshar, a Turkmen tribe in Khorasan, and from nowhere special. He rose as a soldier and warband leader, and in 1726 joined the exiled Tahmasp II, who named him Tahmasp Qoli Khan, 'slave of Tahmasp'. In 1729 he beat the Afghans at Mihmandust and again near Isfahan, and gave the capital back to his master. Then he drove back the Ottomans and got the Russians to hand back the Caspian provinces.

In 1732 he deposed Tahmasp and put the shah's baby son on the throne as Abbas III. On 8 March 1736, at a great assembly on the Mughan plain, Nader had himself proclaimed shah. He even tried to bring Shi'a and Sunni Islam closer together. In 1739 he invaded Mughal India, beat its army at Karnal and entered Delhi. When a riot broke out he ordered a massacre, and tens of thousands were killed in a day.

He came home with the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor diamond. But he grew suspicious and cruel. In 1742 he had his eldest son Reza Qoli blinded, believing he had plotted to kill him. Taxes soared and revolts were crushed savagely. In June 1747, in his camp at Quchan, his own officers broke into his tent and killed him.

claims.text: About 20,000 to 30,000 people were killed in the Delhi massacre.
claims.note: That is the range most historians give. Figures from the time vary much more widely.

claims.text: Nader named the diamond himself, crying 'Koh-i-Noor!', 'Mountain of Light!', when he first saw it.
claims.note: The story comes from later writers. The name certainly dates from his time or soon after.

claims.text: He had his eldest son Reza Qoli blinded.
claims.note: Recorded by his own court historian and by Europeans in Iran. Nader is said to have regretted it bitterly.

reigns.hook: Nader's empire shatters overnight. His heirs turn on each other, and in the Zagros mountains a Zand chief named Karim starts gathering men.

reigns.previously: Nader Shah is murdered in his tent.
paragraphs: Ali Qoli, Nader's nephew, was probably behind his uncle's murder. He became shah as Adil Shah and had most of Nader's family killed, sparing only the teenage grandson Shahrokh.
His brother Ebrahim rebelled, beat him, and had him blinded and later killed.

Meanwhile Nader's grandson Shahrokh was proclaimed in Mashhad. Ebrahim's troops deserted him, and he was captured and killed.

reigns.tagline: The blind shah of Khorasan
reigns.reignEnded: Tortured to death by Agha Mohammad Khan
reigns.previously: Nader's empire breaks up.
paragraphs: Shahrokh, grandson of Nader Shah and through his mother of the Safavids, was proclaimed shah in Mashhad. He was blinded by a rival in 1750 but kept ruling Khorasan for nearly fifty years while others held the rest of Iran.
In 1796 Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar took Mashhad and tortured the old man to reveal Nader's hidden jewels. Shahrokh died of his wounds.
reigns.hook: Shahrokh keeps Khorasan, but the rest of Iran is up for grabs. In the Zagros mountains, a Zand chief named Karim is gathering men.

reigns.tagline: The chief who ruled Iran and never called himself shah
reigns.relationToPredecessor: No relation; a Zand tribal chief
reigns.cameToPower: Won the wars after Nader's death
reigns.previously: Nader's heirs blind and kill each other. Iran falls apart.
paragraphs: Nader Shah's empire did not outlive him. His heirs turned on each other, and his blind grandson Shahrokh was left holding Mashhad in the far east. The rest of Iran became a brawl of warlords. Out of the Zagros mountains came Karim, chief of the Zand, a small Lak tribe. By about 1751 he was the strongest of them, and over the next ten years he beat his rivals one by one.

Karim never took the title of shah. He ruled as Vakil, the deputy, at first in the name of a Safavid boy, Ismail III, whom he kept as a puppet. He made Shiraz his capital and gave it buildings that still stand: the Vakil Bazaar, the Vakil Mosque and the Vakil Bath. Taxes were light and the roads were safe, and Iranians still remember him as the gentlest ruler of a brutal century.

In 1776 his army took Basra from the Ottomans. At his court lived an honoured hostage, the Qajar prince Agha Mohammad, whose tribe were the Zands' great rivals. Karim died in Shiraz on 1 March 1779, in his seventies, and left no son strong enough to hold what he had built.

claims.text: He called himself Vakil al-Ra'aya, 'deputy of the people'.
claims.note: He certainly ruled as Vakil. Historians differ on when he used the fuller title and how official it was.

claims.text: Karim Khan was the most humane ruler of 18th-century Iran.
claims.note: Persian chroniclers and European visitors praised his justice and low taxes. He could still be harsh with rebels, and he looked kind partly because the times were so cruel.

claims.text: A robbed merchant told Karim he had slept soundly because he thought the Vakil was awake, and Karim paid for his loss.
claims.note: A favourite anecdote in later Persian tellings. No record from his own time backs it up.

reigns.hook: Karim Khan is dead, and the Zand princes are already fighting over Shiraz. That same day the Qajar hostage Agha Mohammad slips out of the city and rides north to raise his tribe.

reigns.tagline: Five Zand rulers in ten years
reigns.previously: Karim Khan dies, and his family fights over his throne.
paragraphs: Karim Khan Zand never called himself shah, and when he died his family fell to fighting. His sons Abol-Fath and Mohammad Ali were put up as nominal rulers, then pushed aside by his brother Sadeq.
Ali-Morad Khan killed Sadeq and ruled from Isfahan until 1785; Jafar Khan followed and was poisoned in 1789. Meanwhile the Qajar chief Agha Mohammad Khan was taking northern Iran.

reigns.tagline: The last Zand, betrayed at Kerman
reigns.cameToPower: Took Shiraz after his father's murder
reigns.previously: Jafar Khan Zand is poisoned.
paragraphs: Lotf Ali Khan, a brave young commander, took Shiraz after his father was murdered and fought Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar for five years.
Betrayed by his own minister, he lost Shiraz and held out in Kerman. When Kerman fell in 1794 the Qajar had thousands of its men blinded. Lotf Ali was captured, blinded and killed.
reigns.hook: Agha Mohammad Khan rules all Iran.
