reigns.tagline: The eunuch who forged a dynasty in blood
reigns.cameToPower: Fought the Zands for the throne
reigns.reignEnded: Murdered in his tent at Shusha
reigns.previously: Karim Khan is dead, and his hostage Agha Mohammad has escaped.
paragraphs: Agha Mohammad was the son of a chief of the Qajars, a Turkic tribe from Astarabad near the Caspian. As a boy he was castrated on the orders of Nader Shah's nephew Adel Shah, so that he could never rule. He grew up beardless and high-voiced, and nobody who crossed him forgot it. He then spent years as a hostage at Karim Khan's court in Shiraz, treated well and quietly furious.

When Karim died in 1779 he escaped and gathered the Qajars. In 1786 he made Tehran, then a modest town, his capital. The young Zand prince Lotf Ali Khan fought him for years. In 1794 Agha Mohammad took Kerman, where Lotf Ali had held out, and punished it terribly: thousands of its men were blinded or killed. Lotf Ali was captured, blinded and put to death.

In 1795 he sacked Tbilisi to drag Georgia back from Russia's orbit, and in 1796 he was at last crowned shah. He had Nader's blind grandson Shahrokh tortured to give up the last of Nader's jewels. In June 1797, camped at Shusha in the Caucasus, he condemned two servants to death but put off the execution till morning. That night they killed him in his tent.

claims.text: As a hostage he secretly slashed Karim Khan's carpets with a knife.
claims.note: Told in later Qajar-era and European accounts. It fits his reputation but cannot be checked.

claims.text: The eyes of Kerman's men were brought to him and counted, 20,000 in some accounts.
claims.note: Mass blindings at Kerman are widely reported. The exact number comes from later accounts and may be inflated.

claims.text: He was castrated as a boy on Adel Shah's orders.
claims.note: Reported by Persian chroniclers and accepted by modern historians.

reigns.hook: His killers run off with the crown jewels, but the dynasty holds. Agha Mohammad had already picked his heir: his nephew Baba Khan, governor in Shiraz, who hurries north to take the throne.

reigns.tagline: The great beard who lost the Caucasus to Russia
reigns.previously: Agha Mohammad Khan is murdered by his servants at Shusha.
paragraphs: Fath-Ali Shah looked like a king from a storybook. His court painters showed him life-size, with a long black beard, a tiny waist and jewels on everything. He had an enormous harem, and by the end of his reign his children and grandchildren were counted in the hundreds. Under him Tehran became a proper royal capital.

Outside the palace things went badly. Russia was pushing south into the Caucasus. Two wars ended in defeat. The Treaty of Gulistan in 1813 gave up much of the region, and the Treaty of Turkmenchay in 1828 handed over the khanates of Erivan and Nakhchivan and loaded Iran with a heavy indemnity. The crown prince, Abbas Mirza, tried to build a modern army, but it was not enough.

In 1829 a Tehran mob stormed the Russian mission and killed the envoy, the playwright Alexander Griboyedov. To calm the tsar the shah sent a peace offering: the Shah diamond, which is still in Moscow. Abbas Mirza died in 1833. Fath-Ali Shah died in Isfahan in October 1834.

claims.text: Fath-Ali Shah had hundreds of children and grandchildren.
claims.note: Counts vary a lot between chroniclers and visitors, and the court liked big numbers. Everyone agrees the family was huge.

claims.text: The Shah diamond was sent to Russia as an apology for Griboyedov's murder.
claims.note: The stone, engraved with the names of three rulers including Fath-Ali Shah, is in the Kremlin's Diamond Fund.

claims.text: Turkmenchay set the Aras river as much of Iran's northern border.
claims.note: The treaty text survives, and the line still forms much of the border today.

reigns.hook: His grandson Mohammad Shah takes the throne and marches on Herat. Then, in 1844, a young merchant in Shiraz announces that he is the Bab, the 'Gate' to the hidden Imam.

reigns.tagline: The shah who lost Herat
reigns.cameToPower: Named heir after his father's death
reigns.previously: Fath-Ali Shah dies, with dozens of sons wanting his throne.
paragraphs: Mohammad was the son of the crown prince Abbas Mirza, who died before his father. With Russian and British backing he beat his uncles for the throne in 1834.
He tried to take Herat in 1837, but a British threat forced him to retreat. He left government to his mystic tutor Haji Mirza Aqasi. He died of gout in 1848.
reigns.hook: His 16-year-old son Naser al-Din becomes shah.

reigns.tagline: The photographer shah who ruled for half a century
reigns.reignEnded: Shot at a shrine near Tehran
reigns.previously: Mohammad Shah dies, and the Bab's followers are spreading.
paragraphs: Naser al-Din was a teenager when he took the throne. His chief minister, Amir Kabir, was a reformer in a hurry. He cut waste, went after corruption and in 1851 opened the Dar ul-Funun, Iran's first modern college. Enemies at court turned the young shah against him. Amir Kabir was sacked, sent to Kashan and in 1852 killed in a bathhouse there, his veins cut open.

The Bab was shot by a firing squad in Tabriz in 1850. After a group of Babis tried to kill the shah in 1852, many were hunted down and put to death. Naser al-Din loved new things. He took up photography, and his pictures of his wives and courtiers still survive. He went to Europe three times, in 1873, 1878 and 1889, and kept diaries of everything he saw.

He sold concessions to foreigners for cash. In 1890 a British company won control of all Iran's tobacco. Merchants and clerics protested, and a fatwa told believers to stop smoking. The deal was cancelled in 1892. On 1 May 1896, days before his 50th anniversary on the throne by the Islamic calendar, he was shot dead at the Shah Abdol-Azim shrine by Mirza Reza Kermani.

claims.text: The first volley of the firing squad missed the Bab.
claims.note: Babi and Baha'i accounts, and some European reports, say the bullets only cut his ropes and he had to be shot again. Details differ between versions.

claims.text: Even the women of the shah's harem gave up their water pipes during the tobacco boycott.
claims.note: A famous detail of the protest. It shows how widely the ban was kept, but it is hard to check.

claims.text: Amir Kabir was killed on the shah's orders in the bathhouse at Kashan.
claims.note: Persian and European accounts agree. The bathhouse in the Fin Garden is now visited as a memorial to him.

reigns.hook: The new shah is Mozaffar ad-Din, a sickly man who has waited decades in Tabriz. He inherits debts, angry merchants and a country starting to talk about a constitution.

reigns.tagline: The ailing shah who signed a constitution
reigns.reignEnded: Died days after the Fundamental Law
reigns.previously: Naser al-Din Shah is shot dead at a shrine near Tehran.
paragraphs: Mozaffar ad-Din had spent decades as crown prince, governing in Tabriz. By the time he became shah he was in his forties and often ill. He borrowed heavily from Russia, and a good part of the money went on trips to Europe for his health. In Paris in 1900 a man pointed a pistol at him; the shah was not hurt. In 1901 he sold William Knox D'Arcy the right to look for oil across most of Iran.

Anger was building. In 1905 the governor of Tehran had merchants beaten on the soles of their feet over the price of sugar. Clerics walked out of the capital to the shrine at Qom. In the summer of 1906 thousands of merchants, guildsmen and students camped in the garden of the British legation and refused to leave. The shah gave way. On 5 August 1906 he signed a decree for an elected assembly, the Majlis.

The Majlis opened in October. On 30 December 1906, by now a very sick man, the shah signed the Fundamental Law, which put limits on royal power. He died in January 1907. Iran had a constitution and a parliament. Now it needed a shah willing to keep them.

claims.text: About 14,000 people camped in the British legation grounds.
claims.note: Reports at the time give different numbers; 14,000 is the figure most often repeated.

claims.text: Sugar merchants were beaten in public, and that set off the protests.
claims.note: The beatings in December 1905 are well reported. Accounts differ on how many merchants and on their role in what followed.

claims.text: Iran marks 5 August, 14 Mordad, as Constitution Day.
claims.note: The anniversary of his decree is an official commemoration in the Iranian calendar.

reigns.hook: His son Mohammad Ali Shah takes the throne. He has no love for the Majlis, and he has the Cossack Brigade and its Russian officers at his command.

images.caption: A photograph by the court photographer Mirza Ibrahim Khan, taken in 1901.
images.alt: Photograph of Mozaffar ad-Din Shah standing by a chair in dress uniform, with an inscribed cartouche below

reigns.tagline: The shah who turned the cannon on his own parliament
reigns.previously: Mozaffar ad-Din signs the Fundamental Law and dies days later.
paragraphs: Mohammad Ali had been crown prince in Tabriz, and he hated the constitution his dying father had signed. In August 1907 Britain and Russia carved Iran into zones of influence without asking it. In February 1908 a bomb was thrown at the shah's motorcar; he was not in it. He was sure the Majlis men were behind it, and the two sides headed for a showdown.

On 23 June 1908 his Cossack Brigade, under its Russian commander Colonel Liakhov, shelled the Majlis building. Leading constitutionalists were arrested, and two of the best-known, a fiery preacher and a radical newspaper editor, were strangled in the royal garden. Tabriz refused to give in. Under Sattar Khan, a former horse dealer, the city held out for months against a royal siege.

In July 1909 two armies closed on Tehran, Bakhtiari tribesmen from the south and revolutionaries from Gilan in the north. They took the capital. On 16 July the shah ran to the Russian legation and was deposed. He went into exile in Russia, and in 1911 landed on the Caspian coast to win his throne back. His army was beaten, and he left Iran for good.

claims.text: Colonel Liakhov's Cossacks shelled the Majlis in June 1908.
claims.note: Diplomats and journalists in Tehran reported it in detail at the time.

claims.text: The 1907 Anglo-Russian Convention split Iran into spheres of influence.
claims.note: The treaty text survives: a Russian zone in the north, a British one in the south-east and a neutral zone between.

claims.text: Russia quietly backed his 1911 attempt to return.
claims.note: He sailed from Russian soil, and Shuster and the constitutionalists accused St Petersburg. The Russian government denied it.

reigns.hook: The victors need a new shah fast. They pick Mohammad Ali's son Ahmad, a boy of 11, and crown him with a regent at his side.

reigns.tagline: The boy king who reigned while others ruled
reigns.reignEnded: Deposed by the Majlis in absence
reigns.previously: Tehran falls and Mohammad Ali Shah is deposed in July 1909.
paragraphs: Ahmad was 11 when he replaced his deposed father, so regents ran things until he came of age in 1914. In 1911 the Majlis hired an American, Morgan Shuster, to sort out the finances. He was good at it, too good for Russia. A Russian ultimatum forced him out that December, and the Majlis that had backed him was shut down.

In the First World War Iran declared itself neutral. Russian, British and Ottoman troops marched in anyway. Famine struck in 1917 to 1919, on top of war and disease. In 1919 Britain signed an agreement with the government that would have put Iran's army and finances under British advisers. Uproar followed, and the Majlis never ratified it.

On 21 February 1921 a Cossack officer, Reza Khan, marched on Tehran with the journalist Seyyed Zia and seized power. Ahmad Shah kept his crown, but Reza Khan became war minister, then prime minister in 1923. That year the young shah left for Europe. He never came back. On 31 October 1925 the Majlis voted his dynasty off the throne. He died near Paris in 1930, aged 32.

claims.text: The famine of 1917 to 1919 killed millions.
claims.note: Some historians argue for deaths in the millions and blame the occupying armies; others think far fewer died. Records are thin, and estimates vary enormously.

claims.text: The Anglo-Persian Agreement of 1919 was never ratified by the Majlis.
claims.note: It met fierce opposition in Iran and abroad, and was formally dropped after the 1921 coup.

claims.text: Ahmad Shah took British money to back the 1919 agreement.
claims.note: British documents show payments to the ministers who signed it and a monthly subsidy talked of for the shah. How far he was bought is argued over.

reigns.hook: With the Qajars gone, an assembly hands the crown to the man behind the coup. The Cossack from Mazandaran is about to become Reza Shah.

reigns.tagline: The Cossack who dragged Iran into the modern age
reigns.cameToPower: Voted the crown by an assembly
reigns.previously: The Majlis deposes the Qajars. Reza Khan is the man in charge.
paragraphs: Reza came from a village in Mazandaran, joined the Cossack Brigade young and rose through its ranks by sheer toughness. After the 1921 coup he became war minister, then prime minister in 1923. In December 1925 a constituent assembly gave him the crown, and he was crowned on 25 April 1926. He took the surname Pahlavi, after the language of pre-Islamic Iran.

He wanted a strong, modern state, fast. He built a national army with conscription, the Trans-Iranian Railway from the Caspian to the Gulf, and Tehran University. From 1935 he asked foreign governments to say Iran, not Persia. Men were ordered into Western clothes, and in January 1936 women were banned from wearing the veil in public. When protesters gathered in the Goharshad Mosque in Mashhad in 1935, troops opened fire.

Critics were jailed or worse; his once-powerful court minister Teymourtash died in prison in 1933. In the Second World War Britain and the Soviet Union saw him as too close to Germany, and they wanted his railway to supply Russia. They invaded on 25 August 1941. On 16 September he abdicated in favour of his son. He died in exile in Johannesburg in 1944.

claims.text: Troops killed many protesters in the Goharshad Mosque in 1935.
claims.note: The shooting is well established. Death tolls given range from dozens to many hundreds, and the government released little.

claims.text: By 1941 he was the biggest landowner in Iran.
claims.note: Historians widely report huge estates, many taken under pressure. The exact size of his holdings is argued over.

claims.text: The Trans-Iranian Railway is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
claims.note: It was added to the World Heritage List in 2021.

reigns.hook: Britain and the Soviet Union now have a new shah on their hands. He is 21, his country is occupied, and he will reign for 37 years.

reigns.tagline: The last shah, the oil boom and the revolution
reigns.cameToPower: Father forced out by the Allies
reigns.previously: Britain and the USSR invade and force Reza Shah to abdicate.
paragraphs: Mohammad Reza was 21 and his country was occupied. In 1943 Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin met in Tehran. In 1946 the Soviets backed a breakaway government in Iranian Azerbaijan before pulling out. In 1949 he was shot at Tehran University and survived. After 1953 he ruled more and more alone. The SAVAK secret police, founded in 1957, hunted his opponents, and the torture of prisoners is documented in many accounts.

In 1963 he launched the White Revolution, with land reform and votes for women. A cleric in Qom, Ruhollah Khomeini, denounced him; protests broke out in June 1963, and Khomeini was exiled in 1964. The shah crowned himself in 1967, and in 1971 held a lavish party at Persepolis for 2,500 years of monarchy, linking himself to Cyrus. Oil money poured in after 1973. In 1975 Rastakhiz became the only legal party.

In 1978 protest turned into revolution. In August a fire at the Cinema Rex in Abadan killed several hundred people. On 8 September, Black Friday, troops fired on crowds in Jaleh Square in Tehran. Strikes shut down the oil industry. The shah was secretly ill with cancer. On 16 January 1979 he flew out of Iran. He died in exile in Cairo in July 1980.

claims.text: The 1971 Persepolis celebrations cost a fortune.
claims.note: Critics, Khomeini among them, called it obscene waste. The government gave a much lower cost, and estimates still differ widely.

claims.text: Islamist militants started the Cinema Rex fire.
claims.note: At the time many Iranians blamed SAVAK. After the revolution a court convicted a man who admitted setting it with others, but questions about who was behind it remain.

claims.text: SAVAK tortured political prisoners.
claims.note: Documented by Amnesty International in the 1970s and by many former prisoners. The number of victims is disputed.

reigns.hook: To see how the shah became so powerful, go back to 1951. An elderly aristocrat is leading the fight to take Iran's oil back from the British, and the crowds adore him.

reigns.tagline: The prime minister who took back Iran's oil
reigns.cameToPower: Named prime minister by the Majlis
reigns.previously: Flashback to 1951. Iran wants its oil back from the British.
paragraphs: Mohammad Mosaddegh was an elderly aristocrat, related to the Qajars, with a law doctorate from Switzerland. He wept in public, received visitors from his bed in pyjamas, and the crowds loved him. He led the National Front, and its great cause was oil. The Anglo-Iranian Oil Company, majority-owned by the British government, kept most of the profits. In March 1951 the Majlis voted to nationalise it, and in late April Mosaddegh became prime minister.

Britain hit back with a blockade of Iranian oil, and the giant Abadan refinery fell silent. Mosaddegh flew to New York to argue Iran's case at the UN Security Council, and Time made him its Man of the Year for 1951. In July 1952 he resigned in a row with the shah over control of the army, and the 30 Tir uprising brought him back. He began to rule by decree, and in 1953 dissolved the Majlis after a referendum.

The CIA and British intelligence plotted his fall. A first coup attempt on 15 to 16 August 1953 failed, and the shah fled to Baghdad, then Rome. On 19 August a second attempt, with army units and street crowds, succeeded. Mosaddegh was tried and spent three years in prison, then lived under house arrest at his estate in Ahmadabad until his death in 1967.

claims.text: The CIA organised the 1953 coup together with British intelligence.
claims.note: The CIA formally acknowledged its role in documents released in 2013.

claims.text: Time named him Man of the Year for 1951.
claims.note: He was on the cover of Time's issue of 7 January 1952.

claims.text: His fall was mainly the work of foreign plotters.
claims.note: Some historians stress the CIA and MI6. Others give more weight to the Iranian clerics, officers and politicians who had turned against him.

reigns.hook: The shah flies home stronger than ever. A quarter of a century later the crowds are back on the streets, and this time they are chanting for a cleric in exile.

reigns.title: The Revolution
reigns.tagline: The shah flies out and an ayatollah flies in
reigns.previously: The shah flies out of Iran on 16 January 1979.
paragraphs: The shah left behind a last royal government under Shapour Bakhtiar, a long-time opponent of his. It lasted weeks. On 1 February 1979 Ayatollah Khomeini flew home from exile in Paris, and vast crowds came out to greet him. Asked on the plane what he felt about returning, he answered: 'Nothing.' On 11 February the army declared itself neutral and the old regime collapsed.

A referendum at the end of March asked one question: Islamic Republic, yes or no? The official result was a landslide yes, and the Islamic Republic was declared on 1 April. Mehdi Bazargan led a provisional government, but real power lay with Khomeini and the revolutionary committees. Revolutionary courts executed hundreds of former officials and officers that year, among them the former prime minister Amir-Abbas Hoveyda. Fighting broke out in Kurdistan.

On 4 November students loyal to Khomeini seized the US embassy in Tehran and took its staff hostage. Bazargan's government resigned two days later. In early December voters approved a new constitution built on velayat-e faqih, guardianship of the Islamic jurist: a senior cleric would stand above the elected government as Supreme Leader.

claims.text: Asked what he felt on returning to Iran, Khomeini said 'Nothing'.
claims.note: The exchange was filmed on the plane. What he meant by it is still argued over.

claims.text: About 98 percent voted yes to an Islamic Republic.
claims.note: That is the official figure, and no independent observers checked it. Few doubt that most voters backed the change.

claims.text: Amir-Abbas Hoveyda was executed in April 1979.
claims.note: He was shot after a brief trial before a revolutionary court, as reported around the world. Totals for that year's executions vary by source.

reigns.hook: The constitution is in force, and the man it was written around takes his place at the top. Ayatollah Khomeini is Supreme Leader, and 53 Americans are still hostages.

reigns.tagline: The exile who became Iran's first Supreme Leader
reigns.previously: Iranians approve a constitution with a cleric as Supreme Leader.
paragraphs: Ruhollah Khomeini came from the small town of Khomeyn and spent 14 years in exile, most of them in the Shi'a holy city of Najaf in Iraq. In April 1980 a US mission to rescue the embassy hostages ended in disaster in the desert. The 52 Americans were held for 444 days and freed on 20 January 1981, minutes after Ronald Reagan took office. Iraq had invaded Iran on 22 September 1980.

The revolution turned on itself. President Banisadr was impeached in June 1981. Bombings killed Ayatollah Beheshti and many others that month, and President Rajai in August. In 1981 and 1982 thousands of opponents, many from the People's Mojahedin and the left, were executed. At the front Iran retook Khorramshahr in 1982 and pushed into Iraq, sending young volunteers across minefields. Iraq used chemical weapons.

In July 1988 the USS Vincennes shot down Iran Air Flight 655, killing all 290 on board. Khomeini then accepted a UN ceasefire, calling it more deadly than drinking poison. The war's dead are usually put at several hundred thousand. That summer thousands of political prisoners were executed. In 1989 he issued a fatwa against Salman Rushdie. He died on 3 June 1989.

claims.text: Thousands of political prisoners were executed in summer 1988 after hearings lasting minutes.
claims.note: Estimates range from about 2,800 to more than 5,000; rights groups say more. Survivors and later leaked records describe the hearings.

claims.text: His chosen successor, Ayatollah Montazeri, protested the 1988 executions and was pushed aside.
claims.note: Montazeri's letters and memoirs, later published, record his protests. He lost his post as heir in 1989.

claims.text: At his funeral the crowd tipped his body out of its coffin.
claims.note: Filmed and widely broadcast. The body was recovered and buried later that day.

reigns.hook: Khomeini is dead and his old heir has been pushed aside. The Assembly of Experts meets the next day and picks a cleric still short of the top rank: President Ali Khamenei.

reigns.tagline: Thirty-six years at the top, ended by an airstrike
reigns.cameToPower: Chosen by the Assembly of Experts
reigns.previously: Khomeini dies, and Iran needs a new Supreme Leader fast.
paragraphs: Ali Khamenei grew up in Mashhad, studied under Khomeini and was jailed under the shah. In June 1981 a bomb hidden in a tape recorder went off as he spoke at a Tehran mosque, crippling his right arm. He was president from 1981 to 1989. The day after Khomeini died, the Assembly of Experts chose him as Supreme Leader, though he was not yet a senior enough cleric. The constitution was changed that July.

Six presidents served under him: Rafsanjani, Khatami, Ahmadinejad, Rouhani, Raisi and Pezeshkian. Protest came in waves and was put down each time: students in 1999, the Green Movement after the disputed 2009 election, fuel-price protests in 2019 that left hundreds dead. In 2022 Mahsa Amini died in morality police custody. In the 'Woman, Life, Freedom' protests that followed, rights groups counted 500 or more killed, and protesters were executed.

Iran agreed a nuclear deal in 2015, which the US left in 2018. In January 2020 the US killed General Qasem Soleimani; days later the Revolutionary Guards shot down a Ukrainian airliner by mistake, killing 176. In June 2025 came the Twelve-Day War with Israel and US strikes on nuclear sites. On 28 February 2026, the first day of a new war with the US and Israel, he was killed in an Israeli airstrike in Tehran.

claims.text: A bomb hidden in a tape recorder crippled his right arm in 1981.
claims.note: Reported at the time; he lost the use of the arm for the rest of his life.

claims.text: Iran's Revolutionary Guards shot down Ukraine International Airlines Flight 752 by mistake.
claims.note: After first denying it, Iran admitted three days later that its air defences fired the missiles.

claims.text: He was the longest-serving Supreme Leader, at 36 years.
claims.note: He held the post from June 1989 until his death in February 2026, confirmed by the Iranian government on 1 March. Khomeini, the only other Leader before him, served under ten years.

reigns.hook: Iran is at war with no Supreme Leader. An interim council takes on his duties while the Assembly of Experts meets in wartime to choose his successor.

reigns.tagline: Father to son, at the top of an Islamic Republic at war
reigns.cameToPower: Elected by the Assembly of Experts
reigns.previously: Ali Khamenei is killed on the first day of war with the US and Israel.
paragraphs: Mojtaba Khamenei was born in Mashhad in 1969, the second son of Ali Khamenei. He joined the Revolutionary Guards in 1987 and served in the last part of the Iran–Iraq War. He then trained as a cleric in Qom and later taught at its seminary. For many years he worked in his father's office and was widely seen as one of the most powerful figures behind the scenes.

His father was killed on 28 February 2026, the first day of a war with the United States and Israel. An Interim Leadership Council took on the Leader's duties. On 8 March the Assembly of Experts, meeting in wartime, chose Mojtaba as Iran's third Supreme Leader. It was the first time the post had passed from father to son, in a republic born from the overthrow of a hereditary monarchy.

He was reported injured in the strike that killed his father, and he has rarely, if ever, been seen in public since. Statements in his name have been read out on state television. On 8 April a two-week US–Iran ceasefire, brokered by Pakistan, was agreed, and talks followed in Islamabad. But the war that began in February still hangs over everything. Where Iran goes next is an open question.

claims.text: The Assembly of Experts elected him Supreme Leader on 8 March 2026.
claims.note: Announced by the Assembly and Iranian state media, and reported worldwide.

claims.text: He is the first Supreme Leader to succeed his own father.
claims.note: Only three men have held the post: Khomeini, Ali Khamenei and now his son.

claims.text: An Interim Leadership Council handled the Leader's duties between his father's death and his election.
claims.note: Its creation was announced by Iranian officials on 1 March 2026 and widely reported.
